item.title: [Together AI] Auto repair for Together GPU Clusters: from GPU fault to hea…
item.description: Full title: Auto repair for Together GPU Clusters: from GPU fault to healthy node
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

GPU Clusters

Published 10/27/2026

Auto repair for Together GPU Clusters: from GPU fault to healthy node

Health checks find the fault, the platform picks the lightest fix, and you decide what runs without a person in the loop, down to individual Xid codes.

  • AuthorsPavneet Ahluwalia, Dongsheng Zhang, Barbara Kazanowska
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...
  • Links in this articleTogether GPU Clusters consoleDocs: Node repairDocs: Health checks

At cluster scale, GPU faults are a reality. An Xid error, a double-bit ECC error, a GPU falling off the PCIe bus or a flapping InfiniBand link can stall a distributed training job or take an inference replica down. Spotting that something is wrong is usually the easy part. The hard part is everything between the fault and a healthy node again

Earlier this year, we announced the launch of our fully Automatic node remediation features. Our GPU clusters customers and our internal Inference platform has been using this capability to help drive workload resiliency and minimize down time. Our customers love this capability, and we wanted to take some time break the system down and explain how it works and why we designed it this way.

We first implemented “Passive health” checks system, that watches every node continuously, both inside your VM and on the host underneath it. When a check finds a fault, auto repair recommends the lightest action to fix and shows you supporting evidence behind the recommendation. You decide up front, fault by fault, whether a repair waits for approval or runs on its own. You also decide how long auto repair waits for running workload to finish. Your own detectors can open repairs through the same pipeline by writing a single annotation on a node.

‍Availability Generally available today: passive health checks, repair recommendations, the auto-remediation policy (including per-fault and per-node consent), wait-for-idle controls, the escalation ladder, the safety rails, and API and console repair. Preview: node-label based remediation contracts, which let you bring your own detection systems such as NVSentinel or custom controllers. We are constantly adding new detection signals and remediation actions to ensure maximum coverage and minimum time to recovery.

Why NotReady is not enough

Most node auto-repair keys on a single signal: the node went NotReady. That signal looks the same whether a node is broken or just briefly unreachable. When a storage or network event touches many nodes at once, every impacted node drops to NotReady. Our system has a circuit breaker built in to prevent mass replacement of nodes. NotReady also does not say why the node failed, so there's no basis for choosing between a reboot and a new machine.

So auto repair follows one rule: no node repair occurs without a failed health check behind it, and every repair carries its supporting evidence.

The pipeline

Auto repair pipeline: signals from inside the VM and from the host feed Detect, Decide, and Repair inside your cluster; migrated hosts go to Re-validate on Together infrastructure.

The pipeline has four stages: detect a fault, decide whether and when to act, repair the node, and re-validate the machine. The first three stages run against your cluster. The fourth runs on our side, on the physical host your node just vacated. Node-label requests from your own detection tooling enter at the decide stage and get exactly the same treatment as ours.

1. Detection from both sides of the hypervisor

GPUs in Together GPU Clusters are passed straight through to your VM for bare-metal performance. That means GPU faults are visible from inside the VM, while host and fabric faults are visible from the host. Detection therefore runs on both sides of the hypervisor and lands in one place.

Inside your VM, exporters watch:

  • the kernel log, for Xid errors and GPUs falling off the PCIe bus
  • DCGM, for ECC double-bit errors, row-remap failures, PCIe replay rate, and thermal throttling
  • Node Problem Detector, for read-only filesystems, XFS shutdowns, kernel deadlocks, and repeated kubelet or containerd restarts

On Slurm, an exporter reports nodes marked DOWN or DRAIN.

On the host, we watch InfiniBand rail state and link flapping, attributed to the VM that owns those rails. We also watch host reachability, so a dead host shows up as a problem on your node rather than as silence.

Every alert ships a stable summary, a plain-language description, and a machine-readable evidence payload. For an Xid, that's each code and its NVIDIA mnemonic. For thermal throttling, it's the peak temperature and throttle count. The control plane passes those strings through untouched, so the console, the API (as linked_alerts), and your notifications always say the same thing.

We keep observed separate from actionable. Every repair-relevant alert is recorded and marks your node Degraded. Only signals with an action mapping create a repair. Disk pressure, for example, shows up but doesn't trigger a reboot, because a reboot won't fix it. An alert with no mapping is counted and logged, never silently dropped, and routed to our support team for investigation.

2. Policy: we decide what, you decide whether and when

What is owned by the platform. Each signal maps to the lightest action that fixes it, so you never need to know which Xid means what:

Whether is yours to decide. In the Repairs tab, the Auto-remediation policy defaults to Approve before repair: every recommendation waits for a person, who can accept or override the action. You can switch the default to Fully automatic, but it isn't a blanket switch. The Repair actions checklist groups faults by the repair they trigger, and you select the ones you trust to run unattended. Inside the Xid group, you can set consent per code. A common setup auto-approves reboots for Xid 119 and 95 and keeps migrations gated. The Xid checklist also works under Approve before repair, if you want a short list of faults to run automatically while everything else waits for your review.

When is yours as well. A repair drains the node, so Wait for idle holds it until the node is actually idle. On Kubernetes, that means no running pod on the node is requesting a GPU. On Slurm, it means the scheduler reports no allocation on the node. Maximum wait bounds the hold, with a default of 2 hours and a cap of 24. Do not interrupt running jobs removes the bound entirely. Set the wait to at least your checkpoint interval. If the bound expires, the repair proceeds and the timeout is recorded.

Every repair records who requested it (Together Health Checker for automatic repairs), who approved it (a named user or Auto-Approved), which rule decided, and when.

3. Bring your own detector

Teams running large GPU fleets already have detection they trust: DCGM dashboards, NVSentinel, in-house scanners, job-level checks. Every repair, whatever its source, becomes the same record in our control plane. That gives capacity checks, audit, and safety rails exactly one home.

There are three ways in:

  • API. Create a repair against an instance with a mode, an optional client-supplied ID for idempotency, and optionally the health check run or alert you're citing as evidence. You can also list, get, approve, reject, and cancel repairs.
  • Console. The ⋮ menu on any node opens the Repair dialog with the detected issues and the recommended action.
  • Node labels (Preview). Any detector with RBAC permission to write node metadata can open a repair by adding one annotation and one label to the node. The annotation carries the detector name, a stable request ID, the repair mode, when the fault was detected, and a human-readable reason.

Our cluster operator mirrors the node label up to the control plane. The repair is recorded with the detector as an external requester, so it's always attributable and can never impersonate a user. Detector name plus request ID is the idempotency key across the cluster, finished repairs included, so a detector that re-asserts the same fault on every scan can't reboot a node twice. Authorization is your cluster's own RBAC, with no API key and no onboarding ticket.

Annotation requests can ask for Reboot, Quick reprovision, or Migrate. Remove stays human-only. Like a console click, these requests skip the approval queue, but they still pass the same evidence gate, capacity check, and budgets as everything else. A per-cluster cap means a buggy detector causes limited damage rather than a catastrophe.

4. Repair actions and the escalation ladder

Every repair follows the same lifecycle: cordon, wait (per your policy), drain, act, rejoin. The console shows the node moving through Cordoning → Draining → Repairing / Migrating → Joining → Running.

The actions, from lightest to heaviest:

  • Reboot. Restarts the VM in place. Local /scratch and /tmp data survive.
  • Quick reprovision. Rebuilds the VM from a clean image on a healthy host. Local data is lost.
  • Migrate to new host. Rebuilds the VM on different hardware and sends the old host to re-validation.
  • Remove. Pulls the node for RMA. Always human-initiated.

The same fix doesn't loop. If a fault comes back on the same machine after the same action has already run twice, the next recommendation moves one rung up. A third round of Xid reboots becomes a reprovision, and a third reprovision becomes a migration. The ladder is tracked per machine, cluster, alert, and Xid code. Attempts older than a week don't count, and neither do cancelled or self-resolved recommendations.

Two tries per rung, then one rung up. Migration needs critical-alert evidence.

Migrations are evidence-gated. Migrate is the one action that consumes real capacity. It requires either a critical alert currently firing on the node or a critical alert on the same machine within the last ten days. A request that meets neither condition runs as a Quick reprovision instead.

Host power cycle (Preview). Some faults, Xid 79 among them, need the GPU to lose power, which a VM reboot can't do even though the hardware may be fine. Rather than consuming a new host, we can power-cycle the one you're on. No BMC credentials exist anywhere in the system. A boot-ID check prevents a retry from cycling a host that has already come back.

Clusters that need a guaranteed replacement window can reserve hot spare capacity, so migrations draw from that reserve rather than general availability. Ask your account team for details.

5. Rails that assume the alert storm will happen

A bad driver push, a storage outage, or a network partition can make dozens of nodes look sick at once. Node-level repair can't fix a cluster-level cause, so the rails are layered and independent:

  • Persistence. A signal must hold for a per-signal duration before it becomes a recommendation.
  • Cooldown. After any repair, a node gets roughly 30 minutes before a new recommendation can be generated.
  • Concurrency budget. The budget is sized from cluster node count, and the operator runs one repair per node pool at a time.
  • Circuit breaker. When one cluster generates a burst of correlated automatic repairs, the breaker trips. Many nodes failing at once points to a cluster-level cause, and repairing nodes one by one will not fix it.
  • One target per repair. The schema enforces it, so a bug can't fan out across nodes.
  • Auto-resolve. A recommendation whose alert clears before anyone acts disappears on its own.

The control plane is replicated, and every write is idempotent and checked against the state it expects. Two replicas racing on the same node produce one repair, not two.

6. The machine re-validates itself

When a node migrates off a machine, or is removed from one, that machine shouldn't go straight back into the pool, and it shouldn't sit in a queue waiting for someone to read diagnostics either. As soon as the old VM is gone, the machine moves into validation automatically. A test VM runs the same GPU, NCCL, InfiniBand, and storage checks that every brand-new machine passes before joining the fleet. No person touches the machine between your node leaving and the verdict landing.

Only an explicit failure files a hardware ticket.

There are three verdicts:

  • Passed. The machine returns to the pool. No ticket is filed and no one is paged, so a transient fault stays transient.
  • Failed. A hardware ticket is filed automatically with per-test results and logs attached. The machine stays out until it's fixed and passes again.
  • Aborted. The checks couldn't run, for example because the host was reallocated or the test VM couldn't be placed. The machine is restored to its prior state, and nothing is condemned.

Only an explicit failure produces a ticket.

Built to extend past one accelerator

Repair decisions key on alerts, nodes, and machines, not on the GPU vendor. The GPU type matters for placement and capacity, but recommendations, policy, escalation, budgets, triggers, and re-validation don't special-case it. The vendor-specific parts are detection (the Xid and DCGM exporters) and the diagnostic battery. Bringing up a new accelerator means adding those pieces, and everything downstream carries over.

Using it

Open your cluster in the console and go to the Repairs tab. Pending recommendations and history are there, with the Auto-remediation policy at the top. Each remediation in the API carries its linked_alerts, so your own tooling sees the same evidence the console does.

What's next

  • NVSwitch coverage. SXid faults, coalesced per node, with readable descriptions.
  • Status back on the node. Repair progress written back as node metadata, so external detectors can close the loop where they opened it.
  • One health surface. Click from a failed check to the repair it caused and back, plus a per-node view of health, events, and repair history.

Tell us what fails on your clusters that we don't catch yet. That list drives what we build next.

-> Get started in the console -> Docs: Node repair · Health checks

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Expanding Claude for Nonprofits
item.content:encoded:
Today, we're releasing the Claude for Nonprofits plugin, a set of skills and connectors built with ~30 nonprofits. It helps teams set up Claude responsibly with their organization's context and policies, supports fundraising from research through reporting, and takes on the operational work that stretches small teams. We're also planning to extend Claude Corps (opens in new tab), our program for placing early-career fellows in U.S. nonprofits, through a partnership with Taproot (opens in new tab).

As a public benefit corporation, Anthropic has a responsibility to make sure our products are accessible and useful to organizations working on the world’s hardest problems. Last December, we launched Claude for Nonprofits (opens in new tab) with discounts of up to 75%, connectors for Blackbaud, Candid, and Benevity, and a free AI Fluency course built with GivingTuesday. More than 25,000 nonprofits now use Claude in their work. Most of those organizations are small, local operations: more than 75% of them have fewer than 10 Claude seats. We think today's update will have the biggest impact on these organizations.

Katherine Rodrigues, who leads AI Transformation at the International Rescue Committee (IRC), explains how Claude helped spot a spike in pneumonia cases and mobilize their response.

We’ve spent the last year working directly with nonprofits to meet their needs. We expanded nonprofit plans to the same models as our standard Team and Enterprise plans, lowered the Team plan minimum to orgs with as few as two people, and included Claude Code in nonprofit plans at no additional cost. And during the United Nations General Assembly in September, we launched a new discount of ~90% for verified nonprofits in low- and middle-income countries, bringing standard Team seats to $3/user/month.

Cost is only one barrier. Nonprofits told us two others stood in the way: a lack of people with the skills to put AI to work, and a lack of tools built specifically for how nonprofits operate.

  • Too few people with AI skills. Claude Corps is placing 1,000 early-career fellows in at least 400 US nonprofits to build with Claude alongside their teams. Hosts include a wide variety of organizations, from large organizations to small, local teams, including food banks, art museums, and veteran support organizations. We’re now planning to extend this program through a partnership with Taproot, which would match nonprofits with experienced pro bono consultants for shorter, project-based work. A growing group of partners can support nonprofit adoption, including Accenture, Boston Consulting Group (BCG), The Bridgespan Group, Civis Analytics, Deloitte, fusionSpan, Idealist Consulting, Myridius, SapienAI, Slalom, v4c.ai, and Vera Solutions. And for teams getting started on their own, we’re hosting two live webinars: Claude for Nonprofits: An Admin's Guide to Data Handling and AI Use Policy (opens in new tab), for admins, on November 10, and Claude for Nonprofits: A Staff Guide to Making Claude Useful on Day One (opens in new tab) on November 12.
  • Too few tools built to meet nonprofits where they’re at. We built the skills we're releasing today with the nonprofits in our Design Partner Circle. It includes ~30 organizations, from small teams serving one region of the United States to international organizations operating in dozens of countries, working on education, economic mobility, health, humanitarian response, and more. Many are funders themselves. This fall, fundraisers, operations leads, and chiefs of staff at many of these organizations tried early versions of our skills on real work and told us what wasn't working. We brainstormed, iterated, and updated our solution based on what we heard.

What's in the plugin

We’re starting with three areas nonprofits told us were most urgent, especially as year-end fundraising picks up.

Extend your team

Many nonprofits told us the same thing: there are more jobs to do than people to do them, so everyone covers several roles at once. Claude extends your team, so a small staff can work like a bigger one and spend more of its time on the mission.

  • Marketing: plan a campaign sized to your team’s bandwidth, teach Claude to draft in your organization’s voice, and get a second read on your content before it goes out.
  • Hiring and people: build a job post with an interview guide and scoring rubric, plan a new hire's first 90 days, and answer staff questions from your own handbook.
  • Board and leadership: see what skills your board is missing, draft outreach to the candidates you have in mind, get new members up to speed with an orientation packet, and plan the deck for your next meeting.

Set up Claude responsibly: security, governance, and context

Claude works best when it has your organization’s context, including your mission, programs, workstreams, communication principles, and policies, and when your staff have clear rules for working with it. Start by asking Claude to:

  • Map your organization. Claude asks where you keep each kind of record, like donor data, grant files, finances and policies, and, with memory on, saves that map for each person. It then offers to connect the tools it can't reach yet. Every other skill in the plugin reads the map first, so Claude knows where to look and you don't have to point it to the same source for each task.
  • Check what your AI policy allows. Staff can ask "Can I use Claude for this?" and get the answer based on your organization's own AI policy. (No policy yet? See the Claude Academy tutorial below.)

Fund your mission

Fundraising is the lifeline for nonprofits, and it matters even more toward the end of the year. It's also time-intensive and process-heavy, which can be challenging for small organizations. The plugin supports the full fundraising lifecycle, freeing up your team's time for the irreplaceable human work, like managing relationships and deciding which opportunities to pursue.

  • Find the right funders and grants. Research donors, foundations, companies, and surface open grants, with sources cited.
  • Decide what to pursue. Forward an RFP and get a breakdown on eligibility, requirements, and what it would take to compete.
  • Write proposals and reports. Turn an RFP into a requirements list and a first draft built from your own material. Grant reports include sources for their figures.
  • Keep relationships warm. Get a brief before a funder call, a write-up and thank-you note after, and donor updates in your voice. Ask how to re-engage donors and receive a stewardship plan.

Where nonprofits are seeing impact

“For Start Early, AI is a tool that supports the people who carry out our mission. Claude first helped our staff save time on tasks like formatting. The nonprofit skills take that further, offering a vision of how AI can support whole workflows instead of single tasks. That gives our teams a strong starting point and opportunity for more time to focus on advancing outcomes for children and families.”

Stella Owings, Senior Project Manager, Start Early

“Good investor engagement starts with understanding what a funder is working toward. The nonprofit skills in Claude have been a helpful administrative tool, helping us find funding opportunities, connect a funder’s goals to our programmatic work and pull relationship history from our CRM. This allows our team to spend more time on strengthening the relationships that advance StriveTogether’s mission of helping every child succeed from cradle to career.”

Amanda Jenkins, Senior Manager, Development, StriveTogether

“We built Rumi with Claude so every teacher can have a coach in their pocket. Turning a national curriculum into a year of daily lessons used to take expert teams years. Our agents now do this in a week, then coach teachers daily in their own language. 95% of teachers rate the lesson plans as useful. We support 16,000 teachers and 418,000 learners across 6 countries, and Rumi is open source so others can use it too.”

Haroon Yasin, CEO, Taleemabad

“We think of Claude as a research fellow who never gets tired. With its help, our one-person government affairs team has turned our analysis of more than 750 state anti-trafficking policies into recommendations local advocates can take to their legislators to close gaps that leave people vulnerable.”

John Nehme, President & CEO, Allies Against Slavery

“At Best Friends, we're always looking for ways to remove barriers so our teams can focus on saving lives. Being part of Anthropic's design partner circle gave us the opportunity to help shape tools around real nonprofit challenges, and I was impressed by how quickly Anthropic incorporated feedback and translated it into practical improvements that can help organizations increase their impact.”

Marc Peralta, Chief Program Officer, Best Friends Animal Society

“We want to use AI effectively at Braven, and Claude is a key lever in how we’re getting there. Everyone has access, we ran our own training, and our IT team built Claude skills the whole organization now shares. We believe the best way to harness AI for good is to use it ourselves and constantly test and learn what works and what doesn't.”

Alina Yang, Head of Transformation, Braven

“With a team smaller than a soccer squad, turning thousands of citizen suggestions into credible government policy is no easy feat. Claude Code helped us rapidly prototype and iterate on a tool that turns feedback from WhatsApp, voice notes and forms into traceable, clustered reports—so governments can see not just aggregated suggestions, but the voices that ultimately shape public policy.”

Antaraa Vasudev, CEO & Founder, Civis

“Claude turned our staff retention report into a polished board deck, and the process of refining it felt collaborative and engaging. When the board came back with follow-up questions, we had clear answers ready in about 15 minutes, work that would otherwise have taken far longer.”

Lucy Martinez, Chief Operating Officer, Code the Dream

“At Colnodo, we use Claude to build a platform containing global information on Community-Centered Connectivity Initiatives, to improve the monitoring of our projects, and to take on much more than we were previously able to, all while helping to bring internet access to rural communities in Colombia.”

Julián Casasbuenas G., Director, Colnodo

“Claude Code has helped me pull trustworthy information on crises and our response into up-to-date documents. These are being incorporated in our operational decision-making and have contributed to significant fundraising successes.”

Mila Dorji, Public Health Data Scientist, Direct Relief

“The donor correspondence sounded like us. Rather than repeating the same proposal a third time, Claude suggested a more accessible starting point for the partnership. We also value the option to tailor a skill to how our organization works, which addresses the concern that AI doesn't know us.”

Krystal Brooks, Senior Director, Career Success and Business Development, Forte

“We connected 25 years of grantmaking into one knowledge graph that anyone across the foundation can explore using conversational AI.”

Mike Phipps, Lead AI Engineer, Gates Foundation

“Our teams write their own proposals, so through the design partner circle we asked for a thorough reviewer and better support for go/no-go decisions. We have been very impressed with the result. It strengthens our proposals while keeping the decisions with our people.”

Miles Zinn, Director, Grants Portfolio, International Justice Mission

“Claude helps us find savings we’d never have spotted on our own. We used it to show one of our partner agencies what it was paying at retail compared with buying through us, and that agency now spends 40% less to feed the same neighbors. Claude is making us a much better steward of every dollar.”

Scott Burns, President & CEO, Montgomery County Food Bank

Helen Davies, COO, Operation Fistula

1/16

Safety and security for your mission

Nonprofits hold sensitive information about the people they serve. Admins manage who has access and which connectors your organization can use, and we don’t train our models on your data by default. IT teams can find our security and compliance documentation in the Anthropic Trust Center (opens in new tab), and our new Claude Academy tutorial, Claude for Nonprofits: Data handling and your AI use policy (opens in new tab), walks admins through how Claude handles their data and how to draft and roll out a simple AI use policy.

Help us shape what’s next

This plugin is the first of several releases that we will continue to build with nonprofit organizations. Thank you to every organization that has given its time to date. Tell us what would help your team most here (opens in new tab) and let us know if you want to work closer with us to shape our upcoming releases.

The Claude for Nonprofits plugin is installed automatically for nonprofits on Team and Enterprise plans, at no additional cost. item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Anthropic files S-1 with the SEC for proposed initial public…
item.description: Full title: Anthropic files S-1 with the SEC for proposed initial public offering
item.content:encoded:
Today, Anthropic, PBC filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission relating to its proposed initial public offering of its Class A common stock.

Anthropic intends to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” The number of shares of Class A common stock to be offered and the price range for the proposed offering have not yet been determined.

The proposed offering will be made only by means of a prospectus. Copies of the preliminary prospectus, when available, may be obtained from: Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 200 West Street, New York, NY 10282, by telephone at (866) 471-2526, or by email at prospectus-ny@ny.email.gs.com; or Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 180 Varick Street, 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10014.

A registration statement relating to these securities has been filed with the SEC but has not yet become effective. These securities may not be sold, nor may offers to buy be accepted, prior to the time the registration statement becomes effective. Today’s announcement does not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy these securities, nor shall there be any sale of these securities in any state or jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation, or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or jurisdiction.

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMa…
item.description: Full title: Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMaker SDK v3
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMaker SDK v3

Fleet-wide computer vision model lifecycle management is a problem that shows up the moment a quality inspection proof of concept succeeds. One camera and one model work fine. Then the plant asks for the same result on 40 lines, each with several cameras, and every camera sees the world differently. Each has a different angle, different glare off the same stainless surface, and different ambient light depending on which bay door is open. In production deployments we have worked on, a single model trained on pooled footage underperforms enough individual cameras that each camera ends up with its own fine-tuned model. Now the real problem is no longer training one model well. It’s training, evaluating, versioning, and shipping thousands of them without a human in the loop for each one.

This post updates the pattern introduced in the 2023 series Build an end-to-end MLOps pipeline for visual quality inspection at the edge for the current Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3. It replaces the since-deprecated Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager with Amazon SageMaker Neo for edge optimization. I walk through a dual-branch Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that trains an anomaly detector and a defect classifier per camera, with quality gates that block underperforming models. An in-pipeline SageMaker Neo compilation step ensures every registered model ships with a device-optimized artifact, and an AWS Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training. You deploy everything with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), and a full pipeline run on synthetic data costs about $0.07 in compute.

The complete sample is available in the aws-samples GitHub repository.

Solution overview

The following diagram shows the sample’s fleet-wide model lifecycle. An orchestration layer queues re-training requests and limits concurrent work. A per-camera training pipeline prepares data, trains and evaluates an anomaly detector and a classifier, and produces versioned model artifacts for edge devices.

Figure 1: Solution architecture

The training half is a single SageMaker Pipeline, parameterized by camera, that runs 13 steps per execution. Three entry steps run in parallel: Preprocess, Fetch Latest Anomaly, and Fetch Latest Classifier. The pipeline preprocesses that camera’s images and fetches the camera’s most recent approved model for each branch, then trains two models. The first is a small convolutional autoencoder that learns what normal product looks like and flags anomalies by reconstruction error. The second is a ResNet18 classifier fine-tuned to confirm the defect. Each branch exports its model to ONNX, evaluates the exported artifact against held-out data, and passes through a quality gate. Past the gate, the model is compiled with SageMaker Neo for the configured edge target, and only then registered in the SageMaker Model Registry. As a result, every approved package has a device-ready compiled artifact. Packages carry the camera ID as metadata, and each branch’s warm-start fetch filters on it, so re-training always resumes from that camera’s own history.

The orchestration half paces the fleet. Re-training requests land on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue, and an AWS Lambda function starts a Step Functions execution per request. Each execution acquires a slot through a DynamoDB semaphore before starting its pipeline, so a burst of requests drains at a steady rate instead of all launching at once. Completions publish to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), and operational failures reach the same topic through an Amazon EventBridge rule with the original error preserved.

The output of the system is versioned, quality-gated, per-camera model artifacts. The Model Registry holds the portable ONNX, and S3 holds the Neo-compiled build of that model, which is a device-optimized shared library loaded by the DLR runtime rather than ONNX. Both are ready for whatever delivery mechanism your plant uses.

Prerequisites

To deploy the sample you need the following:

  • An AWS account with permissions to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles.
  • An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket.
  • An Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository.
  • The SageMaker AI, AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon DynamoDB resources in the stacks.
  • Python 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12, Docker.
  • The AWS CDK CLI version 2.1131.0 or later.

Previous CLI versions fail with a cloud assembly schema mismatch against recent versions of aws-cdk-lib. No service quota increase is needed. The orchestration layer admits at most five pipeline executions at a time by default, which keeps concurrent SageMaker training jobs inside the standard account quota.

If you deploy to an AWS Region other than your CLI default, set all three of AWS_REGION, AWS_DEFAULT_REGION, and CDK_DEFAULT_REGION on the deploy command itself rather than in your shell profile, for example, AWS_REGION=us-east-2 AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-2 CDK_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-2 cdk deploy --all. The CDK CLI, Boto3, and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) resolve the Region from overlapping but not identical variable sets, and a mismatch produces confusing partial deployments. Prefixing the command sets all three for that invocation only, so your own default Region is left unchanged.

Defining the training pipeline with SDK v3

The code in this section is excerpted from the CDK application in the repository rather than a standalone script, and it runs during cdk deploy, when the stack synthesizes the pipeline definition. Environment setup and the deploy commands come later, under Deploying and running the sample. SDK v3 reorganized the SageMaker Python SDK into modular packages, and the imports show the new shape of the library:

from sagemaker.train import ModelTrainer
from sagemaker.train.configs import InputData, Compute, OutputDataConfig
from sagemaker.core.training.configs import MetricDefinition
from sagemaker.serve.model_builder import ModelBuilder
from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.pipeline import Pipeline
from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.steps import ProcessingStep, TrainingStep
from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.model_step import ModelStep
from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.condition_step import ConditionStep
from sagemaker.core.workflow.conditions import ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo
from sagemaker.core.workflow.functions import JsonGet

Installing sagemaker>=3.0.0,<4 pulls in sagemaker-core, sagemaker-train, sagemaker-serve, and sagemaker-mlops as separate packages. Training configuration that v2 spread across Estimator constructor arguments now lives in typed config objects passed to ModelTrainer. This is the anomaly branch’s trainer, verbatim from the sample:

anomalib_trainer = ModelTrainer(
    training_image=custom_training_image_uri,
    compute=Compute(
        instance_type=training_instance_type.to_string(),
        instance_count=1,
    ),
    base_job_name="cv-pipeline-anomalib-train",
    sagemaker_session=pipeline_session,
    role=role_arn,
    hyperparameters={
        "program": "train_anomalib.py",
        "model_name": "autoencoder",
        "image_size": "256",
        "num_epochs": "3",
        "batch_size": "16",
        "learning_rate": "0.001",
    },
    input_data_config=anomalib_input_data,
    output_data_config=OutputDataConfig(
        s3_output_path=run_prefix("anomalib-training")
    ),
).with_metric_definitions(
    [
        MetricDefinition(
            name="image_auroc",
            regex=r"validation:image_auroc=([0-9]*\.?[0-9]+)",
        ),
    ]
)

anomalib_input_data wires four channels (train, validation, test, pretrained_model) from upstream step properties, and run_prefix scopes every S3 path to the pipeline execution ID so concurrent fleet runs never collide. Both are in the repository.

Two v3 behaviors matter when the pipeline lives inside a CDK application, and neither appears in the changelog as a breaking change. First, SDK v3 validates the pipeline’s execution role against live IAM while building the pipeline definition. This validation happens at synthesis time rather than execution time. A CDK app can’t create the role and the pipeline in one deployment, because the role doesn’t exist yet when the SDK validates it. This is separate from cdk bootstrap, which provisions the CDK toolkit resources once per account and Region and might already be done in your account. The sample’s own two-phase deploy is driven by a context flag that happens to share that name. An initial pass with -c bootstrap=true creates the role, bucket, and ECR repository, and the second pass synthesizes the pipeline against the now-existing role. The role Amazon Resource Name (ARN) embedded in the pipeline definition must also be a concrete string, not an unresolved CDK token.

Second, the v3 role validator simulates ECR pull permissions without a resource ARN, so an execution role scoped to a single ECR repository fails validation even though it would work at runtime. The sample’s role carries a broader ECR grant for this reason.

Lastly, one v3 habit the sample uses: constructing the pipeline with PipelineSession(default_bucket=your_bucket) routes SDK-managed uploads, such as step code, into the pipeline’s own bucket, so every artifact lives in one place and the execution role’s permissions cover a single bucket. (Granting the role access to the SDK’s default bucket works too. This approach is tidier.)

Quality gates that match how defect data behaves

Every trained model is evaluated before registration, and the evaluation runs against the exported ONNX artifact rather than the in-memory PyTorch model. That distinction matters: the artifact you gate is the artifact you ship, so an export problem can never slip a broken model past a healthy-looking training run.

The anomaly branch gates on AUROC of at least 0.8. The classifier branch gates on two metrics at once, and the choice of metrics is shaped by the defining property of defect data: heavy class imbalance. In this sample roughly 90 percent of images are good, which is realistic for a production line. Against that distribution, plain accuracy is meaningless, because a model that predicts “good” for every image scores about 0.9 while catching zero defects. Balanced accuracy, the mean of per-class recall, corrects for that, but it has its own blind spot. A model with perfect recall on good parts and only 20 percent recall on defects still scores (1.0 + 0.2) / 2 = 0.6. So the gate requires balanced accuracy of at least 0.6 and defect recall of at least 0.5, together:

step_check_classifier = ConditionStep(
    name="CheckClassifierQuality",
    conditions=[
        ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo(
            left=JsonGet(
                step_name=step_eval_classifier.name,
                property_file="evaluation",
                json_path="balanced_accuracy",
            ),
            right=min_accuracy,
        ),
        ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo(
            left=JsonGet(
                step_name=step_eval_classifier.name,
                property_file="evaluation",
                json_path="defect_recall",
            ),
            right=min_defect_recall,
        ),
    ],
    if_steps=[step_compile_classifier, step_register_classifier],
    else_steps=[step_fail_classifier],
    depends_on=[step_eval_classifier],
)

A ConditionStep ANDs its conditions, so both must pass. The thresholds are pipeline parameters, adjustable per execution without redeploying. If a gate fails, a FailStep marks the execution failed and that branch’s model never reaches the registry (the two branches gate independently, so the other branch’s model may still register). The fleet keeps serving the previous approved model for that camera.

The training code addresses the same imbalance from the other side. The classifier is a fine-tuned resnet18 with ImageNet weights and a two-class head. At per-camera dataset sizes, fine-tuning pretrained weights is what keeps the model from collapsing onto the majority class. The training code balances training batches with a WeightedRandomSampler using inverse class frequencies, while the loss stays unweighted. Combining a weighted loss with weighted sampling over-corrects toward the minority class.

Compiling for the edge with SageMaker Neo, inside the pipeline

Notice the gate’s if_steps in the preceding code: past the gate, compilation runs first and registration depends on it. Both training scripts export ONNX with dynamic batch axes. The quality gates score those exported artifacts under ONNX Runtime, and then a CompileAnomalibNeo or CompileClassifierNeo step hands the gated artifact to SageMaker Neo. The invariant is gate, then compile, then register. A model only becomes an Approved package if it also compiled for the fleet’s edge target, so the registry never advertises a model the devices cannot run.

The compile step encapsulates three error-prone details. Neo requires the input tarball to contain only the model file, but training jobs emit model.tar.gz with the checkpoint and metrics alongside the ONNX model. The step repackages an ONNX-only tarball first. Neo also requires concrete input shapes while the exports declare a dynamic batch axis, so batch size 1 is pinned in the compilation request. And because pipeline steps can retry, the compilation job name derives deterministically from the execution ID, so a retry resumes polling the job it already started instead of orphaning it.

The target is a pipeline parameter: NeoTargetDevice selects a named device such as jetson_xavier or rasp4b, and its default compiles for the NeoTargetOs/NeoTargetArch platform, LINUX/X86_64 by default. The compiled package contains the optimized compiled.so plus the DLR runtime for loading it. The default output runs on any x86_64 Linux host, so you can validate it before committing to device-specific targets. Compilation itself incurs no charge. You pay for the processing instance that drives it and the S3 storage of the outputs. For compiling an already-registered model for additional device types later, without re-training, the repository includes an ad-hoc script that runs the same flow against the Model Registry.

Per-camera models in the Model Registry

Each branch registers into its own model package group, and every package carries the camera ID and its evaluation metrics. From the sample, with the metrics wiring elided:

classifier_model_builder = ModelBuilder(
    s3_model_data_url=classifier_model_data,
    image_uri=custom_training_image_uri,
    sagemaker_session=pipeline_session,
    role_arn=role_arn,
)
step_register_classifier = ModelStep(
    name="RegisterClassifierModel",
    depends_on=[step_compile_classifier],
    step_args=classifier_model_builder.register(
        model_package_group_name="sm1k-classifier-model-group",
        approval_status="Approved",
        model_metrics=classifier_metrics,
        customer_metadata_properties={"CameraId": camera_id},
    ),
)

Camera identity in customer_metadata_properties is what turns two shared package groups into a fleet catalog. Packages from all cameras live in the same groups, and per-camera history is recovered by filtering on the metadata. Each branch has a fetch step that pages through approved packages newest-first until it finds the requesting camera’s latest model, because ListModelPackages cannot filter on customer metadata server-side. On a camera’s first run the fetch finds nothing and training falls back to its cold-start initialization (ImageNet weights for the classifier, random initialization for the autoencoder). Every later run resumes from that camera’s own prior model, which is what makes frequent, cheap, incremental re-training viable across a fleet.

Note what these registry entries are and are not: they catalog versioned, quality-gated artifacts, but their container reference is the training image, which serves no inference endpoints. They exist for a fleet workflow where a downstream system pulls artifacts and ships them to devices, not for CreateEndpoint.

Orchestrating fleet training requests

Every AWS account has service quotas on concurrent SageMaker training jobs, and each pipeline execution here launches several jobs, so fleet re-training needs pacing. Something has to keep a burst of 500 requests from becoming 500 simultaneous pipeline launches. The sample uses a semaphore, a counter of available slots that works like a parking lot with five spaces. Before the Step Functions state machine starts a pipeline, it takes a slot by atomically incrementing a counter in DynamoDB, with a condition that refuses the increment once the cap is reached:

acquire_semaphore = tasks.DynamoUpdateItem(
    self, "AcquireSemaphore",
    table=semaphore_table,
    key={"LockName": tasks.DynamoAttributeValue.from_string("pipeline-concurrency")},
    update_expression="SET ActiveCount = if_not_exists(ActiveCount, :zero) + :one",
    condition_expression="attribute_not_exists(ActiveCount) OR ActiveCount < :limit",
)

If all slots are taken, the execution waits and retries. When its pipeline finishes, it decrements the counter to release the slot. One detail is worth carrying into your own designs. The DynamoDB condition expression enforces the cap in a single atomic operation, rather than the state machine reading the counter and deciding, which would leave a race window between the read and the write. The repository implements the rest of the operational hardening, including releasing slots on every failure path and forwarding failed executions to Amazon SNS through Amazon EventBridge. Its README covers sizing the wait bounds.

The cap of five is a stack parameter, set low so the sample deploys and runs in any standard account without requesting quota increases. Adjust it to whatever your account’s training-job quotas support. Past a single account’s quotas, scaling fleet training is its own topic. The standard levers are raising the service quotas, spreading training across instance types or Regions, and distributing the fleet across multiple accounts. You can also hold the backlog in SQS and admit work only as capacity frees up. Those choices depend on your fleet’s size and shape. The sample gives you the working skeleton to extend.

Deploying and running the sample

The walkthrough in the repository README is the authoritative version. The following short form starts from a clean checkout and sets up the environment before the first deploy:

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-sagemaker-fleet-cv-pipeline
cd sample-sagemaker-fleet-cv-pipeline && python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cdk bootstrap                                           # once per account/region
cdk deploy SageMakerCVPipelineStack -c bootstrap=true   # roles, bucket, ECR
cdk deploy --all                                        # pipeline + orchestration
./scripts/push_ecr_image.sh                             # build and push training image

By default the pipeline generates synthetic production line images, so you can validate the whole system end to end with no dataset and no data approvals. A full run executes all 13 steps, including both Neo compilations, in about 15 minutes and costs roughly $0.07 in billed ml.m5.xlarge time (US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2), July 2026, on-demand). The orchestration resources together cost well under $0.10 per month at sample scale.

To exercise the pipeline on real images, the repository includes a downloader for the BCCD dataset. The dataset is a collection of 364 annotated blood smear microscopy images originally open sourced on GitHub and reorganized into Pascal VOC format under an MIT license. The same dataset is also distributed by Roboflow as public domain. The script maps platelet presence to the defect class, optionally splits the images per camera to simulate a fleet, and uploads training tarballs to the pipeline bucket. The accompanying notebook runs the full pipeline on the real data and does side-by-side ONNX inference on a normal and an anomalous sample. Treating platelets as defects is an illustrative stand-in for a manufacturing defect distribution, not a clinical claim.

Cleaning up

Model packages are created at pipeline runtime, so AWS CloudFormation cannot delete them. Remove them with the AWS CLI first, then destroy the stacks with cdk destroy --all -c bootstrap=true --force. The README lists the exact commands.

Conclusion

In this post, I showed a working SageMaker SDK v3 reference architecture for the fleet-scale computer vision lifecycle. The architecture includes a dual-branch training pipeline where every model is quality-gated on its exported ONNX artifact, compiled with SageMaker Neo, and only then registered. A Model Registry layout uses camera metadata to turn shared package groups into per-camera warm-startable history, and a Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training within account quotas. For teams whose needs are met by managed options such as Amazon Lookout for Vision, that is the simpler path. This pattern targets the per-camera, fleet-scale constraint that managed options do not cover. The design rules transfer beyond computer vision: gate on balanced accuracy plus minority-class recall rather than accuracy, evaluate and compile the artifact you ship, and make operational failures notify rather than terminate silently.

The sample deploys in minutes and a full validation run costs about seven cents of compute, so a low-cost next step is to clone the repository and run it. From there, point the BCCD downloader at a real bucket, set NeoTargetDevice for your hardware, or size the orchestration bounds to your fleet. For the SDK v3 migration itself, the SageMaker Python SDK documentation and the two-part series announcing the new SDK are the references I kept open throughout.

If you want help adapting this pattern to your production environment, reach out to your AWS account team.

About the author
