One dimension detail is worth calling out, because the typed API won’t catch it for you: the AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases namespace expects a prefixed id, knowledge-base/<id>, while the solution’s own BMKB/* namespaces use the bare id. Both are only strings as far as CDK is concerned.

# L1 — AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases wants the prefixed form.
dimensions_map={"Operation": "Retrieve", "KnowledgeBaseId": f"knowledge-base/{kb_id}"}

# BMKB/* — our own namespaces use the bare id.
dimensions_map={"KnowledgeBaseId": kb_id}

Layer 5: The span tree

Layer 5 is the raw OTEL span tree in aws/spans, and it is the layer that shows you the agentic loop directly. It is worth reading carefully, because the nesting isn’t obvious: one LLM call produces three spans. The Strands invoke_agent span wraps the turn, an internal chat span wraps the model call, and a chat <model> span of kind CLIENT is the actual call, and all three repeat the same gen_ai.usage.* token attributes.

The following screenshot shows the span tree in aws/spans, with the three-span nesting visible in the top rows.

Figure 14: Layer 5 span tree in aws/spans, showing the three-span nesting of a single LLM call

Reading the top three rows: an invoke_agent Strands Agents aggregate, then an internal chat span, then a CLIENT chat span, all reporting an identical 7,299 input and 268 output tokens. That is the same LLM call appearing at three levels of the tree, which is why aggregation needs care.

That structure matters the moment you aggregate. To count each LLM call once, filter to the CLIENT leaf:

fields attributes.gen_ai.request.model as model,
       attributes.gen_ai.usage.input_tokens as in_tok,
       attributes.gen_ai.usage.output_tokens as out_tok
| filter ispresent(in_tok) and kind = 'CLIENT' and name like /^chat /
| stats sum(in_tok) as input_tokens, sum(out_tok) as output_tokens,
        count(*) as llm_calls by model

Without that filter the same query reports three times the tokens and three times the calls.

Applying that CLIENT-leaf filter, the following screenshot shows generation token usage by model with each LLM call counted once.

Figure 15: Generation token usage by model, with each LLM call counted once

With the filter in place, the run shows 14 LLM calls totaling 60,472 input and 2,709 output tokens. Without it, the same query would report three times the calls and three times the tokens.

Evaluate: On-demand and continuous

Quality is measured two ways, and both are provisioned by the app.

On-demand: The driver notebook calls AgentCore There is no deploy script in this version, and that is the point: (LLM-as-judge) over each session’s spans for built-in evaluators, Correctness, Faithfulness, Tool-Selection Accuracy and publishes the scores to CloudWatch, where they appear as Layer 7 on Dashboard A.

The following screenshot shows Layer 7 on Dashboard A: on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, with the Layer 5 OTEL span table on the same dashboard.

Figure 16: Layer 7 on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, beside the Layer 5 span table

Layer 7 shows the on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, with the Layer 5 OTEL span table alongside, so the scores and the spans that produced them read together on one board.

Continuous (online): The agent stack also provisions an AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OnlineEvaluationConfig that samples live sessions and scores them automatically, no notebook run required. The configuration itself is visible in the Bedrock AgentCore console under Assess → Evaluations → Evaluation configurations. Results land in the log group /aws/bedrock-agentcore/evaluations/results/<config-id>, and every score is also published as a CloudWatch metric in the Bedrock-AgentCore/Evaluations namespace, keyed by evaluator name and configuration id, so you can graph the scores or alarm on them without parsing logs.

The following screenshot shows the online evaluation configuration in the AgentCore console, under Assess, then Evaluations, then Evaluation configurations.

Figure 17: The online evaluation configuration in the AgentCore console, with four built-in evaluators at 100 percent sampling

The configuration lists four built-in evaluators, Tool-Selection Accuracy, Faithfulness, Correctness, and Response Relevance, set to 100 percent sampling and shown as ACTIVE and enabled.

Because the scores are ordinary CloudWatch metrics, they graph like anything else, no log parsing, and the same widget could carry an alarm. The following screenshot shows those four evaluator scores graphed as ordinary CloudWatch metrics.

Figure 18: The four continuous evaluator scores graphed as ordinary CloudWatch metrics

The four evaluator scores appear as metrics in the Bedrock-AgentCore/Evaluations namespace, each keyed to the evaluation configuration id and the agent’s service name, so you can graph them or alarm on them without parsing logs.

Online results only arrive after a session closes. Scoring runs on the completed session, so the results log group stays empty for roughly the session idle timeout (~30 minutes) after you drive traffic. An empty group right after a run is expected, not a misconfiguration. Each result event carries session.id, so it joins to every other layer. The on-demand path in the notebook has no such wait, which is why both are here.

Across the four built-in evaluators on this run, the continuous path scored 1.00 on Correctness, Faithfulness, Response Relevance, and Tool-Selection Accuracy, five scored traces per evaluator, each result carrying a written explanation.

⚠️ Sampling and cost. This app sets SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE = 100 purely for the blog experiment, so every session is scored and the results are immediately visible. This isn’t a production recommendation. Online evaluation invokes an LLM-as-judge per sampled session, so cost scales with the sampling rate and traffic volume. For a real deployment, choose a sampling percentage that fits your quality-monitoring needs and budget, and align the configuration with your organization’s own policies and cost-governance requirements before enabling it. The rate is a single constant, EvalConfig.SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE, in config.py.

Clean up

When you’re finished, remove the solution so it stops incurring charges, since stored KB data, the agent image in ECR, and the still-active online evaluation all cost money while the stacks sit idle. One command tears everything down:

cdk destroy --all

CDK deletes the stacks in reverse dependency order on its own, dashboards, then agent, then gateway, then kb: the same graph it derived for the deploy, walked backward. There is no teardown script to keep in agreement with the deploy script, which is one of the more quietly valuable properties of modelling the dependencies once.

Two removal behaviors are worth knowing, because both replace hand-written cleanup code:

self.source_bucket = s3.Bucket(
    self, "SourceBucket",
    removal_policy=RemovalPolicy.DESTROY,
    auto_delete_objects=True,  # replaces a list_object_versions delete loop
)

self.repository = ecr.Repository(
    self, "AgentImageRepo",
    removal_policy=RemovalPolicy.DESTROY,
    empty_on_delete=True,  # replaces an image-delete loop
)

Both are set for sample hygiene, for anything you care about, switch the bucket to RemovalPolicy.RETAIN.

The CDK bootstrap stack (CDKToolkit) and its staging bucket aren’t removed. They are shared account-wide infrastructure that other CDK apps may depend on.

What changed since the single-shot solution

Both this post and the 2024 solution are CDK applications in Python, deployed with cdk deploy. The authoring tool is the constant here, what changed is the architecture underneath it, and most of the change is subtraction:

Concern2024: Single-shot RAGThis solution
Vector storeAn OpenSearch Serverless collection and index you provision, scale, and pay OCU forNone. Type: MANAGED, Amazon Bedrock owns storage and indexing
Index lifecycleA custom resource creates the index and waits for it to become searchableNothing to create
Embedding modelYou select it and grant model accessService-managed by default
Stacks3: KB role → OpenSearch infra → KB + data source4: kb → gateway → agent → dashboards
RetrievalOne Retrieve, top-k chunks by vector similarityAgenticRetrieveStream, reranked internally, returns a synthesized cited answer
Choosing a knowledge baseNot applicable, there is one indexThe agent routes semantically across two
Second look at the corpusNot possible in one shotThe agent retrieves again before answering
TelemetryNone provisionedSeven layers, two dashboards
EvaluationManual: sync, pick a model, ask questionsOn-demand and continuous, both provisioned
Cost floor when idleOCU charges accrue whether or not you queryStorage only

The trade is real in both directions. A single index answering single-shot questions is cheaper per query, simpler to reason about, and entirely sufficient when one corpus holds the answer. Reach for this design when it doesn’t.

The CDK constructs doing the work

Four constructs carry most of the weight in this app, and they are worth naming because each replaces something people otherwise hand-write:

  • Provider – For custom resources that outlive the 15-minute ceiling of an AWS Lambda function. The on_event / is_complete split means nothing sleeps in a poll loop, and the response protocol back to CloudFormation is the framework’s job rather than a vendored urllib callback in every handler.
  • BucketDeployment – Uploads the corpora, so the ingestion custom resource only ingests.
  • auto_delete_objects=True and empty_on_delete=True, replace the hand-written list_object_versions and image-delete loops that a stack otherwise needs to be destroyable at all.
  • repository.grant_pull_push(project) – One line for the eight ecr:* actions CodeBuild needs, spelled correctly by construction.

And typed dashboards, from the Observe section: Metric / GraphWidget / Row objects instead of a DashboardBody JSON string, which moves an invalid widget combination from “renders broken on the console” to “fails at cdk synth.”

Two things CDK doesn’t change, and both are worth knowing before you start:

  • Free-form JSON stays camelCase. connector_parameters and parameter_values are passed through verbatim, so the AWS CDK snake_case to PascalCase conversion does not apply inside them. Keys like bucketName and inclusionPrefixes must be spelled exactly as the API expects, and nothing will tell you otherwise until the resource fails.
  • String-typed values are still strings. The knowledge-base/<id> versus bare <id> dimension difference from the Observe section is invisible to the type system. Typed constructs check structure, not semantics.

Neither is a reason to prefer one tool over the other. They are the boundary of what “typed” buys you, and knowing where that boundary sits is most of what makes CDK pleasant instead of surprising.

Conclusion

We built a complete enterprise agentic retrieval solution on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base and AgentCore: multi-KB semantic routing, a reasoning agent, seven layers of observability, and both on-demand and continuous evaluation, and deployed all of it as a single AWS CDK application.

Two things are worth taking away. The managed knowledge base removed infrastructure rather than adding it: no vector store to provision, no index to create and wait on, no OCU line item accruing while the system sits idle. It is also the knowledge base type that supports agentic retrieval and the AgentCore Gateway connector, as described in the Amazon Bedrock documentation. And once retrieval became agentic, observability stopped being optional. Roughly half of what this app provisions exists to answer what the agent actually did and whether the answer was any good, which isn’t overhead on an agentic system. It’s the part that makes one operable.

The CDK authoring model earned its place on the seams. Seven values cross stack boundaries in this architecture, and every one of them is a construct reference rather than an export/import pair, which is also why there’s no deploy script, no teardown script, and no fixed order to remember.

From here you can point the data sources at your own corpora, place the agent in a virtual private cloud (VPC), tune the online-evaluation sampling rate to your budget and policies, or add more knowledge bases to the router. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock detail page and the Amazon Bedrock documentation. The app, the driver notebook, and the self-contained utilities are all in the accompanying GitHub repository, so you can clone it and deploy your own copy with one command.

About the authors

item.title: [Anyscale] KubeRay in production: best practices from the field
item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

KubeRay in production: best practices from the field

By Naila Khan | October 26, 2026

Part 2 of our KubeRay series, from the field. Part 1: Running Ray at scale on Kubernetes with KubeRay covers what KubeRay is, its custom resources, and how to deploy your first RayJob.

Part 1 ended on a good moment: a RayJob reaching SUCCEEDED. This post picks up from there, with what changes when that one job becomes hundreds, spread across teams and clusters. KubeRay handles that growth well; a public Ray Summit 2024 talk showed Ray Train scaled to 10,000 Kubernetes nodes.

If you've run Ray on Kubernetes for a while, you may know the moment. Somewhere past a handful of nodes and a second team, a failed GPU job stops being a quick kubectl logs. The cluster that held the answer may already be gone, and the GPUs reserved for the rerun keep billing while someone works out whether it was the code, the data or the hardware.

As a field engineer, I spend a lot of time with two kinds of teams: enterprises fitting Ray into clusters built for something else, and digital natives pushing Ray further than it has been pushed before. They tend to meet the same handful of scenarios, and they've taught me which practices hold up. That's what this post shares.

LinkFrom the quickstart to production

Part 1's example trains Fashion MNIST on CPUs. A production RayJob uses the same resource, with four changes: it requests GPUs, queues behind team quotas through Kueue, keeps work off the head node, and scales workers from zero.

1apiVersion: ray.io/v1
2kind: RayJob
3metadata:
4  name: nightly-train
5  labels:
6    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: team-ml   # same quotas as every other GPU workload
7spec:
8  entrypoint: python train.py
9  shutdownAfterJobFinishes: true         # GPUs go back to the pool when done
10  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 300
11  rayClusterSpec:
12    enableInTreeAutoscaling: true
13    headGroupSpec:
14      rayStartParams: { num-cpus: "0" }   # keep work off the head node
15      template: { ... }
16    workerGroupSpecs:
17      - groupName: gpu-workers
18        minReplicas: 0
19        maxReplicas: 16
20        template: { ... }                # nvidia.com/gpu requests go here

At this scale, the features from Part 1 do more of the work: GPU nodes shared across jobs, workers that scale back to zero, and quotas that keep teams fair. For one team on one cluster, this spec is often all you need.

Note the shutdownAfterJobFinishes: true line, though. It is good for cost, and it is also where the first production scenario starts.

LinkFive production scenarios to plan for

Once Ray becomes shared infrastructure, with more teams, more clusters and GPUs you can't afford to waste, the same pattern shows up in the field: defaults that work well at small scale need returning under production parallelism and contention. These are not KubeRay issues. Each sits on the boundary between Ray, Kubernetes and the organization running both.

  • Debugging data is tied to the cluster's lifetime. A RayJob that cleans up after itself also deletes its Ray dashboard. The hardest case is a driver that exits in its first few minutes: GPU workers come up, receive no tasks, and the cluster is torn down before anyone captures the driver log. That leaves little to investigate afterward.
  • Hardware faults surface as application errors. A PCIe or NVLink fault, or a hung NFS mount, can interrupt a training run while the pod still reports Ready. Ray continues to schedule work there, so the failure presents as an application error. Some teams have built a modified operator and a custom resource to detect failing hardware.
  • Default settings need tuning at scale. With 20 clusters competing for one GPU pool, an idle GPU worker can be reaped while its placement group is still forming, and training can't begin. A maxReplicas set with no headroom can stall the autoscaler when Ray Train retries an out-of-memory task. Each retry can also leave a placement group behind. Teams in the field report weeks of platform engineering before reliability stabilizes.
  • Head node disruptions affect the whole cluster. Node drains for node-image updates and security patches can take Ray nodes down, and memory pressure can evict the head pod, as Klaviyo's engineering team describes from a year of running Ray Serve on KubeRay. Without GCS fault tolerance, the whole cluster fails. With it, workers keep running only if the head recovers within about ten minutes, KubeRay's default worker reconnect timeout.
  • Ray shares the cluster with existing platform services. Service meshes, shared namespaces, quotas and audit requirements were there first. One enterprise team serving thousands of models on Ray Serve found its Envoy sidecars creating a listener for every Ray port, which strained the mesh control plane and affected neighboring services.

LinkSix best practices for production KubeRay

None of these needs new tooling. Each practice maps to one of the scenarios above and uses what the Kubernetes ecosystem already gives you.

Link1. Persist logs and events before the cluster goes away

Plan for the Ray dashboard of an ephemeral cluster to go away. Turn on the History Server from Part 1 so Ray events and logs land in object storage, and test it against short-lived runs: a driver that crashes in its first minutes is the case teams most often miss. If your team debugs in an existing log stack, also ship logs there with a sidecar such as Fluent Bit. For a job you are actively debugging, raise ttlSecondsAfterFinished so the cluster outlives the failure long enough to inspect.

Some context on why this matters. Seeing logs and dashboards for a finished RayJob is one of the oldest asks in the KubeRay community; users were raising it as early as 2023. It is hard because ephemeral clusters are the whole point of RayJob, so the evidence has to leave the cluster before the cluster does. The History Server is the community's answer, built with contributors from several large platform teams. It was introduced as alpha in KubeRay v1.6 and promoted to beta in v1.7. It writes Ray events and logs to object storage and lets you inspect them after the cluster is deleted.

Link2. Treat GPU health as a scheduling signal

Run NVIDIA's DCGM exporter and alert on GPU Xid errors, not only on utilization. Use node health checks to taint or cordon a failing node so new Ray pods stop landing there. Then use the label-aware scheduling from Part 1 to keep new Ray work on healthy nodes. KubeRay maintainers are also discussing forwarding Kubernetes Pod events, including device-related failures, to RayCluster resources for remediation (issue #5304).

Link3. Tune for contention, not for a quiet cluster

Test your configuration at production parallelism, not on one cluster. Five settings come up repeatedly in the field:

  • Gang scheduling: use one of the gang schedulers from Part 1 (Volcano, YuniKorn, scheduler-plugins or NVIDIA KAI Scheduler) so a job's workers start together or not at all. This stops early workers from sitting idle while a placement group forms.
  • Idle timeout: if you don't gang-schedule, raise the idle timeout so early GPU workers survive while the rest of a placement group forms.
  • maxReplicas headroom: leave room for the replacement worker Ray Train requests after an out-of-memory kill. Size it for your needed workers plus at least two.
  • Bounded retries: cap out-of-memory retries with RAY_task_oom_retries so repeated retries can't run for hours.
  • Mixed CPU and GPU pools: watch whether the autoscaler adds CPU nodes while GPUs are the bottleneck, and whether idle CPU nodes scale down during GPU-bound stages.
1autoscalerOptions:
2  idleTimeoutSeconds: 600   # default is 60
3workerGroupSpecs:
4  - groupName: gpu-workers
5    maxReplicas: 10          # 8 needed + headroom for retries

Watch for placement groups left behind after retries, too. They hold resources the autoscaler can't reclaim.

Link4. Design for losing the head node

  • Set num-cpus: "0" on the head so CPU tasks and actors aren't scheduled there.
  • When you enable GCS fault tolerance, give each critical workload its own external Redis so a Redis issue stays contained to one workload.
  • Bake dependencies into the image instead of installing them at runtime, which can fill ephemeral storage and get pods evicted.
  • For Ray Serve, set max_replicas_per_node so a single node failure affects only part of a deployment.

Link5. Fit Ray into the cluster you already have

  • Give Ray its own namespace, with the RBAC and NetworkPolicy controls from Part 1, so Ray workloads stay isolated from neighboring services.
  • If you run a service mesh, keep it at the edge. Exclude Ray's internal ports from the sidecar, and encrypt Pod-to-Pod traffic with Ray's own TLS or KubeRay's mTLS support (alpha in v1.7) instead. A sidecar listener for every Ray port can overload the mesh.
  • Label every RayJob and RayService with its team and cost center, so the Kueue quotas from Part 1 also give you attribution and chargeback.

Link6. Alert on the failures that matter, and automate the first response

Alert on RayJob Failed status, head pod restarts and GPU Xid errors. Start from what Part 1 covered: KubeRay's Kubernetes-native status fields and Events already report RayJob and RayCluster state, and kubectl ray gives on-call engineers a quick view. Where the response is always the same, such as cordoning a node with a failing GPU, automate it so the on-call engineer starts from an answer instead of a dashboard.

LinkWhen the glue starts to cost you

In Part 1, KubeRay replaced the glue between Ray and Kubernetes. At fleet scale, a new layer of glue appears. Every practice above is doable. Each one is also glue: something a person on your team builds, maintains and supports. With one team on one cluster, that's manageable. It changes with the second team and the second cluster, when a failed job, a three-hour queue wait or an auditor's question each take real time to answer.

A quick self-check. Do you:

  • Maintain a pipeline just to capture logs before ephemeral RayJobs terminate?
  • Spend hours working out whether a failure was the GPU, Kubernetes or Ray?
  • Hand-tune autoscaler defaults to keep production jobs from stalling?
  • Run redundant clusters or a custom health checker to keep Ray Serve up?
  • Map workloads to teams by hand for audit or chargeback?
  • Operate Ray across several clusters, clouds or regions, beyond what MultiKueue covers?

If two or more describe your week, a platform layer is likely worth a look.

LinkWhat comes next: KubeRay Connect

We built Anyscale KubeRay Connect, now in private preview, so teams don't have to keep building that layer themselves. It sits on top of the KubeRay you already run. Your operator keeps reconciling your CRs, you keep submitting with kubectl apply, and your Kueue queues and GitOps stay as they are. Nothing is rewritten.

Whether you're just starting with KubeRay or already running it in production, keep your existing Kubernetes and KubeRay stack and extend your platform with full-stack observability, multi-cloud orchestration, security, governance, and enterprise support, so your developers stay productive and ship faster.

KubeRay Connect installs with a Helm chart as a thin layer beside your workloads. A small Anyscale Connector patches your KubeRay specs at admission and injects lightweight telemetry sidecars. A collector ships metrics and Kubernetes events to the Anyscale platform.

Here is how Connect maps to the five scenarios:

ScenarioWhat KubeRay Connect does
Debugging data is tied to the cluster's lifetimePersisted task and actor dashboards, aggregated logs, and job, service and autoscaler events, managed for you and viewable in the Anyscale console without kubectl access
Hardware faults surface as application errorsCorrelates GPU metrics, Kubernetes events and Ray signals in one place, so a hardware fault appears next to the affected task
Default settings need tuning at scaleShows autoscaler events and GPU utilization per job, so you can see when idle timeouts and replica limits are wrong. Orchestrate adds single-cluster job submission, scheduling and status tracking alongside your Kueue queues. Automated tuning of Ray settings is on the roadmap.
Head node disruptions affect the whole clusterShows the events around a failure; your resilience design stays yours
Ray shares the cluster with existing platform servicesInstalls beside your existing stack: outbound-only connections, no control-plane ingress, and your Kueue queues and GitOps unchanged. Identity passthrough for RBAC and attribution is on the roadmap.

Connect works alongside your cluster design: mesh configuration, Redis topology and image size stay your choice, and the practices above still apply. Mapping identity to people and placing work across a fleet stay with you today, and preview users are shaping what comes next.

The security model is built for review. Every connection starts inside your cluster, so the control plane needs no ingress. Authentication uses projected ServiceAccount OIDC tokens instead of API keys. Admission is fail-closed by default, so a workload is never silently admitted without telemetry.

LinkGet started

KubeRay is a strong foundation, and the six practices above will take you a long way. When you'd rather spend your team's time on models than on glue, a maintained platform layer gives that time back.

  • Running KubeRay in production? Apply for the KubeRay Connect private preview.
  • At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 (November 9–12, Salt Lake City)? Register and come say hello. We'd love to hear about your clusters and what your team is working through.
  • New to KubeRay? Start with Part 1: Running Ray at scale on Kubernetes with KubeRay.
  • Join the community. Share what you've learned in #kuberay on the Ray Slack, or at the bi-weekly KubeRay community meeting.

Table of contents

  • From the quickstart to production
  • Five production scenarios to plan for
  • Six best practices for production KubeRay
  • 1. Persist logs and events before the cluster goes away
  • 2. Treat GPU health as a scheduling signal
  • 3. Tune for contention, not for a quiet cluster
  • 4. Design for losing the head node
  • 5. Fit Ray into the cluster you already have
  • 6. Alert on the failures that matter, and automate the first response
  • When the glue starts to cost you
  • What comes next: KubeRay Connect
  • Get started

Sharing

item.title: [AI21 Labs] Why we built a benchmark before training for instruction fol…
item.description: Full title: Why we built a benchmark before training for instruction following
item.content:encoded:
In Brief

Train a model on standard instruction-following (IF) rewards, and it learns to satisfy the constraints and skip the task. One of our runs answered a request for a history chapter with a single word, and got full reward. In this post, we walk through how we trained it right. That meant building LIFT-Bench first, a benchmark where every constraint is scoped to one section of a document and the task itself is scored, and then using the same score as the RL reward. Trained that way, the model didn’t collapse, and it held steady on outside benchmarks where IFTrain slipped.

The run that looked perfect

Say you decided to train a model that drafts documents. Your users give it a topic, an outline, and a few rules: this section in German, a comparison table here, the summary under 100 words. You picked the best base model you could find, took IFTrain, the go-to open dataset for instruction following, and ran RL with its checkers as rewards.

It works! The reward climbs to 1.0, IFEval goes up 5 points, IFBench 16. Then you actually read the outputs (like you should). Asked for a chapter of alternate history about the Xinhai Revolution, with no word repeated more than four times, your model answers: “China”.

This is not a thought experiment; it happened when we ran this (real) experiment. It taught us the lesson behind everything that follows: an instruction-following reward has to check whether the task was done, not just whether the rules were followed. Getting there meant building a benchmark first.

What went wrong: the reward never saw the task

“China” wasn’t a fluke: by step 390, the median answer had shrunk from 114 words to 18. The reason is simple. IFTrain’s reward, like IFEval’s, checks constraints with code (no commas, a keyword three times) against the whole response. Nothing checks whether the task was done, so dropping it costs nothing, and RL finds that out.

The usual patches don’t close the gap. IFBench adds a reward-model classifier, but it scores general quality, not this task. AdvancedIF gets closer: it trains on content rubrics from a fine-tuned rubric generator. But the generator, the training data and the RL code are all closed, so you can’t build on any of it.

So before training anything, we needed an eval that could see the task.

Step 1: Build an eval that sees the task

Drafting has one big advantage here: structure. Instead of checking every constraint against the whole response, we attach each one to a section of the outline and score it only against that section’s text. That’s the difference between “a paragraph in French somewhere” and “section 2.1 in French”. We call these scoped constraints, and they’re the core of LIFT-Bench.

Each section carries two kinds of constraints. Verifiable ones are checked by code (e.g. write in German, use “tournament” at least three times). Judged ones are checked by an LLM and describe what the section has to cover (e.g. trace the championships back to their first official tournament). The judged constraints are the task, written down section by section, and they count in the same score as the formatting.

Figure 1: Example of a LIFT-Bench task. Each constraint is attached to one section and scored only against that section’s text, and the LLM-judge ones spell out what the section has to cover.

Scoping also gives us a knob no existing IF benchmark has: density, the number of constraints on a single section. We set it when generating tasks, separately from the total number of constraints in the document.

Everything is synthetic. Topics come from Wikipedia, outlines and constraints from an LLM, and a sampler controls how many constraints land on each section. The same pipeline also produces flat tasks, with no outline and every constraint applied to the whole response, the way IFEval does it. LIFT-Bench has 784 test tasks in ten splits: short and long documents (about 4 and 9 sections) at four density levels, plus two flat splits.

Step 2: Make sure the judge works

Judged constraints need a judge, and a reward is only as good as its judge. The default setup hands the judge the full prompt, the full response, and one criterion. We tested that against 305 human-labelled examples, and it said yes to almost everything. Gemma-4-31B accepted 292 of them when only 227 were actually satisfied. Unscoped Qwen2.5-32B scored 0.44 macro-F1, about the same as always answering yes (0.43).

So we scoped the judge too. Instead of the whole document, it gets a short request for one section and only the text the constraint applies to:

Figure 2: Judges scored against 305 human-labelled examples. Scoping the judge to the text a constraint governs lifts macro-F1 for both models, and the weakest scoped judge beats the strongest unscoped one.

Scoping added 11–19 points, the biggest effect of anything we varied, including the judge model itself. Our read: the unscoped judges weren’t failing at judging so much as at finding the right paragraph in a long document. We went with scoped Gemma-4-31B.

This matters more than usual here, because the same judge also hands out the RL reward. A judge that says yes to almost everything would pay for the same collapse we started with.

Step 3: Rethink the base model

Back to the start: you picked the best base model. Best according to what? Most IF leaderboards use flat, IFEval-style prompts, where every constraint applies to the whole response. LIFT-Bench lets us compare that setup with scoped tasks in one pipeline. We evaluated 17 models, 8 samples per task.

On structured tasks, the top models are close to ceiling: GPT-5.5 averages 0.96. On flat tasks, nobody passes 0.85, and the leading closed models average 0.65–0.72. That isn’t about load. Flat tasks carry far fewer constraints, and when we restrict both to tasks with 10 constraints or fewer, all but one model still scores lower on flat. The outline points that only structured tasks can earn are 10% of the score, too little to explain a gap this size.

The rankings change too. Among our nine main models, GPT-5.5 is first on structured tasks and fifth on flat, and the two best overall averages belong to open-weight models, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 Pro. The best model on a flat leaderboard isn’t necessarily the best model for your drafting task.

Figure 3: At 10 constraints or fewer, every model but Qwen3.8-A95B scores significantly lower on flat tasks than on structured ones, so the gap isn’t a matter of load.

Load elsewhere in the document matters too. Keep a section’s own constraints fixed and add more to other sections, and frontier models barely move (Kimi K3 loses 0.4% per density step, GPT-5.5 1.5%), while GPT-5 nano loses 5.5%. A model that handles one constrained section well can slip once the rest of the document is loaded too.

Step 4: Train on what you measure

With an eval we trust, the next step follows: use the same score as the RL reward, unchanged. That’s LIFT-Train, 34,258 tasks from the same generator. We trained Qwen2.5-7B with GRPO on LIFT-Train and on IFTrain, and looked first at what happened during training.

The two runs went in opposite directions. IFTrain’s reward hit 1.0 by step 180, while its median answer fell from 114 words to 18 by step 390, with 38% of answers scoring at least 0.8 in under 30 words. On LIFT-Train, the median answer stayed around 390–530 words, and not one high-scoring answer came in under 30 words. The reward curve won’t warn you about this, so if you’re running RL for instruction following, track answer length next to it.

Figure 4: Rollout health during GRPO on Qwen2.5-7B. On IFTrain, the median answer shrinks from 114 words to 18, and 38% of answers score at least 0.8 in under 30 words. On LIFT-Train, answers stay long and none degenerate.

Now, some of this is by construction: a reward that scores content can’t be maxed by deleting it. The real question is whether content is what makes the difference, since LIFT-Train also differs from IFTrain in format and topics.

So we ran a control. A flat-only slice of LIFT-Train matches IFTrain’s surface, with flat prompts and IFEval-style constraints, but keeps content in the reward. It trained cleanly too. Topics still differ (Wikipedia vs. WildChat), so it’s not a perfect control, but it points to the content in the reward, not the format, as the part that matters.

Not collapsing is the minimum bar. The harder question is whether our reward helps beyond our own benchmark, so we compared both runs on five benchmarks, including two outside ones that also score content:

Figure 5: Scores after 180 GRPO steps on Qwen2.5-7B. Each recipe wins its own benchmark. On AdvancedIF and ComplexBench, which also score content, IFTrain slips and LIFT-Train holds steady.

Each recipe does best on its own benchmark, as expected. On AdvancedIF and ComplexBench, IFTrain slips and LIFT-Train holds steady. The deltas are small, so we read this as LIFT-Train avoiding a regression rather than as a general win, but it’s the pattern you’d expect when one reward sees the task and the other doesn’t.

The flat/structured split from Step 3 matters for training data too. We trained Qwen3-32B on each scope and on a mix. Each single-scope run helps the other scope, but less than the mix: structured-only reaches 0.805 on flat tasks and flat-only 0.798 on structured ones, against 0.896 and 0.919 for the mix. An easy-to-hard curriculum made no difference.

Summary

The lesson isn’t just “build a better benchmark”. The reward decides which parts of the task a model learns to care about. If it measures the rules and ignores the task, a rising reward can hide a model that’s getting worse at what you asked.

What we’d tell another team training for instruction following:

  • Measure the task, not just the rules. Scope each constraint to the text it governs, and score content next to formatting.
  • Check your judge against human labels. It also hands out your reward.
  • Pick the base model on that eval, not on a flat leaderboard.
  • Use the eval as the reward, and track answer length, not just the reward curve.

LIFT-Bench, LIFT-Train and the pipeline are available here. Read the full technical paper here.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Claude Cowork and chat come together for Enterprise
item.content:encoded:
Chat and Cowork first came together for Pro and Max plans in September. The same unified Claude experience is now generally available for Claude Enterprise plans.

Chat and Cowork are now one Claude on web, desktop, and mobile, so your team can ask a quick question or hand over a full project in the same conversation. Agentic work runs in a cloud environment that Anthropic manages, and Claude Enterprise admins control access by role and manage usage with a new Efficient mode.

One Claude for every task

Team members no longer choose between chat and Cowork before they start work with Claude. Conversations begin as a chat, and a simple question still gets a quick answer. When a task needs to run code or work with files, Claude continues in the cloud and returns the finished document, analysis, or deck. Because the work runs in the cloud, it keeps going after someone closes their laptop, and they can pick it up on the web, desktop, or mobile. Chats, projects, connectors, skills, and plugins carry over to the new unified experience.

Organizations are already seeing value from the unified Claude experience across their teams:

“Before chat and Cowork capabilities were unified, they were separate experiences that had to be used and managed independently. Bringing them together has made everything simpler, both for our users and administrators. The transition was seamless, nothing broke across our connectors, skills or MCPs, and we’re confident rolling it out more broadly.”

Daniel Padilla, CTO of LabX

“We no longer have to choose between chat and Cowork. With under ten minutes of prompting, Claude worked through stacks of county, state and federal budgets and public meeting documents, mapped how the funding streams connect, and produced a comprehensive report that would have taken our team weeks. I never had to decide which tool to use for which step. That report will shape our strategic plan and upcoming budget process.”

Paul Simpson, CFO and Head of Technology

“Bringing chat and Cowork together answers what clients kept asking us, ‘which Claude should I use’ and ‘which one does what’. It adapts to how and where you work across mobile, desktop and browser. At Quantium, it’s helping us scale our own AI ambitions and what we can do for our clients.”

Harley Barnes, Executive Manager, AI Technology

“Work at Carvana doesn’t happen only behind a desk. The unified Claude experience lets employees start a task on their computer and pick it up on their phone, with notifications when Claude has results or needs their input. It fits the way our teams work, whether they’re at their desks or visiting a site.”

Charles Sellers, Senior Director, Engineering

“Before chat and Cowork capabilities were unified, they were separate experiences that had to be used and managed independently. Bringing them together has made everything simpler, both for our users and administrators. The transition was seamless, nothing broke across our connectors, skills or MCPs, and we’re confident rolling it out more broadly.”

Daniel Padilla, CTO of LabX

“We no longer have to choose between chat and Cowork. With under ten minutes of prompting, Claude worked through stacks of county, state and federal budgets and public meeting documents, mapped how the funding streams connect, and produced a comprehensive report that would have taken our team weeks. I never had to decide which tool to use for which step. That report will shape our strategic plan and upcoming budget process.”

Paul Simpson, CFO and Head of Technology

“Bringing chat and Cowork together answers what clients kept asking us, ‘which Claude should I use’ and ‘which one does what’. It adapts to how and where you work across mobile, desktop and browser. At Quantium, it’s helping us scale our own AI ambitions and what we can do for our clients.”

Harley Barnes, Executive Manager, AI Technology

“Work at Carvana doesn’t happen only behind a desk. The unified Claude experience lets employees start a task on their computer and pick it up on their phone, with notifications when Claude has results or needs their input. It fits the way our teams work, whether they’re at their desks or visiting a site.”

Charles Sellers, Senior Director, Engineering

“Before chat and Cowork capabilities were unified, they were separate experiences that had to be used and managed independently. Bringing them together has made everything simpler, both for our users and administrators. The transition was seamless, nothing broke across our connectors, skills or MCPs, and we’re confident rolling it out more broadly.”

Daniel Padilla, CTO of LabX

“We no longer have to choose between chat and Cowork. With under ten minutes of prompting, Claude worked through stacks of county, state and federal budgets and public meeting documents, mapped how the funding streams connect, and produced a comprehensive report that would have taken our team weeks. I never had to decide which tool to use for which step. That report will shape our strategic plan and upcoming budget process.”

Paul Simpson, CFO and Head of Technology

1/4

Maintaining security

If your organization has already approved Claude chat, this builds on the enterprise controls you already use, including single sign-on (SSO) and the Compliance API. Anthropic still encrypts data in transit and at rest and doesn’t use it for model training by default.

Claude does agentic work in cloud sessions, each running in its own isolated virtual machine with network egress off by default for Claude Enterprise and connector credentials kept outside the sandbox. Because that work runs in one environment that Anthropic manages, your security team gets central visibility and controls over it. The security best practices guide on the Anthropic Trust Center covers the full architecture.

Managing cost

Claude Enterprise pricing stays usage-based. The newest Claude models are more efficient than their predecessors: billed through usage, Claude Opus 5.5 costs 40% less to run than Claude Opus 5 on typical workloads, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs up to 30% less than Claude Sonnet 5 for most work.

Depending on the task, agentic work can use more tokens than a quick chat. Claude Enterprise admins have four controls for managing this usage. Efficient mode is a new setting that keeps the unified Claude experience on Sonnet and Haiku models. Model entitlements set which models each role can use. Spend limits apply at the organization, group, and member level, and pooled group budgets give a group one shared monthly amount to draw from.

Getting started

The unified Claude experience is generally available today for Claude Enterprise plans. Admins can manage the rollout in Organization settings. Organizations that use zero data retention for Claude Code, a HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys stay on their current configuration.

See the admin setup guide for details. If you're an existing Claude Enterprise customer, you'll receive an email about the rollout for your organization.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Claude Duet Safety, Privacy, and Security
item.content:encoded:
Claude Duet (opens in new tab) is an agent, currently in research preview, that uses a cloud-based computer to do work for you. It can use all the apps and services you've chosen to connect to Claude, and it runs continuously even after you close the app. It can read your inbox, draft replies, book things, and run routines while you are away. Our team runs Claude Duet on our own accounts and we use it for work every day.

We built Claude Duet on three principles to guide the agent's behavior:

  • Your information, and what other people share in your connected apps, is handled with discretion, using a new classifier that checks messages Claude Duet drafts before they go out.
  • You stay in control of what it does on your behalf.
  • Claude Duet never sees your passwords, browser cookies, sign-in tokens, or other credentials.

Claude Duet is new but the thinking behind it is not. In 2025 we published our framework for safe and trustworthy agents (opens in new tab), which puts people in control and treats privacy and secure interactions as basic requirements. Since then, we have written about why no single defense is enough (opens in new tab) and why protection inside the model can’t stand alone (opens in new tab). We also build and operate the infrastructure businesses use to run agents in production through Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab), and Claude Duet keeps credentials separate from the agent in the same way. It builds on this work, adding the protections that an agent acting for you needs. This post walks through what we added and what we’re still working on.

You approve important actions

An agent that acts while you’re away has to know when to stop and ask for permission before proceeding, and to do it at the right cadence. Before Claude Duet does something like sending a potentially sensitive message, paying for something, or deleting anything, it shows you the action, the destination, and the content, including every recipient. It then waits for you to approve the action.

A separate, automated check runs alongside each action, built on the auto mode classifier from Claude Code (opens in new tab) and extended for Claude Duet. It assesses whether the action matches your intent. The check runs outside the model doing the work so instructions hidden in a page cannot affect the outcome.

Some actions stay off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities, banking actions such as moving money between accounts, and accessing someone else's account. Some other steps aren’t covered by a "don't ask me again" rule, however often you have approved them, like paying or sending money, deleting an order, or creating an account. The routines that run while you are away have the same safeguards.

We spent a lot of time calibrating how often Claude Duet asks for approval. Approval fatigue is a serious issue, because too many requests teach people to tap through them, sometimes without adequate consideration. We will continue to adjust this calibration over time.

For purchases, Claude Duet pays with a one-time card from a wallet like Link from Stripe, limited to that merchant and amount. You see the item and the total, and you approve the purchase in your Link app. Your real card number isn’t shared with Claude Duet or the merchant.

Figure 1. Approval flow: the approval card and the separate check sit outside the model, so nothing the agent reads can answer the card.

Your information is handled with discretion

An agent that reads your email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where different types of information should go. If you ask Claude Duet to send your team a weekly recap, it should include only things everyone on the team already has access to and never private details, like your performance review conversations.

To address this, we built a new safety classifier that runs separately from the main model and checks whether each message Claude Duet is about to send contains potentially sensitive information. We categorize this information into two tiers:

  • Never share: We give the most sensitive protection to information like sign-in credentials, full card and bank account numbers, and government ID numbers. Claude Duet is instructed never to share these with anyone, even if you ask.
  • Needs consent to share: Claude Duet will share other private information, such as health or finances, only if you’ve explicitly approved it. Your own request counts as consent, so “send a note to my dentist about my tooth pain” generally won’t need additional approval.

Figure 2. Where your information can go: before anything is sent, the check weighs how sensitive the information is and whether you’ve given consent.

If Claude Duet is blocked for either reason, it can decide to rewrite the message without the sensitive information and share with you for approval.

Claude Duet is still in research preview and these safeguards will occasionally miss something or flag a harmless message. That’s why they work alongside the approval mechanisms above, which are designed to keep you in control of what Claude Duet sends on your behalf. We expect to continue iterating on our classifier as we learn more about how people use Claude Duet.

You have visibility into tasks and connected apps

You can see what Claude Duet has done and is doing in its task list, where each task has its own page, and steer it mid-task. Claude Duet keeps your conversation history and its memory so it can carry context between tasks, until you delete your history or reset it. Deleting your account wipes everything Claude Duet has stored.

The apps you have connected to Claude carry over to Claude Duet, and switching an app off in one place switches it off in both. Disconnecting an app stops new access from that moment, but what Claude Duet already learned from it stays until you reset its memory, which you can do anytime from the app’s settings. Claude Duet also uses the memory from your Claude account, so details Claude remembered from your earlier chats are visible.

Credentials and the browser are isolated from the model

Claude Duet never sees your passwords, browser cookies, or the sign-in tokens for your connected apps, and it can’t save them to its memory. They only ever pass through separate machines the model can’t access, and the approvals and safety checks that govern what it does run there too.

Passwords

When a site asks for a password, you type it into a form inside the Claude app. The form encrypts it with a single-use key that exists only on our secure cloud browser machine, for that one single use. It passes the encrypted password unopened to the browser, which types it into the site. The model doesn’t see the password and can’t save or repeat it. Soon you will also be able to sign in with 1Password; Claude Duet will ask for a credential, you will approve that request in 1Password, and the credential will go to the browser without passing through the model.

An agent that signs in for you changes phishing in two ways. On one hand, Claude Duet doesn’t hold credentials for you so it can’t be phished for a password, and no hidden instruction can make it reveal a secret it doesn’t have. On the other hand, the sign-in form is itself a target, because anything that asks for a password can be imitated. So Claude Duet’s sign-in form only appears inside the app, during a sign-in you asked for. It never arrives as a link, a text message, an email, or a website other than claude.ai. If something that looks like Claude Duet asks for your password anywhere else, it’s not legitimate.

Sign-in tokens

When Claude Duet works in a connected app, it follows our Claude Managed Agents design (opens in new tab) so credentials stay out of reach of the agent’s work. Credentials that the agent uses on your behalf, such as a sign-in token for a connected service, never enter the machine where the agent works. A placeholder for the credential sits there instead and a proxy outside that machine puts in the real value only as a request is made.

The browser

Your browser in Claude Duet runs in its own dedicated virtual machine in the cloud, separate from the model and from the cloud computers the agent works on. The agent drives the browser only through a fixed set of commands: open this page, click here, type this. Whatever a site runs stays on the browser machine (opens in new tab). The site’s code and cookies don’t reach Claude Duet’s memory or your connected apps, and none of the agent’s commands can read cookies out of the browser. What does come back is the page's text and downloads, because the agent has to read them to do its job. That’s why the other checks exist, and why Claude Duet also uses the prompt-injection safeguards described in our browser-use research (opens in new tab). Files it uploads through the browser get the same sensitive-information check as its messages.

Figure 3. The browser boundary: fixed commands go across, page text comes back, and the site's code, cookies, and downloads stay on the browser machine.

Claude Duet is also designed to identify itself as an agent. Today, requests that its web browser sends include a distinct User-Agent header, and we publish the public IP addresses it browses from, so sites can recognize it and decide how to treat it. Before launch, we also contacted several large websites and gave them the option to prevent Claude Duet from visiting their sites, and some chose to. We’ll keep refining how Claude Duet identifies itself as we learn from the research preview.

Figure 4. Credential path: the password is encrypted on your phone, opened only on the browser machine, and never passes through the model.

How we tested Claude Duet

Testing started well before the research preview and continues now. Our Safeguards team built evaluations from routine-shaped tasks, each in three variants: an innocent version, one with injected instructions, and one that tempts the agent to do more than it was asked. Those run alongside shadow traffic from real use.

Red teams further tested whether Claude Duet would leak information, act without approval, or follow malicious prompts. We built a threat model of the whole system, across the repositories and trust boundaries it touches. An external penetration-testing firm tested Claude Duet with access to our source code, and a follow-on engagement covering the cloud browser and the sign-in form is running now. Each new credential feature is red-teamed on an isolated rig before it ships to anyone.

Claude Duet is also in scope of Anthropic’s public bug bounty program, which rewards valid reports and offers safe harbor for good-faith research, under our responsible disclosure policy. If you find a security vulnerability, we want to hear about it: report it through Anthropic’s bug bounty program on HackerOne (opens in new tab).

Building this with you

We’re releasing Claude Duet as a research preview because we want to learn what you value in a personal agent, including the protections and controls you’d like to see next. Some of what’s described here is still changing: how often it asks for approval, how you sign in, and how well the sensitive-information checks tell what’s private from what’s harmless. Tell Claude Duet in plain words what you’d like to see or what went wrong, and it will file a report for our team.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

Published October 23, 2026

Update on GitHub

9

David Corvoysier

dacorvo

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

Look up a model

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Run it yourself

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:

python3 run.py

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:

hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache

What "runs" means

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

The results are a dataset

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_parquet("hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data")
df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B"][["neuronx_cc", "library", "library_version", "neuron_cores", "result"]]

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

item.description: Full title: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape

Enterprise Article

Published October 23, 2026

3

Kyle Wiggers

Ai2Comms

allenai

📄 Paper

Encountering a new paper can change a research idea's trajectory. The researcher may discover that someone has already addressed their proposed contribution, or find an unresolved problem in the paper that inspires a new direction of inquiry.

We call this process a literature-initiated pivot: a change in research direction prompted by reading prior work. It connects two activities that researchers often have to manage separately: developing an idea and deciding which literature to measure it against.

With collaborators at the University of Pennsylvania, we developed LitPivot, a system that helps researchers navigate these pivots. Using papers retrieved through Asta Paper Finder, LitPivot organizes literature around the part of a proposal being edited, offers critiques supported by excerpts from selected studies, and suggests revisions that researchers can accept, edit, or reject. LitPivot is intended to be used for early-stage research ideation, but the idea could possibly extend to longer writing tasks (i.e., writing the introduction section of a paper).

In a study with 17 researchers, domain experts rated research ideas developed with LitPivot as better grounded in the literature than those developed with a text editor and an AI chat tool. Participants also perceived their revised research ideas as more novel and useful, and reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature.

LitPivot will be presented at UIST 2026 in Detroit. Read the paper here.

Why pivoting is hard

Research ideas evolve through engaging with the literature. In our analysis of meeting notes from four completed computer science research projects, we identified 21 literature-initiated pivots across all four projects. These fell into two types: differentiating an idea from existing work to establish an idea’s novelty, and aligning an idea with existing work to build on it. This project itself went through two pivots before we settled on its contributions.

These changes can be difficult to navigate. In a formative study, five researchers developed proposals using a text editor and standard search tools. They struggled to develop their ideas while critically evaluating them against the literature. When a paper challenged an idea’s novelty, they wanted concrete suggestions for how to revise it, supported by prior work. These findings shaped LitPivot’s assessments, which pair literature-supported critiques with specific suggestions for revising the selected part of an idea.

How LitPivot works

In LitPivot, a researcher starts by writing a short proposal in an editor and enabling what we call facet highlighting, which segments an articulated idea into different facets (i.e., a problem, contribution, and evaluation). To check a proposed facet, the researcher clicks that segment in the draft. An adjacent panel groups related papers based on the selected facet (e.g., grouping papers by the evaluation methods they use when the evaluation facet is selected) and highlights the most relevant groups. The researcher selects papers, requests an assessment, and reviews a suggested revision alongside excerpts supporting the critique. The literature is then reranked based on relevance to the revised facet.

In particular, LitPivot separates a research idea into its problem, proposed contribution, and evaluation plan. Each facet has its own set and relevance ranking of related literature. LitPivot groups retrieved papers around the facet being edited, letting the researcher choose which ones the system should use to assess the draft.

Alongside scientific-writing environments such as Prism and agentic assistants such as Claude Code, LitPivot explores a new workflow for developing an early research idea: choosing literature to assess it against, using that evidence to revise it, and reconsidering which papers matter as the idea changes. Its paper groups and linked critiques make those steps explicit for each part of the proposal, while researchers control both the draft and the evidence used to assess it.

For a problem statement, LitPivot looks for evidence that the problem exists and reasons it matters. To assess a proposed contribution, it compares what the selected papers have already addressed with the limitations and future work they describe, looking for remaining gaps. For an evaluation plan, it checks whether the proposed tests address the research question and how similar work has been evaluated. The system then suggests a rewrite with supporting quotes attached.

Changing one facet of an idea can leave another out of date. LitPivot flags passages that may need revision, such as an evaluation plan that no longer adequately evaluates a revised contribution. Researchers can accept, edit, or reject suggestions, and request new papers or refresh the literature ranking as their proposal develops.

Paraphrased example from one study participant.

Our findings

In our lab study, 17 researchers each developed one assigned idea with LitPivot and another with a baseline tool—a text editor and an AI tool for asking questions about selected papers. Both conditions used the same collection of papers. Two domain experts, unaware of which system had been used, rated the resulting proposals on a single criterion: how well they used relevant literature to support and justify the idea. Proposals developed with LitPivot received higher ratings.

Participants in the same study also reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature and greater self-reported improvements in their ideas’ novelty and usefulness with LitPivot than with the baseline. Domain experts also reviewed the participants’ ideas and rated the ideas revised using LitPivot to be significantly better grounded in relevant literature.

One participant in our lab study started with a proposal to generate consistent, factual synthetic medical notes. LitPivot identified consistency across multiple hospital visits as a potential gap in the selected literature. The participant reviewed abstracts and removed papers about single-visit notes. After another assessment, they narrowed the proposal to detecting contradictions across notes from multiple visits. The example shows how revising an idea and choosing the literature used to assess it can inform each other.

In a follow-up study, five researchers used LitPivot on their own ongoing projects during 30-minute sessions. Participants used LitPivot across multiple project phases, not just at the beginning. Two used it to vet new ideas against the literature, while three used it to refine the framing of more mature ideas. One researcher highlighted how seeing parallel concepts from different domains helped them reframe their contribution.

These studies suggest that LitPivot can support both early exploration and the refinement of an existing research direction.

Supporting scientific discovery

At Ai2, we’re developing AI to help researchers formulate testable ideas and examine the evidence behind them. Asta supports that effort through theory generation from published findings (Theorizer), synthesis, and hypothesis generation and testing on data (AutoDiscovery), while HARPA generates promising hypotheses informed by emerging research trends. Scideator lets researchers recombine elements of prior work into new ideas and assess their novelty, and IdeaSynth supports iterative refinement with feedback grounded in the literature.

Our recent study, Old Ideas, Novel Problems, examines the limits of automated novelty evaluation, showing how small prompt changes can alter an AI judge’s verdict on the same ideas. LitPivot extends this line of work by making the choice of relevant literature part of the revision process. Researchers can change which papers they use to assess a proposal as their idea develops, then use critiques and supporting excerpts to decide how to revise it. The system connects those decisions across the proposal’s problem, contribution, and evaluation plan.

We hope insights from LitPivot help scientists build on existing knowledge and turn early ideas into new contributions to their fields.

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A…
item.description: Full title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide

Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome.

Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder. The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result.

This post uses Wordle, a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting.

In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models. All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository.

Solution overview

The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect.

Figure 1: MTRL on SageMaker AI, where the training job invokes the AgentCore-hosted agent once per rollout to sample the policy model, play the game, and report a reward

For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, guess_word, and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter on the policy model.

Three design points matter for what follows:

  • The agent and reward live in one place. A single Python file deployed to AgentCore holds the environment, the tool, and the scoring function.
  • The dataset carries only the secret word. The word lists bundled with the agent are built from the open-source SCOWL word lists and are used only for scoring.
  • The reward is outcome-dominant. A solve pays 1.05–1.55 depending on speed, a loss pays -0.5, and never making a valid guess pays -1.5. A small shaping term rewards good strategy within each tier.

Supported models and AWS Regions

MTRL is serverless: you pick a base model and the service provisions the training and sampling infrastructure. At the time of writing, it supports the following base models, each trained with a LoRA adapter:

Base modelAWS Regions
Amazon Nova 2 LiteUS East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2)
GPT-OSS-20BUS East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2)
Gemma 4 31B (instruction-tuned)US West (Oregon) (us-west-2)
Qwen 3.6 27BUS West (Oregon) (us-west-2)

We chose GPT-OSS-20B because it has the lowest per-token price of the four and its reasoning effort is controllable per request. See the MTRL documentation for the current list.

Pricing

You don’t choose instances or size a cluster. You pay per million tokens in three dimensions, priced by base model:

  • Prefill: input tokens the policy model processes. These accumulate in a multi-turn task, because every turn re-reads the history.
  • Sample: tokens the policy model generates, including reasoning tokens.
  • Train: tokens processed in the backward pass that updates the LoRA adapter.

The 100-step run consumed 491.6 million prefill, 159.7 million sample, and 643.3 million train tokens across 105,486 rollouts in 12 hours 40 minutes. At GPT-OSS-20B list prices in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) at the time of writing, that is about $339:

DimensionTokensPrice per 1MCost
Prefill491,616,806$0.12$58.99
Sample159,737,098$0.30$47.92
Train643,308,554$0.36$231.59
Total1,294,662,458$338.50

The train dimension dominates and scales with trajectory length, so shorter games and less verbose reasoning cut the bill. The AgentCore runtime bills separately for the vCPU and memory the agent uses. For this run, that was about $79, from the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics at us-east-1 list prices. DescribeJob reports the token counts under BillableTokenUsage. See Amazon SageMaker AI pricing for current rates.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need the following. See also the MTRL prerequisites.

  • Python 3.10 or later, uv, Node 20 or later, and the AgentCore CLI (npm install -g @aws/agentcore). See Get started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for installation and the IAM permissions the CLI needs.
  • botocore 1.43.37 or later, on the machine that launches the job. This is the first version that includes the AgentRFT CreateJob operation.
  • Two AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, described in Step 1.
  • An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket in the same Region as the agent. The training job must also run in that Region, because CreateJob rejects a cross-Region runtime ARN.

Step 1: Create the IAM roles

MTRL uses two roles, and one of them has a trust policy that the general SageMaker AI documentation doesn’t mention.

Agent runtime role. agentcore deploy creates this role for you. It trusts bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com and needs the AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess managed policy, which lets the agent call the policy model and report rewards. The CDK stack in the sample repository attaches this policy automatically.

Training job role. You create this one. It must trust job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com with both sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession, and it needs the AmazonSageMakerJobFullAccess managed policy.

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [{
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Principal": {"Service": "job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com"},
        "Action": ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession"]
    }]
}

Note: The trust principal is job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com, not sagemaker.amazonaws.com. With the generic principal, CreateJob fails with “Could not assume role,” and the message names the correct principal only after retries.

Step 2: Deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Clone the sample repository, set your account and Region in Wordle/agentcore/aws-targets.json, and deploy:

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-multi-turn-rl-wordle
cd sample-multi-turn-rl-wordle/Wordle
agentcore validate
agentcore deploy

The CLI builds the agent’s dependencies for the runtime’s Linux ARM64 platform, creates the execution role with AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess attached, and deploys through AWS CloudFormation. We recommend it over uploading a code package on the console, where it’s common to get the roughly 700 MB of compiled dependencies or the policy attachment wrong. Note the runtime ARN in the output for the training job.

Figure 2: The Wordle agent runtime in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console with status Ready

The runtime reads two environment variables from agentcore.json. REASONING_EFFORT=low sets reasoning_effort on every request to the policy model. In our evaluation jobs, low effort used 63 to 83 percent fewer sample tokens per game than medium. REASONING_PROMPT_HINT=true also adds “Reasoning: low” to the system prompt, which is how gpt-oss reads the setting in its Harmony chat format. Neither variable gives the model any hint about the secret word.

Figure 3: Runtime environment variables showing REASONING_EFFORT set to low

The agent is one file, main.py. Simplified, its entrypoint looks like the following. For your own task, you change the task parsing, the tools, and the reward:

app = BedrockAgentCoreApp()

@app.entrypoint  # outermost: starts the HTTP server AgentCore invokes
@sagemaker_rft_handler  # reports the returned reward to SageMaker AI
def handle_rollout(payload):
    prompt, answer = parse_task(payload["prompt"])
    game = WordleGame(answer)

    @tool
    def guess_word(guess: str) -> str:
        """Submit a 5-letter Wordle guess and get feedback."""
        return game.guess(guess)

    agent = Agent(model=build_model(), system_prompt=SYSTEM_PROMPT, tools=[guess_word])
    agent(prompt)
    return {"reward": game.final_reward()}

Important: The sagemaker_rft_handler decorator does not start an HTTP server by itself. Wrap it with BedrockAgentCoreApp and @app.entrypoint, with the entrypoint decorator outermost. Without this, every invocation times out after 30 seconds.

Step 3: Verify the runtime

Before spending GPU time, confirm the whole chain works with a payload shaped like the one the training service sends. The repository includes one as Wordle/payload.json:

{
  "prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"beach\", \"id\": \"smoke-test\"}",
  "metadata": {
    "jobArn": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-east-1:111122223333:job/AgentRFT/smoke-test",
    "rolloutId": "r1"
  }
}
