item.title: [Inference.net] Introducing AutoEvals: Automatically find the best model for…
item.description: Full title: Introducing AutoEvals: Automatically find the best model for your task
item.content:encoded:
Aug 5, 2026

Introducing AutoEvals: Automatically find the best model for your task

A

Amar Singh

It's the Summer of 2026. A new frontier model is released nearly every month. Each one comes with a new set of benchmark numbers, some hype on X, and the same nagging question for teams running LLMs in production: should we switch?

Most teams never really answer it. Answering it honestly means building a dataset that represents your real traffic, standing up API access to every provider you want to test, writing a rubric, wiring up judging infrastructure, burning the tokens to run it all, and then interpreting the results. That's a week of work, per model, per task, every time something new ships. So the question gets shelved. The model that was chosen months ago, based on a price point and vibes, keeps running because swapping models in production is both hard and risky.

And the risk is real. Benchmarks are averages over someone else's tasks. A model can top the leaderboards and still fumble your tool schemas, your output format, your edge cases. The only benchmark that actually matters is your own traffic, and until now, nobody had time to run it.

We're introducing tooling to fix this. Introducing AutoEvals - the plug-and-play toolkit to find the right model for your task. Sign in or read the docs to get started.

Real production traffic is the best benchmark

AutoEvals is designed to help developers find the best model for a given task or agent. Not the best on a public benchmark you never heard of - better on the exact requests your users sent last week.

Integrate with Inference Gateway (in 2 minutes), collect data, click one button in the dashboard, and a few minutes later you have a definitive answer about which model you should use, with real numbers on the difference in quality, cost, and latency.

Every model release becomes free upside instead of homework. When something new ships, you no longer weigh the announcement against a week of eval work. Run a comparison over lunch and know by the afternoon whether it matters for you.

Switching stops being scary. The recommendation isn't a leaderboard rank. It's your own traffic, replayed and judged, with every sample inspectable. You can understand exactly how a new model handles requests compared to your current model before a single production request touches it.

You stop paying for intelligence you don't need. Plenty of tasks are quietly overserved by expensive models. AutoEvals shows you the quality-cost frontier for your specific task, so you can see when a more affordable model offers the same level accuracy.

The verdict: a concrete recommendation for your task, with the reasoning behind it

How AutoEvals work in practice

An AutoEval runs in three moves. It starts by sampling your recent production traffic, which is then replayed by a set of candidate models. Afterwards, LLM judges score each output for both quality, meaning how well the model did the task, and similarity, meaning how closely it behaves like the model you run today. It then summarizes these results into a model verdict, key findings, and per-model summaries.

The two scores together tell you how safe a switch is. High quality with high similarity is a drop-in upgrade. High quality with low similarity means the model is good but behaves differently, so it earns a closer look first. When you do want to inspect the outputs individually, the Sample Viewer gives you side-by-side model responses and the judge's reasoning for each score.

The Sample Viewer: side-by-side model responses and the judge's reasoning for each score

Getting your traffic in front of Inference platform is the only setup, and it's one integration: route your LLM calls through our Gateway (our CLI can instrument your project automatically), or report traces with our tracing SDK. From then on, comparing models is a button, and switching is a single line change.

Running on our own agents

We built AutoEvals for our own agents before we built it for anyone else, and two findings genuinely changed how we think about model selection.

The gap between model generations is bigger than you think. One of our GTM agents had been running on the same well-regarded model for months. It felt fine, until we ran an AutoEval on it. Models at a fraction of the cost blew it out of the water with better long-horizon trajectories, tighter tool-schema adherence, and more precise results across the board. We left better results on the table because we didn't look.

Some tasks have a skill ceiling. On that same task, the top frontier models landed on identical quality scores. Past a certain capability level, they were all simply taking the right action, and paying more bought nothing. Once you can see the ceiling, the model decision makes itself, and it's rarely the most expensive option.

Past a certain capability level, quality converges - paying more buys nothing

Put those two findings together and the conclusion is hard to escape: if you're building with LLMs, your application should be getting more accurate and cheaper over time, just from the pace of model releases. The teams that capture that compounding advantage will be the ones for whom evaluation is effortless. That's what we built.

Run your first comparison today

AutoEvals are live now for every Inference account, free to start. Connect your traffic, click Run Comparison, and in a few minutes you'll know something most teams never find out: whether the model you're running is actually the best one for the job.

Read the guide or sign up free to get started.

The best model for your task might have shipped last week. Now you can actually find out.

CONTACT

Meet with our research team

Schedule a call with our research team to learn more about how Specialized Language Models can cut costs and improve performance.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Building agents: When to fold subagents into your main agent…
item.description: Full title: Building agents: When to fold subagents into your main agent loop
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve built an agent in Claude Platform that includes multiple subagents, see which may make sense to fold into the main agent loop using our migration kit. It runs a guided workflow to identify your patterns, evaluate alternatives, and verify the best approach. It includes a demo that you can try on a mock system before running on your agent.

Subagents – agents with their own context window, tools, and instructions, orchestrated by a coordinator – are a core component of agent design. They are effective at verification, parallel work, and modular permissioning. We use them in many of our own agents that we build using Claude Platform, for example our multi-agent research system.

However, recently the Applied AI team has found a pattern of enterprise agent deployments that have benefited from folding routers, planners, and domain subagents into the main agent loop. In our comparisons across several enterprise deployments, a single agent with skills frequently outperformed both the one-prompt-for-everything design and the subagent design on quality, and often at a lower cost and latency per task.

For example, one company found the dozen of specialist subagents within its customer-facing agent made a consistent on-brand experience difficult to maintain and added latency that hurt the user experience.

We also often see proposed agent designs that follow a familiar progression: an intent classifier, a fixed multi-step reasoning pipeline, user-segment buckets, separate recommendation branches, and a multi-agent orchestrator on top.

In these cases feedback is often that most of this structure was doing work the model no longer needed done for it, and that one clear system prompt, 4-5 thin data tools, and firm output guardrails would cover most of the use case.

To be clear, subagents still have their place, including at the research frontier. Use them when:

  • A single agent loop hits measurable performance degradation from context bloat, or
  • Multiple tasks need to be tackled in parallel with fresh context windows that can be discarded once the task is done, or
  • A single agent struggles to select appropriate tools or there are conflicting instructions in the system prompt.

But too often we see enterprises give each team or problem type its own subagent, with the agent architecture becoming a copy of their org chart (Conway’s law at work).

This post explains when to consider folding subagents into your main agent loop with best practices we’ve learned from building agents in large organizations.

Agent building failure modes for large organizations

Companies often want to build an agent that unites multiple products and capabilities into a single customer interface.

Typically, each capability is owned by a separate team, so companies start by letting each individual team build their own agent, then a central platform team builds an orchestrator on top. This can take on several structures including orchestrator-subagent or a single agent with specific agents exposed as MCP tools.

This looks like the simplest solution but introduces immediate complexity around:

  • Context management: You need to decide what context is exchanged between agents and often lose details in the back and forth.
  • Subagent sprawl: Every team ships its own subagent, so companies end up with hundreds of overlapping subagents with no enforced standards and no specific owner.
  • The Frankenprompt: Every team adds a sentence to the system prompt, resulting in conflicting rules and no consistent voice.
  • Unvetted, overly localized evals: Everyone adds their own evals that are overly optimized for their subtask. No one owns or maintains the whole set, and leadership makes decisions based on watered-down, overly localized scores.
  • Latency: Multi-agent architectural complexity adds latency. One customer that evaluated their multi-agent harness against a single agent loop saw a roughly 2x faster runtime with the latter.

Using an agent loop with progressive disclosure

The orchestrator-subagent design described above is a reasonable approach to coordinating specialists built across teams, but often a more effective approach can be progressively disclosing context via skills and progressively disclosing tools via tool search. In other words, the agent sees short descriptions of the skills and tools, which are fully loaded only when needed.

There are three reasons why this approach can make sense:

  • Shared context produces better answers: for longer-running agents, we want the context from several different tasks to sit in the main context window. An agent that has seen the result of each earlier step can connect them, which leads to richer outputs and better insights than a set of summaries handed back by subagents. It also means fewer context windows and fewer lossy handoffs.
  • Progressive disclosure prevents context bloat: this technique allows teams to build single agents that can accomplish a wide variety of tasks without requiring all of the context to be immediately loaded into one long system prompt. This removes the main reason teams previously split work across subagents. In fact, we reduced Claude Code’s system prompt for more advanced models by over 80% which included cuts related to progressively disclosing skills and tools.
  • Models are more capable: starting with Opus 4.5, models became capable of managing far more in a single loop than most teams expected. You cannot turn off thinking on Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1, and recent models increasingly narrate their progress and check their work as they go, which makes some harness elements redundant. Each new model lets you move more of the decision-making out of the harness and into the model itself. A simpler loop is also easier to move to the next model; in migrations we have helped customers with, rigid multi-agent structures were often what stopped the new model from doing more of the work.

The single agent loop design requires discipline: a carefully managed system prompt, skill and tool descriptions that trigger at the right times, and deliberate handling of context windows, memory, and note-taking. This article goes deeper into migration and design considerations in subsequent sections.

One central team should own end-to-end quality and the system prompt, vetting every new tool and eval before it ships. Keeping that central team small helps iteration move quickly and lowers coordination cost across a large org.

If you go the multi-agent route, start with the simplest pattern (generator-verifier, orchestrator-subagent, or other) that could work. Decompose boundaries effectively by dividing by context: give each subagent a piece of work that needs little from the rest of the system and have it hand back a compact result (good candidates are independent research paths, separate components with clean interfaces, or black-box verification). When agents are split by problem type, they engage in a "telephone game," passing information back and forth with each handoff degrading fidelity.

How to fold subagents into the main agent loop

Many teams already have an orchestrator and a set of specialist agents in production. The following is the single loop design we'd suggest working toward:

  • One model and one context window running an open-ended tool loop, with limits (turn and cost budgets, write gates) set in the harness.
  • Each turn, the model emits a batch of tool calls. The harness runs them in parallel and returns raw results to the same model, which decides the next step: another batch, a question to the user, or an answer.
  • The loop stops when the model answers or hits a budget. A goal or verifier check can optionally run after the answer.
  • The model writes its plan in context on the first turn and revises it as results arrive. This is the main change from the orchestrator and specialist agents setup: the model that writes the plan is also the one carrying it out, so it can change the plan mid-turn.
  • Context still gets loaded, and is managed by the agent itself:A code step that rewrites the plan from a catalog of rules is no longer needed, since the model decides each step.Ordering and domain procedure move into skills.Hard limits (validation, approval gates) and anything else that comes up mid-conversation (e.g. memory lookup) move into the tools.Code can still be used to load anything cheap and almost always relevant (e.g. an entity resolution step), and to handle any mechanical parts (payload construction, stream parsing, resuming a clarification) inside tools the loop calls.

This single loop design also helps with the end state many teams are working toward (an agent that understands a user's high-level goals and acts on their behalf), since it keeps everything the agent has learned in one context.

The suggestions below are how a team could get from a multi-agent system to a single agent loop in stages, and how several teams can keep contributing to that agent along the way.

Task-completion evals

The first step is to create an eval set that can help you determine whether you should fold a subagent into the main agent loop. The eval structure we’ve seen work is one shared end-to-end set owned by a central team with smaller eval sets shipped with each skill by the team that owns it. Even a set of 10 golden examples is enough to start.

Grading the agent's final message against a rubric is a good starting point for tracking answer quality. While you still have an orchestrator, you should also track routing accuracy (did it pick the right subagent?). Once a subagent is folded in, check instead whether the agent loaded the right skill or called the right tool. Working toward task-completion evals over time is helpful as this matters most when comparing architectures.

This can be complex in environments where internal systems are difficult to replay and user engagement is difficult to simulate. One approach that has worked for us internally is to record timestamps on important events, so they can be replayed later to run as targeted evals.

Reducing subagents over time

Evolving toward a single agent loop involves folding the subagents into tools and skills. This can be done by merging domain subagents, calling them as tools, or replacing them with skills and tools.

Combining domain agents

Build a small end-to-end eval before the first merge. Then fold in by shared context starting with subagents that have the most use.

Merge specialists that chain on each other's output, touch the same data, or are often called together. For example, if a significant share of production traffic is one specialist followed by a second, that is a tightly coupled pair, which makes it a candidate to merge into one domain agent.

Subagents called as tools

When one of the three conditions above applies and you keep a subagent, it can be effective to have the main agent call subagents as tools so it can continue holding the conversation with the user.

We’d only recommend a full handoff, where the subagent takes over the conversation, when it needs to talk to the user directly. Everything else can be a skill plus tools in the main loop.

This will allow you to define a shared response schema for subagents, verify the conclusion against real data with the main agent, and trim the input to any final synthesis step. This is a good first step, as you don’t need to rewrite the subagents. It also gives you a baseline on the task-completion eval before deciding to fold any subagents into the main agent.

However, some failure modes will remain:

  • Each specialist has its own prompt, context, owner team, and evals
  • Each call still hands back a lossy summary
  • Every call is a nested model loop that adds latency

Folding subagents into the main agent via skills and tools

Fold subagents into the main agent one at a time by turning each one’s prompts into skills and API calls into MCP tools. Compare eval performance with and without the subagent. Then decide which to keep.

When you compare, don’t just examine the final score, take a look at which tasks flipped. When we tested this on a sample support agent, folding one subagent into another lowered latency, but also broke a process that had been passing. The main agent was holding the order lookup tool and answering on its own, without asking the shipping specialist for the delivery date.

Before each change, make sure your eval has a task for every chain of agents that runs together in production and for every rule the agent must not break, and run each task more than once, since a break like this one only showed up in one run out of two.

How several teams can contribute to a single agent

Domain reasoning can be retrieved from knowledge bases, skills, and MCP tools. Individual teams can shift their ownership from agents to skills and tools, with one small central team keeping ownership of the system prompt and end-to-end quality. This involves vetting new skills, tools, and evals before they ship.

MCP tools

Tools are the right fit when the agent needs to take an action, read live data from a system, or return a result in a fixed shape. You can also use tools as a way to keep calling subagents while you migrate. We recommend tools grouped by user intent (not one tool per API) because once you exceed 30-50 tool definitions in the system prompt, tool choice tends to degrade.

Use tool search with deferred loading, limit hard preconditions, and move any needed ones into the tools. For example, if Y needs X's output, Y's tool checks for it and returns an instruction the model can act on. Per-user permissions work the same way. Each tool checks what the calling user may see or do and returns a plain refusal the model can read, so one loop can serve users with different access without a separate agent per permission level.

Skills

Skills are the right fit when the agent needs to know how a team does work, like the steps, rules, and judgment calls a specialist subagent's prompt used to hold.

Our approach to growing skill libraries is to give the maintenance work back to the people writing the skills. Claude can do the heavy lifting with skills that can build, test, and prune other skills.

To prevent skill sprawl, you can have DRIs per team own their skills and make sure they are well crafted, distinct, and shipped with appropriate evals.

  • /skill-creator allows you to author new skills that start well-formed, and audit existing ones to trim, deduplicate, and restructure them.
  • /skill-doctor allows you to see what each skill in your library costs and how often it’s actually used, and delete dead weight.

Knowledge bases

Knowledge bases are the right fit for reference material the agent only needs some of the time. Facts and reference material (policies, metric definitions, product specs) can sit behind a search or lookup tool the model calls, or ship as reference files inside a skill. Avoid having code retrieve and paste this context into prompts.

Tools to accelerate this work

We recently released a set of Claude API skills that can help with most of the work mentioned above. Our migration kit chains these skills together in one guided workflow for assessing and moving multi-agent systems to a single agent loop. It includes a demo you can try before running it on the real thing:

  • /claude-api build-eval: can help create a first end-to-end set owned by the central team or small evals each team ships with its skill
  • /claude-api prompt-audit: can flag instructions written for older models in your prompts, skills, and tool descriptions and propose fixes as a diff. This can be run on your system prompts to find any rules that were added for an earlier model and are now making the agent slower or more rigid. Each team's DRI can also run it on their own skills and tool descriptions.
  • /claude-api hillclimb: can iteratively improve an app against an existing eval. This can be used for the "folded in vs kept" comparison (after folding one subagent into a skill plus tools, let it iterate on the skill and tool descriptions and see if the folded version matches or beats the subagent), as well as your system prompt.
  • /claude-api cost-optimize: profiles where your calls go and proposes savings from options such as prompt caching, trimming unneeded input and output tokens, effort, and model choice, one change at a time. This can help bring cost and latency down on a given design.

As models evolve, our understanding of how to best use them and guidance around best practice evolve as well. That makes any one architecture less important than the principle behind it: measure, change one thing at a time, and keep what holds up.

This is one of those cases. As models get more capable and agents get longer running, more of your subagents can be skills and tools. You don’t have to make that move in one step, though. Build a small end-to-end eval, fold in one subagent, and keep it as a subagent only if the folded version scores worse, then rinse and repeat.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] The full Claude Platform, available on Google Cloud
item.content:encoded:
Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) is now generally available, giving Google Cloud customers the full set of Claude Platform features, with Google Cloud IAM credentials, billing, and commitment retirement. Claude also remains available via the Google managed offering, where Google is the data processor.

Access the complete Claude Platform on Google Cloud

With the Anthropic managed offering, Google Cloud customers now receive the full set of Claude API features, with new features and betas shipping the same day they go live on the native Claude Platform.

The Anthropic managed offering works with existing Google Cloud IAM credentials, so teams can stay within the tools and permissions they already manage. Billing is through a single Google Cloud invoice and Claude usage draws down your existing Google Cloud commitment.

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) is currently available with US and Global endpoints.

“With the Anthropic managed offering, we get the native Claude API with Google Cloud as the access layer. Accessing new features on day one is important. We build AI agents and assistants for Enterprises, and need to bring new Claude capabilities into our product quickly. Using our existing IAM set-up and knowing usage counts towards our Google Cloud commitment made it an easy decision for our team.”

Arvind Sundararajan, CTO

“Moby, our AI harness for ecommerce brands, runs on Claude. With the Anthropic managed offering, we run Moby on Google Cloud on the same Claude API our team already builds on. Prompt caching is central to how we run Moby cost-effectively at scale, and we’ve kept it while running billing and access through Google Cloud.”

Maksim Gorev, Head of AI Engineering

What’s included

Google Cloud customers using the Anthropic managed offering get the full set of Claude Platform features, so they can:

Build and deploy agents with:

  • Claude Managed Agents (beta) (opens in new tab) to power long-running agents, without managing infrastructure
  • Code execution (opens in new tab) to run Python code, create visualizations, and analyze data within an API call
  • Computer use (opens in new tab) to allow Claude to operate a browser or desktop to complete tasks
  • Agent skills (opens in new tab) to teach Claude repeatable workflows so it delivers consistent results
  • Advisor strategy (beta) (opens in new tab) to give agents an intelligence boost by consulting an advisor model

Connect to systems and knowledge with:

  • Files API (opens in new tab) for uploading and referencing documents across conversations
  • Citations (opens in new tab) for grounding responses in source documents
  • Web search (opens in new tab) and web fetch (opens in new tab) to augment Claude’s knowledge with current, real-world data from across the web
  • MCP connector (beta) (opens in new tab) to connect Claude to other tools without writing client code

Manage cost and performance with:

  • Prompt caching (opens in new tab) for reducing costs and latency on repeated context
  • Batch processing (opens in new tab) for high-volume, asynchronous workloads

Fast Mode on Claude Opus 5.5 is also generally available for customers using Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed). Fast mode prioritizes speed, offering up to 2.5x faster output token generation, for rapid iteration, live debugging, and interactive agents where output speed results in a better user experience. Input and output tokens are $8 and $40 per million.

See the full list of features available on Claude Models on Google Cloud in our documentation (opens in new tab).

Customers using the Anthropic managed offering also get access to the Claude Console, Anthropic’s development environment for observing and managing agents with Claude. The Console includes tools to write prompts and configure agents, run them on hosted environments, monitor usage and costs, and manage access and security per workspace.

Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are available, with new models shipping on the Anthropic managed offering as they launch.

Two paths to build with Claude

There are two ways to build with Claude on Google Cloud.

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) is built for customers who want day zero access to all beta and generally available Claude Platform features. It’s best for customers who want full Claude Platform feature parity, accessed through Google Cloud. Anthropic operates the service and acts as the data processor.

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed) remains the best choice for customers who need Google Cloud as the data processor, have strict regional data residency requirements, or want native Google Cloud integrations like Model Armor or Agent Engine.

Get started

The Anthropic managed offering is generally available today. To get started, open Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) (opens in new tab) or explore the documentation (opens in new tab).

If you have an existing discount, please contact your Anthropic or Google Cloud account executive before getting started with the Anthropic managed offering, to ensure your discounts are applied correctly. Discounts cannot be applied retroactively to usage.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.

Agent interoperability through simplicity

A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.

Donating Agent Skills to AAIF

We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.

We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.

Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.

What comes next

We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s Discord to give feedback on proposed specification changes.

Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at agentskills.io and join the discussion on GitHub.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Open call for guest investigators in the life sciences
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re inviting members of the life sciences community to apply to work with us on special projects. We’re looking for proposals from principal investigators and their research groups at academic institutions, nonprofits, or government labs who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in causal human biology, structural and computational molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, drug discovery, and clinical science.

You can submit a proposal for a project here.

Over 8–12 weeks, guest investigators will work directly with Anthropic researchers on a problem of interest and produce the analyses, artifacts, and tools that will be most helpful for them in their work. Our team will run our models and harnesses at no cost to them.

We’ll work together to publish these outputs and open-source the accompanying data and code. Guest investigators retain the rights to their data at every step during their project. They will also have the rights to any independent follow-on research that might come out of our collaboration.

We’re looking for applicants who can clearly explain how they would benefit from direct collaboration with Anthropic’s researchers. Applicants should also make a reasonable case that their outputs (e.g., preliminary discoveries, answers to open questions, open-source datasets, or public resources) can be produced within the 8- to 12-week collaboration period. There may be an option for extension beyond the initial collaboration period for some projects.

We understand that the results for most open problems of interest will take much longer to validate, but we’re looking for proposals that can produce some preliminary evidence in a relatively short amount of time.

We aren’t asking for guest investigators to give us their data, either in the application or during the collaboration, and we’re requesting that applicants include only publicly available information in their application materials.

Applications will be open for approximately 14 days, and we’ll strive to notify selected participants by email approximately 14 days after applications close. We look forward to potentially expanding this effort in the future as we learn more about how we can best support the scientific community.

This program is one of several initiatives Anthropic is pursuing to invest more heavily in the life sciences and the broader scientific research community. Scientists who would like direct access to our most capable publicly available models for biology can apply to join our Life Sciences Verification Program. We’ve also continued to support researchers through our AI for Science initiative, which provides scientists with Claude credits to accelerate their progress toward making scientific discoveries.

item.title: [Cohere] Introducing Confidential Computing on Cohere Model Vault
item.content:encoded:
Oct 22, 2026

4 minute read

Introducing Confidential Computing on Cohere Model Vault

Now in public beta with NVIDIA Confidential Computing with NVIDIA GPUs on Microsoft Azure, bringing hardware-backed protection and verifiable security to sensitive enterprise AI.

Key takeaways

  • Protect data in use: Model Vault extends protection beyond data at rest and in transit to prompts, documents, responses, and model execution while inference is running.
  • Encrypt sensitive request contents end-to-end: Application payloads remain encrypted through intermediary infrastructure and can only be decrypted inside the attested confidential environment.
  • Verify before you trust: Customers can cryptographically verify the hardware and software environment before sensitive data leaves their infrastructure.
  • Use confidential AI as a managed service: Cohere operates the serving platform on Microsoft Azure infrastructure with NVIDIA H100 GPU Confidential Computing capabilities.
  • Start today in public beta: Customers can start deploying encrypted Model Vault workloads today.

Today, we are announcing the public beta of Confidential Computing on Cohere Model Vault, bringing hardware-backed protection and independently verifiable security to managed enterprise AI.

Model Vault gives enterprises dedicated, fully managed model inference. With Confidential Computing, we are extending that experience to some of an organization's most sensitive workloads and data, including financial information, clinical records, privileged documents, proprietary source code, and intellectual property.

The goal is simple: enterprises should be able to use the capabilities and operational simplicity of managed AI without giving the infrastructure that operates it access to their sensitive plaintext data.

Protecting data in use

Encryption traditionally protects data in two places: while it is stored and while it travels across a network.

Confidential Computing on Model Vault is designed to protect the third state: data in use.

Inference runs within a hardware-backed confidential environment spanning the CPU and GPU. Hardware-enforced isolation protects workload memory from everything outside the confidential boundary, including privileged infrastructure software and operators. With NVIDIA Confidential Computing, GPU memory is protected and traffic between the CPU and GPU is encrypted as the model performs inference.

This enables enterprises to bring more sensitive workloads to AI while reducing the number of parties and systems they need to trust with their data.

**Verify before you trust

**

Protection alone is not enough. Enterprises also need a way to know that those protections are actually in place.

That is why remote attestation is a core part of Confidential Computing on Model Vault.

Before sensitive data is sent, customer-side software verifies cryptographically signed evidence about the environment that will process it, including its hardware, firmware, and software configuration. That evidence is checked against an approved security policy.

If the environment does not satisfy the policy, the client refuses to send the request.

This changes the trust model from "trust us" to "verify it yourself."

“Enterprises should not have to choose between the simplicity of managed AI and control over their most sensitive information. With Model Vault and Confidential Computing, customers can verify the environment that will process their data before they send it. With hardware attestation, customers not only have cryptographic proof that workloads are running in a secure, confidential computing environment, they also can verify that their data is protected from unauthorized access, even from Cohere.”- Phil Blunsom, CTO at Cohere

End-to-end protection for sensitive request contents

Confidential Computing protects what happens inside the compute environment. Model Vault also protects sensitive request contents on their way there.

Rather than relying only on connection-level encryption, Model Vault encrypts application payloads end-to-end to the attested confidential environment. The encrypted request can pass through intermediary infrastructure without exposing its contents, and only the confidential environment can decrypt it. Responses are protected on the return path as well.

This preserves the operational advantages of a managed AI platform without exposing the plaintext contents of customer requests to intermediary infrastructure.

Customers continue to use the Model Vault API and familiar request formats. The additional protection is built into the client and infrastructure layers rather than requiring applications to redesign their payloads.

Built with Microsoft Azure and NVIDIA

The public beta is powered by NVIDIA H100 GPUs on Microsoft Azure.

Microsoft Azure provides the underlying confidential computing infrastructure.and NVIDIA Confidential Computing extends those capabilities to the NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Cohere brings these technologies together through Model Vault's managed model serving, encrypted request path, remote attestation, and customer-side verification.

The result is a managed AI platform that combines the operational simplicity of cloud AI with stronger technical control over access to sensitive data during inference.

“Enterprises need confidence that their most sensitive AI workloads are protected by more than contractual promises. Our work with Cohere on Model Vault demonstrates how confidential computing can combine the simplicity of managed AI with independently verifiable technical controls.”- Vikas Bhatia, Head of Product, Azure Confidential Computing at Microsoft
“Confidential Computing opens new possibilities for enterprises that need to run AI on highly sensitive data. NVIDIA Confidential Computing on NVIDIA GPUs provides hardware-backed protections that help platforms like Cohere Model Vault bring confidential AI inference to enterprise workloads.”- John Fanelli, vice president, Enterprise Software at NVIDIA

Unlocking AI for sensitive enterprise workloads

For many organizations, the question is no longer whether AI can perform a task. The question is whether the data required for that task can safely be used with AI at all.

Confidential Computing on Model Vault is designed to protect workloads where security, contractual, or regulatory requirements may have kept valuable data outside managed AI platforms, including:

  • Fraud investigations in financial services
  • Privileged document search and due diligence in legal services
  • Sensitive public-sector information
  • Patent and research material
  • Proprietary engineering design documents (EDD), Interface design documents (IDD) and architecture materials
  • Search and analysis across proprietary source code

These are the kinds of workloads where reducing privileged infrastructure access and giving customers independently verifiable evidence can make previously restricted AI use cases practical.

Confidential computing does not eliminate all risk, nor does it replace application security, compliance, contractual controls, or data-residency requirements. It provides a hardware-enforced and verifiable protection boundary around data and computation while inference is taking place.

Available now in public beta

Confidential Computing on Cohere Model Vault is now available in public beta, powered by NVIDIA H100 GPUs on Microsoft Azure.

Customers can create and manage encrypted vaults through Model Vault and integrate them using the same Cohere APIs, with customer-side verification and end-to-end encryption protecting sensitive request contents before they leave the customer's environment.

For a deeper look at the confidential compute architecture, encrypted request path, remote attestation, trust boundary, and threat model, read Inside Cohere Model Vault: Building Verifiable Confidential AI Inference.

Get started at vault.cohere.com

item.title: [Cohere] Can AI understand culture?
item.content:encoded:
Oct 22, 2026

5 minute read

Can AI understand culture?

A retired teacher and high schooler put AI to the test

Consider this age-old riddle: “What kind of house do you enter blind and leave seeing?” While English speakers may instantly recognize the answer as “a school,” AI models can struggle with the same riddle if asked in another language. A Cohere Labs open science project revealed the complex nature of interpretation, and the results were surprising.

The word "riddle" comes from the Old English "rædan" which means "to interpret" or "to advise,” suggesting that riddles are about interpretation and insight rather than just guessing. Riddles thrive on ambiguity but have specific solutions. Just as humans get better at riddles through practice and feedback, AI improves its abilities through machine learning.

“We could not believe our eyes… It is not ‘just’ research anymore, it IS a movement.”- Boczka Károly

Hungarian diplomat Boczka Károly was actively exploring opportunities in AI research. When he decided to build tricky, Hungarian trivia-style riddles to test if AI models recognized cultural clues, he received stunning results. The models’ answers sounded right, but they weren't right. The models were missing culturally specific facts, and in certain instances, were hallucinating. In an open-science community discussion around culture in AI hosted by Cohere Labs, Boczka shared his findings with Julia Kreutzer. Kreutzer, the Staff Research Scientist at Cohere Labs, saw immediate potential to test the gap between AI fluency and cultural knowledge. Together, they globally scaled a project to test the fluency, logic, and reasoning within models trained mostly on English data and the blind spots behind each answer.

Participation in the project did not require expertise beyond identification with a culture and a commitment to writing and evaluating riddles, which opened the door for research participants of any age and background. An open call on social media and within the Cohere Labs existing research communities invited people to join the project with no entry criteria, deliberately removing barriers that typically restrict participation. The community gathered on Discord and built its own benchmarks across cultural segments like sports, history, and politics, with each question designed as a riddle.

Mr. Boczka's idea quickly grew into an international initiative. “We could not believe our eyes,” he says. “We had more than 100 contributors from more than 50 countries. It is not “just” research anymore, it IS a movement.” He continues, “Our collective was so dedicated, independent, and cooperative that the whole project grew like a well-planted plant.” Two contributing members within that well-rooted community were 15-year-old American Henry Gagnier and Canadian retired schoolteacher Jane Smith.

While most teenagers might be hesitant to join a global research team of this magnitude, Henry Gagnier’s infectious enthusiasm outweighed any preconceived notion of what a “typical” research team member should be. “I'd say that AI research is for everybody. There are so many different aspects of AI research. We needed people from many different cultures, and it's not ‘AI skills’ that are helpful for building this benchmark, it is real cultural knowledge.” When asked if he was intimidated or surprised by the group, he says, “What surprised me most was their inclusivity and openness, because I was always kind of intimidated as a high school student, joining this project and saying I want to be a lead for this team. But everyone was so nice. It was an amazing experience.”

This project, while grounded in cultural and semantic nuance, provided him with more insight into research and a possible future within it. “It gave me a nice sneak peek into what actual researchers are doing,” Gagnier says. “I want to continue research in this field. I'm doing some projects to further my knowledge in this field now, so I think this project is a good educational experience, and it's definitely changed my outlook on where I want to go in the future.”

As a retired teacher, Jane Smith took what she calls a “teacher approach” to her research. “When I would evaluate kids if they got something wrong, I always tried to back think it, like okay, ‘Where did it go wrong?’ ‘What led to this completely wrong answer?’ There must have been something that led them there, and so I found myself doing that a lot of the time with the evaluating.” She also tried to anthropomorphize her process by incorporating things like tigers or crabs within her riddles to gamify the logic as a powerful teaching tool.

Each solved riddle or generated puzzle became a data point that refined the project’s understanding of language and logic. What made the riddles project particularly meaningful was that it wasn’t just about entertainment, but it demonstrated interpretive capabilities that define both riddles and AI.

AI’s struggle with cultural riddles across different languages and contexts is potentially one of the most significant challenges in developing models. “I was kind of surprised because it wasn't just a lack of cultural understanding,” Gagnier says. “These models don't know this language at all, and I think Buginese is a fairly frequently spoken language. I'm surprised that these models still had virtually zero knowledge of the language, and that translated to zero knowledge of the culture as well with how we were evaluating it.”

The project underlines that intelligence isn't just about solving puzzles, but about understanding the human experience and languages behind them. The etymology of "rædan" (to interpret) takes on new depth when we consider that interpretation must be culturally grounded to be meaningful.

Mrs. Smith reveals a widely shared societal concern regarding AI cultural model accuracy. “I was surprised at how few times the models answered, "’I don't know’. But instead, it gives these quite authoritative sounding [answers] which would lead one to think, ‘Oh, this thing knows what it's talking about’.”

What the team found unsettling were finite conclusions from models that sounded unwaveringly confident despite wrong answers. Recognizing this blind spot, Mrs. Smith says, “The scary part to me is that it sounds so authoritative and people are looking for authoritative answers.” She adds, “I don't think it's AI that's going to kill us. It’s our lack of critical thinking that's going to kill us.”

In an age where some worry that the human elements of daily life are quickly disappearing, the riddles research pushes for a rethink surrounding any resolution that lacks a human touch. In her wisdom, Mrs. Smith poses what may seem like an amusing play on words, but what just might be the decisive outlook on an AI cultural conundrum: “To err is AI. To critically think is human.”

There is an interesting space between human cognition and AI’s thinking. Cohere Labs is working on better contextual understanding by delving into confidence in today’s models. The riddles demonstrate that as AI grows more confident in its answers, we must remember that critical thinking keeps us human.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agen…
item.description: Full title: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

Enterprise Article

Published October 22, 2026

-

Tuhin Kundu

tuhink

microsoft

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Mirco Milletari and Xiang Jiang from Microsoft, Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former intern Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

What happened after training

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

MetricBaseRL fine-tunedChange
Observed 20/2038 (7.50%)→107 (21.10%)+69 tasks
pass@1 (successful attempts)5,242 (51.70%)→6,163 (60.78%)+9.08 pt
pass@20 (tasks solved at least once)453 (89.35%)→446 (87.97%)−7 tasks

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

Contents

  • What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds
  • Results: the dependability column moved
  • Where the gains landed
  • What dependability costs
  • The training loop
  • Offline policy-relative difficulty
  • What earns a reward
  • Run the training stack
  • Where this goes next

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

Results: the dependability column moved

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

ModelRetailAuto insuranceTravelNeobankConsultingOverallObserved 20/20
Claude Opus 5.580.9768.4054.2871.2561.5867.16241 (47.53%)
Claude Opus 580.7165.8049.9570.6266.1966.50241 (47.53%)
GPT-5.476.3362.6568.1265.3454.6065.36128 (25.25%)
GPT-5.6 Sol67.6565.3060.3459.0957.5261.9182 (16.17%)
Qwen3.8-27B RLFT67.9156.4562.6962.4054.5160.78107 (21.10%)
Claude Sonnet 4.672.3554.4058.9456.3954.3159.19102 (20.12%)
GPT-6 Astra71.7346.5555.8760.8756.8358.31231 (45.56%)
Kimi-K382.2450.8061.8341.3551.6357.3768 (13.41%)
Qwen3.8-27B64.0347.8553.4147.8845.6951.7038 (7.50%)

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Where the gains landed

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

What dependability costs

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

MeasureBaseRL fine-tunedChange
Campaign cost, 20 runs$925.80→$855.58−7.6%
Cost per successful attempt$0.177→$0.139−21.4%
Tasks passing 20/2038→1072.8× as many
Cost per dependable task$24.36→$8.00−67.2%

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

The single-attempt view

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

The training loop

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Offline policy-relative difficulty

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Estimating difficulty from limited probes

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:

  • Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop
  • Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep
  • Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep
  • Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT
  • Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

One task, end to end

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

What earns a reward

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict
Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed.
Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test.

Run the training stack

We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:

  • docs/data-preparation.md for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting;
  • docs/reference-q38-run.md for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration;
  • docs/evaluation.md for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20.

Before you start

Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

Install

Keep the three repositories side by side:

mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace
cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace

git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git
git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training

git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1
git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0

Create the validated environment

The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:

cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training

uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy
uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox
uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \
  -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools
uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \
  -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606

python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install
python scripts/verify_verl_install.py
uv pip check

The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.

Prepare the training data

Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:

cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training
source .venv/bin/activate
python data/prepare_data.py --help

The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.

Configure and inspect the launch

Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history.

Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command:

DRY_RUN=true ./scripts/run_train.sh \
  trainer.total_training_steps=50 \
  trainer.save_freq=5

It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run.

Train

The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray:

# head node
ROLE=head NODE_IP="$HEAD_IP" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \
  ./scripts/start_ray.sh

# each worker node
ROLE=worker NODE_IP="$WORKER_IP" \
  HEAD_ADDRESS="$HEAD_IP:6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \
  ./scripts/start_ray.sh

After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node:

export RAY_ADDRESS=auto
export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7

./scripts/run_train.sh \
  trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \
  trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \
  trainer.total_training_steps=50 \
  trainer.save_freq=5

Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv

The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md, then serve it with vLLM.

From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration:

vllm serve "$MERGED_MODEL" \
  --served-model-name q38-rlft \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8001 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --max-num-seqs 16 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --language-model-only \
  --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml

In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001:

cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training
source .venv/bin/activate
bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh

Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness:

curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz

Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration:

orchestrator:
  agent_model:
    type: aoai
    endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions
    deployment: q38-rlft
    credential:
      type: api-key
      api_key: <your_api_key>
    is_reasoning: true
    temperature: 1.0
    top_k: 20
    top_p: 0.95
    max_completion_tokens: 8192
    timeout: 1800

Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA. Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:

uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen \
  thinkingbox-eval \
  --config "$PWD/thinkingbox.yaml" \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  --dataset "$THINKINGBOX_DATA" \
  --output q38-rlft-full.jsonl \
  --errors-output q38-rlft-full-errors.jsonl \
  --repeat 20 \
  --coverage-profile full \
  --aggregate-output q38-rlft-full-aggregate.json \
  --message-timeout 1800

The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation.

Where this goes next

The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.

If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records:

  • Probe before you train. Take your own agent task set, run the base policy against it n times, and look at the band histogram. In our experience teams often have not inspected this distribution, and it is usually more lopsided than expected.
  • Check your parity. Replay the same recorded model output through the training and evaluation parsers, and verify that both extract identical tool names and arguments. Otherwise, training may reward behavior that evaluation interprets differently.
  • Report both coverage and repeatability. State how many tasks pass at least once in k attempts and how many pass all k. A model that occasionally finds a solution is not necessarily one that repeats it consistently.

Further details can be found in the following links:

  • Environment: envs/thinkingbox_env
  • OpenEnv: ThinkingBox environment documentation
  • Framework: microsoft/thinkingbox · tutorial
  • Benchmark: microsoft/thinkingbox-data · v1.0 release
  • Dataset viewer: microsoft/ThinkingBox-Bench
  • Paper: arXiv:2608.19741 or HF
  • RL training: microsoft/thinkingbox-training
  • Blog: The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

Cite the paper

@article{li2026thinkingbox,
  title   = {One Success Isn't Reliability: Thinkingbox, a Sandbox and Benchmark for Agents in Stateful Business Workflows},
  author  = {Li, Zhuochun and Ko, Youngmin and Keramati, Ali and Kundu, Tuhin and
             Tsai, Liang-Chun and Ferri, Nicola and Milletari, Mirco and Liu, Jiaxiang and
             Lopez Pelaez, Susana Palmaz and Wang, Yuepeng and Smolyakov, Vadim and
             Jiang, Xiang and Olafsson, Kjartan and Guy, Tommy},
  journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2608.19741},
  year    = {2026},
  url     = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19741}
}

ThinkingBox code is MIT-licensed; the benchmark data is CDLA-Permissive-2.0.

Disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real enterprise agent patterns; the customers are not real.

ThinkingBox, ThinkingBox-Bench and ThinkingBox-Training is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com.

  • A minority of tasks also include narrow binary rubric requirements for outcomes that the database cannot capture cleanly; those checks can invoke the configured LLM judge.

++ That zero-gradient problem has a standard batch-time fix: oversample, discard the degenerate groups, refill. The full-parameter run did exactly that, similar to DAPO with replacement of zero-variance groups. But refilling still pays full price for every wasted rollout before throwing it away.
