item.description: Full title: Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI

A traffic spike hits your self-hosted text-to-speech (TTS) endpoint, and requests start queueing. Latency climbs past your service level objective (SLO) right when the most callers are listening. The auto scaling policy behind that endpoint was supposed to prevent this, but the target value it scales on was a guess, and guesses like that fail silently until real traffic proves them wrong.

Get that number wrong, and it’s paid for in one of two ways, and neither shows up as an alarm. Guess too conservative, and the fleet runs GPU instances that sit mostly idle. That cost lands on every invoice but never trips an incident report. Guess too aggressive, and the fleet carries a risk nobody sees. Each instance holds more concurrent requests than it can serve inside its latency promise. Nothing looks wrong until a real traffic spike pushes queueing time past the SLO. That happens right when the most callers are listening. That’s the hidden gap. A policy that looks fine on the console can already be failing the people it’s supposed to serve.

In this post, we deploy Kokoro-82M, an 82-million-parameter TTS model, as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) stacks handle the deployment. We replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint. Q_max is the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and T_total is how long a scale-out takes end to end. We derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Every number in this post comes from an actual deployment and measurement run of the aws-samples repository referenced in this post.

Why default auto scaling metrics don’t work for TTS

Most public guidance on Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling targets short synchronous request/response calls, or large language model (LLM) serving, where the natural metric is tokens generated per second. TTS synthesis fits neither pattern: a single request holds a connection open for several seconds with no token-generation loop to attach a metric to. Kokoro-82M is non-autoregressive, a StyleTTS2 derivative with an ISTFTNet decoder, trained adversarially rather than by autoregressive next-token prediction or iterative denoising. It produces a full utterance from one duration-aligned pass. There’s no generation loop to instrument with a per-token metric in the first place. What determines whether a TTS instance is overloaded is simpler than it sounds: how many requests are queued and executing on it right now.

The deployed policy scales on ConcurrentRequestsPerModel, a native metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes itself rather than one this project’s own container code has to emit. Scaling on a metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes removes an entire class of failure where a custom metric configuration looks correct on paper but nothing is actually publishing to it.

ConcurrentRequestsPerModel publishes a Maximum statistic over a 10-second window, a different quantity from the mean in-flight count a benchmarking client measures directly. The tooling accounts for this. At every rung of the concurrency ladder it measures both quantities against the same load and records the ratio between them. It then uses that ratio to convert the client-measured threshold into Amazon CloudWatch units before writing it into the deployable configuration. For the Kokoro-82M run in this post, the measured ratio came out to exactly 1.0 at every rung, so the client-measured and Amazon CloudWatch-reported thresholds match directly.

Solution overview

This solution deploys Kokoro-82M in a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, then replaces a guessed auto scaling target with one derived from two measurements taken against that live endpoint: Q_max, the concurrency ceiling one instance serves inside the SLO, and T_total, how long a real scale-out takes. A synthesis request flows through four layers: a client, the Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint, a custom container on a GPU instance behind that endpoint, and the Kokoro-82M model inside the container.

Figure 1: The Kokoro-82M request path, from client through the Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint and custom container to the model

The container supports two wire transports: response streaming (InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream), which streams audio back as it’s synthesized so playback starts before the utterance finishes, and bidirectional streaming (InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream), which holds one long-lived session open for multiple messages.

Running Kokoro-82M in a custom container, rather than behind a managed inference toolkit, is what makes the rest of this post possible. A container you control can enforce its own admission limits and expose the exact concurrency signal Amazon SageMaker AI already publishes, instead of retrofitting a borrowed metric onto a workload it wasn’t built for. The AWS CDK stacks that deploy this endpoint only attach auto scaling resources once a real, measured plan exists for the model, so a guessed configuration can never reach production silently. The rest of this post is that measurement.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need:

  • An AWS account with permissions to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories, and Amazon SageMaker AI resources. Note: the sample container pins an earlier PyTorch with a known advisory (PYSEC-2026-2286, fixed in torch 2.10.0). Review and upgrade the pin before any non-proof-of-value use.
  • AWS CDK v2, installed and bootstrapped in your target account and region.
  • Python 3.11 or later, uv, and Docker to build the container image.
  • A ml.g5.xlarge service quota with at least one spare slot above your baseline before running the scale-out measurement in this post.
  • The deployment code from the GitHub repository referenced in this post.

Walkthrough

By the end of this walkthrough, you will have a live Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling policy for Kokoro-82M, derived entirely from two measurements taken against your own endpoint rather than from a guess.

Deploy the endpoint stacks

The endpoint deploys through three AWS CDK stacks, applied in order: SpeechFoundationStack creates the IAM roles and the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights, SpeechModelCacheStack syncs a model’s Hugging Face weights into that bucket once, and SpeechEndpointStack builds the container image, pushes it to Amazon ECR, and creates the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint.

Figure 2: The three AWS CDK stacks and the gate that decides whether auto scaling resources get synthesized

The gate on the third stack keeps a default, unmeasured scaling configuration from reaching production. scaling_enabled is a static flag, true whenever max_instances is configured greater than min_instances, and it says nothing on its own about whether the numbers behind it were ever measured. The stack adds a second, independent check at synthesis time: does a real, feasible plan artifact exist for this model? Only when both conditions hold does the stack synthesize scaling resources: an EndpointAutoscaling construct that wires the scaling policy and alarms, and an EndpointObservability construct that adds the dashboards and alarms used to monitor it. A model with scaling_enabled=True but no measurement behind it gets the same no scaling resources output as one with scaling_enabled=False.

The project’s CLI wraps the three stacks behind a single command, applying them in dependency order:

uv run speech-infra deploy kokoro-82m

SpeechModelCacheStack runs an AWS CodeBuild project that syncs the model’s Hugging Face weights into the cached Amazon S3 bucket once. A cold endpoint start doesn’t need to pull them from the internet. Gated by the preceding scaling_enabled check, SpeechEndpointStack builds the container image, pushes it to Amazon ECR, and creates the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint.

The methodology packages as a command-line tool chain, run in a fixed order:

Figure 3: The tool chain, run in order, each command handing an artifact to the next

Step 1: Check for drift

drift runs first, every time, before anything that costs money or holds an endpoint under load. It’s a read-only reconciliation between what’s actually deployed (scalable targets, scaling policies, alarm states) and what the config file says should be deployed. An orphaned policy from an earlier model, or a stopped or canceled qmax or ttotal run, would otherwise silently move capacity mid-measurement and corrupt the numbers being measured.

uv run tts-bench drift

A clean result reports no mismatches and exits with a preflight-ok status, clearing the way for qmax. A stopped or canceled qmax or ttotal run is the most common source of a reported mismatch, because it can leave auto scaling frozen on a single instance. uv run tts-bench thaw --endpoint speech-kokoro-82m restores the deployed policy before you proceed, since qmax and ttotal both assume the deployed state matches the config file exactly.

Step 2: Measure Q_max, the concurrency ceiling

Q_max is the largest concurrency, requests queued plus requests executing on one instance, at which a request still reaches first audio byte inside the SLO at the 95th percentile. It’s measured with a closed-loop load ladder: hold a fixed concurrency N exactly, and walk N upward one rung at a time until the SLO breaks. A closed loop avoids coordinated omission, the flaw in fixed-arrival-rate tests where a slowing server makes the client send fewer requests instead of surfacing real queueing delay.

uv run tts-bench qmax --model kokoro-82m --dry-run
uv run tts-bench qmax --model kokoro-82m

--dry-run prints the schedule and a wall-clock estimate with zero AWS calls, so you can budget the roughly 36-minute cost of a live run first. The live command freezes auto scaling and pins capacity to one instance for the duration, restored automatically on exit, so the number it produces is a genuine per-instance ceiling.

The load ladder recorded the following results:

Concurrencyp95 TTFAB (ms)Meets 3,000 ms SLO?
165.4yes
5286.2yes
10568.5yes
201,129.3yes
301,689.8yes
402,245.0yes
502,805.7yes (Q_max)
603,374.8no (breach)

Figure 4: p95 time-to-first-audio-byte against concurrency, with the SLO line and the breach point at concurrency 60

Q_max = 50, and it’s a bracketed result: rung 60 actually crossed the SLO, which makes 50 a real ceiling rather than a lower bound. The same run measured the uncontended service time, the time one request takes with no queueing at all: mean 61.3 ms, p95 66.1 ms. That number drives a second, independent alarm described later in this post.

Step 3: Measure T_total, the real scale-out time

T_total is how long it takes, wall clock, from the moment more capacity is requested to the moment that capacity serves healthy traffic. It’s measured by forcing a scale-out directly, bypassing the deployed policy’s own detection logic, then timestamping every distinguishable stage.

uv run tts-bench ttotal --model kokoro-82m --qmax <qmax-artifact>

ttotal requires the qmax artifact as input, since its recovery judgment reads off that ladder’s own measured rungs, and refuses to run against a ladder measured on a different wire transport.

The forced scale-out broke down into eight measured stages:

StageDurationShare of T_total
capacity requested to desired_set30.0 s9.4%
desired_set to instance visible in logs180.8 s56.5% (dominant)
instance visible to container started3.7 s1.2%
container started to framework_init0.0 s0.0%
framework_init to weights_ready6.5 s2.0%
weights_ready to warmup_done1.0 s0.3%
warmup_done to in_service20.7 s6.5%
in_service to traffic recovered47.4 s14.8%
measured total (t_total_s)260.2 s
+ policy detection lag, bounded (not measured)60.0 s
T_total, planned against320.2 s

Figure 5: The eight measured stages of a real scale-out, from capacity request to recovered traffic

The dominant stage is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance provisioning plus the container image pull, at 181 seconds, 56 percent of the planned-against total. The highest-impact way to reduce T_total isn’t application code, it’s reducing image size or using warm capacity pools. Everything downstream of “instance visible in logs” is a comparatively small 79 seconds combined.

The 60-second addition on top of the measured 260.2 seconds isn’t measured in this run. It’s bounded from the policy’s own configuration (alarm evaluation period times evaluation periods, plus cooldown), because this run bypassed the policy’s detection logic on purpose to isolate pure provisioning time. plan sizes surge headroom against the full 320.2-second total, because that reaction time is a real part of any production scale-out even though this measurement excluded it.

Step 4: Derive the deployed policy with plan

plan is the only command that never touches AWS. It reads the qmax and ttotal artifacts, combines them with two operator-chosen inputs, an SLO of 3,000 ms p95 TTFAB and a surge ratio of 1.25x (the fleet tolerates traffic growing 25 percent within one scale-out cycle without breaching the SLO), and does the following arithmetic. It then prints a report with a verdict for each finding: ok, warn, or, for a genuinely infeasible plan, stop.

uv run tts-bench plan --qmax <qmax-artifact> --ttotal <ttotal-artifact> --peak-rps 5000

The --peak-rps flag (5,000 requests per second here, alongside an assumed trough of 10) sizes the fleet’s instance count. It doesn’t factor into the threshold arithmetic below.

h  = surge_ratio - 1                    = 1.25 - 1 = 0.25

C_scale_max = (1 - h)     x Q_max       = 0.75 x 50   = 37.50
C_scale_min = (1 - 2h)    x Q_max       = 0.50 x 50   = 25.00

W_max = SLO - S_p95                     = 3.000s - 0.066s = 2.934s

C_scale_max is the concurrency at which one more instance is added, below Q_max by the surge fraction h, so the fleet still has queue headroom when it asks for more capacity. C_scale_min is the concurrency at or below which one instance is removed, set at (1 - 2h) of Q_max so scale-in triggers only once load has fallen well below where scale-out would trigger again.

The final deployed configuration, exactly as produced by the tooling:

"kokoro-82m": ModelEndpointConfig(
    model_name="kokoro-82m",
    instance_type="ml.g5.xlarge",
    min_instances=1,             # trough 10 rps; 3 is the smallest safe floor for scale-in
    max_instances=9,             # peak 5000 rps
    scaling_target_value=37.500, # C_scale_max, in Amazon CloudWatch units (ratio measured as 1.0)
    scale_in_threshold=25.000,   # C_scale_min, in Amazon CloudWatch units
    ttfab_slo_ms=3000,
    queue_max_depth=50,          # enforced by the container's own admission gate
    scale_out_cooldown_s=30,     # short: one instance added at a time
    scale_in_cooldown_s=960,     # long: see below
)

The two cooldowns are asymmetric on purpose. Scaling out is cheap to be wrong about: worst case, you paid for one instance you didn’t need for thirty extra seconds. Scaling in isn’t symmetric in cost, since capacity removed and later needed again costs a full T_total (320 seconds) to replace. The scale-in cooldown is set to roughly three times T_total, so a scale-in decision only fires once load has genuinely, sustainedly dropped.

The container’s own admission control separately enforces queue_max_depth=50, equal to Q_max: past that depth, a request is refused immediately with a 503 queue_saturated response rather than left to queue past the point it could meet the SLO. A FirstChunkLatencyP95 alarm, thresholded at 65 ms (the measured p95 service time at concurrency 1), watches service time on an instance already serving, tighter than the end-to-end SLO, which includes queuing.

Two findings from the Kokoro-82M run are worth including, because they’re the tool correctly surfacing a known, accepted trade-off rather than a defect:

  • surge_survival (warn): Holding C_scale_max (37.5) against Q_max (50) puts one instance at 97.4% utilization the moment a scale-out triggers, and a replacement takes a full T_total to arrive. The surge ratio reserves extra queue slots, but surviving a real surge is about flow, how fast the queue drains, and there’s little flow headroom left at 97.4 percent utilization.
  • scale_in_safety (warn): Removing one instance from a fleet of N multiplies every remaining instance’s concurrency by N / (N-1). Scale-in stays stable only once that ratio holds under C_scale_max / C_scale_min (1.5 here), which requires N >= 3. With a floor of 1 instance, a scale-in from 2 to 1 lands the survivor at exactly Q_max, right back at the ceiling that triggers another scale-out. The long cooldown damps this flapping without eliminating it. Raising the floor to 3 would remove it structurally, at the cost of standing capacity during low traffic.

Every qmax or ttotal artifact’s file name encodes the configuration it was measured against, instance type and container image digest condensed into a slug (for example, g5xlarge-8b1b96bc). ttotal and plan both refuse to pair artifacts whose fingerprints disagree. That’s downgradable to a warning with --allow-config-mismatch, but refusal is the default.

Step 5: Confirm the deployed policy with validate

validate is the last command in the chain, and the second one, alongside drift, that never mutates anything. It compares the scaling policy actually deployed against the values in the plan artifact, confirming the two match before you treat the configuration as live.

uv run tts-bench validate --model kokoro-82m --plan <plan-artifact>

A clean result confirms scaling_target_value, scale_in_threshold, and both cooldowns on the deployed scalable target match what plan derived. Any mismatch means the deployed policy and the measured plan have drifted apart, and should be resolved before relying on the endpoint’s auto scaling behavior.

Testing and validation

Every qmax, ttotal, and plan artifact referenced in this post is a committed file in the repository, not a one-off local output. The preceding worked example, including every number, is independently reproducible by re-running plan against the two committed measurement files, with zero AWS calls and zero new spend:

$ uv run tts-bench plan --qmax <qmax-artifact> --ttotal <ttotal-artifact> --peak-rps 5000
scaling_target_value : 37.500 (C_scale_max)
scale_in_threshold    : 25.000 (C_scale_min)
surge_survival        : warn
scale_in_safety       : warn

Clean up

To remove the resources created in this walkthrough, tear down the stacks in reverse order with a single command:

uv run speech-infra destroy kokoro-82m

speech-infra destroy removes the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, endpoint, and any auto scaling or Amazon CloudWatch resources attached to it. It doesn’t empty the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights or delete the Amazon ECR repository holding the container image, since both can be shared across models. If you no longer need them, empty and delete the Amazon S3 bucket and remove the Amazon ECR repository manually, since a stored model checkpoint and container image continue to incur small storage charges until removed.

Conclusion

Deploy Kokoro-82M as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, and replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint: Q_max, the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and T_total, how long a real scale-out takes. You derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Scaling on ConcurrentRequestsPerModel, a native, AWS-published metric, and measuring its unit conversion directly rather than assuming it, is what keeps this configuration tied to real concurrency.

The result is an auto scaling policy where every number traces back to a real measurement against your own endpoint, not an assumption carried over from a different workload shape. That distinction is what turns a config-file guess, one that silently overpays or silently breaches its SLO, into a policy you can defend with a specific concurrency ceiling and a specific scale-out time, both measured, not asserted.

Nothing about this four-number model, SLO and surge ratio chosen, Q_max and T_total measured, the rest derived, is specific to TTS. It generalizes to latency-sensitive, concurrency-bound, real-time Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints. For example, a real-time image-embedding endpoint that holds each request open through a GPU forward pass is bound by the same concurrency ceiling, not by a throughput metric. The same qmax/ttotal/plan chain applies unchanged. The real bottleneck there is concurrent in-flight requests rather than a throughput metric borrowed from a different workload shape. The specific numbers here, Q_max=50 and T_total=320s, are true for Kokoro-82M on ml.g5.xlarge. They will differ for a different model or instance type. The methodology and tooling that produce them don’t. The five-command tool chain, drift, qmax, ttotal, plan, and validate, carries over unchanged to the next model you deploy this way.

Clone the sample repository, then run the five-command chain, drift, qmax, ttotal, plan, and validate, against your own endpoint to produce a measured policy. Review the Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling documentation to adapt the thresholds to your SLO, and open the SageMaker AI console to watch the policy react to live traffic. If you’d like help building a similar measurement-driven deployment, contact your AWS account team.

About the author

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and…
item.description: Full title: How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and AI-DLC
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and AI-DLC

Every engineering team knows the ritual, and Rescale was no exception. A nightly test suite fails. An on-call engineer pulls the logs, classifies the root cause, and routes it to the right team, only to repeat the process the next morning. At scale, across distributed services and dozens of repositories, this ritual becomes a full-time job hiding inside an on-call rotation.

Rescale is the digital engineering platform built for the AI era. R&D and engineering teams across aerospace, automotive, energy, life sciences, semiconductor, and manufacturing use the Rescale platform to accelerate innovation, bringing intelligent HPC, advanced modeling and simulation, agentic digital engineering, and AI physics together on a single platform.

Beyond coding, Rescale uses AI across the engineering lifecycle, from planning and design through implementation, testing, review, and operations, while keeping engineers accountable for the result. AI can propose and execute, but people define scope, validate the work, and approve production changes. Engineers can then focus on architecture, product judgment, and the context required to operate complex distributed systems.

In this post, we show how Rescale used the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) framework on AWS to build an intelligent triage agent. They went from problem definition to staging deployment in five days, and to production within weeks. The post also covers how Rescale is extending AI-DLC across their engineering organization.

The challenge

As Rescale’s platform grew, so did the operational overhead of keeping it running. Engineers were spending significant time on a repetitive but critical task: classifying automated end-to-end test failures. Hundreds of test cases run in the suite, and when failures appeared, every alert, bug report, and escalation needed to be classified, prioritized, and routed to the right team. After routing, engineers would need to gather evidence from multiple logging and monitoring systems, along with several source repositories before debugging could even begin. Passing end-to-end tests were required to deploy services to production and thus debugging these system failures was in the critical path to getting new changes to production.

In the manual workflow, engineers moved from the test report to logs, historical patterns, and source code to classify failures and identify the likely owning team. Because these integration tests gate weekly production releases, unresolved failures could pull several teams into hours of coordination before a deployment was allowed to proceed.

The team had a clear idea of what a solution looked like: an intelligent agent that could classify and route issues automatically. What they were looking for was a structured way to go from that understanding to a working system in production, with enough structure to extend the approach to other use cases afterward.

Why Rescale chose AI-DLC

Rescale’s triage agent was a well-scoped problem with a tight timeline. The team needed a development approach that could move at that pace without skipping the architectural decisions that would determine whether the system worked in production.

The AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) is an open source, AI-centric methodology for software development built around two ideas:

  • AI executes, humans decide: AI generates work plans, writes code, and proposes architecture, but it surfaces decision points and asks clarifying questions rather than guessing. Humans validate and steer at each step.
  • Team sessions replace async handoffs: Instead of one person building alone and requesting review later, AI-DLC uses focused group sessions: Mob Elaboration (defining requirements together) and Mob Construction (building together while AI handles implementation). Decisions happen in real time.

AI-DLC fit because the hard part wasn’t writing code. It was making sure the AI understood what the team wanted to build. In mob sessions, Rescale engineers answered the AI’s questions together and approved each plan before the AI moved on, so nothing was left to assumptions.

Solution overview

Rescale’s triage agent automates the classification and routing of nightly end-to-end test failures. It runs as a step within Rescale’s existing Argo Workflows continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When a nightly Playwright suite of hundreds of test cases produces failures, the pipeline triggers the triage agent pod.

The agent performs the following steps:

  • Invokes Claude Opus 4.8 on Amazon Bedrock to classify each failure into a root cause category: infrastructure issue, code bug, flaky test, or environment problem.
  • Retrieves relevant historical failure patterns from a knowledge base for additional context.
  • Queries pod logs through Model Context Protocol (MCP) for runtime evidence supporting the classification.
  • Generates a structured remediation report with specific file references, function names, and recommended fixes for engineer review before any action is taken.

The agent completes this workflow in seconds and outputs directly into the team’s existing reporting pipeline. The following diagram shows how these components fit together:

Figure 1: Architecture for Rescale’s AI triage agent, running on Amazon EKS with Amazon Bedrock for classification, a knowledge base for historical failure patterns, and MCP-based log retrieval through Amazon CloudWatch integration

The AI-DLC workshop experience

The engagement was structured as a five-day, in-person workshop. AWS architects guided the build while Rescale engineers worked hands-on-keyboard, co-building in real time.

Inception phase (days 1–2): From vision to validated requirements

The team started by scoping requirements, capturing the intent in a vision document and a technical environment document that grounded the work before any building began. That intent began as a single statement, “We want AI-powered test triage that classifies failures and recommends remediation”. Working collaboratively in mob format, the team answered 20+ clarification questions generated by AI. This produced a scoped requirements document with Phase 1 boundaries explicitly defined and Phase 2 items deferred. Five user stories were consolidated into four units of work:

  • Knowledge base for historical failure patterns.
  • AI triage agent as the core classification and remediation engine.
  • Argo Workflow Integration for trigger, infrastructure, and deployment.
  • Evaluation Harness for accuracy measurement and regression gating.

Human decisions drove the critical boundaries: what belongs in Phase 1 versus Phase 2, priority ordering, and deferred features like automated pull request (PR) generation.

Construction phase (days 2–4): Architecture to running code

The team defined interface contracts and data schemas, completed functional and non-functional design questions, and signed off on the architecture. Two architecture pivots emerged during the build, and the team validated each one before changing course.

First, the team planned to host the agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, then moved it to Amazon EKS, where Rescale already runs its Argo Workflows CI/CD pipeline. Keeping the agent in the existing cluster meant no new runtime to operate and a direct trigger path from Argo. Second, in the early build the agent pulled log evidence from a third-party logging service through MCP. The team moved log retrieval to Amazon CloudWatch, which simplified the dependency chain. The MCP pattern stayed the same. Only the source behind it changed. Because AI-DLC keeps requirements and design decisions in shared documents, the team updated them in place and kept building without losing context.

The agent was built using the Strands SDK, supporting concurrent failure analysis with structured output in JSON and HTML, containerized on Amazon EKS.

By Day 4, the full pipeline was running in staging: Argo workflow trigger, triage agent pod, MCP log query, knowledge base retrieval, and structured triage output.

Operations phase (day 5): Evaluation and handoff

The team built a PyTest-based evaluation framework with live and stubbed test modes, establishing an initial classification-agreement baseline to measure the agent against and improve from. The agent was demoed live to Rescale’s CTO and VP of Engineering, correctly classifying both an infrastructure failure and a real code bug with specific file-level fix recommendations.

How AI-DLC scaled rigor to complexity

Not every unit of work gets the same treatment. The knowledge base needed minimal design and deployed using Terraform in hours. The Triage Agent got full rigor: architecture review, interface contracts, 12 design questions, and iterative code review. Argo Integration focused on infrastructure contracts and IAM. The Evaluation Harness used lightweight design but heavy implementation. AI-DLC matched depth to complexity automatically.

By the end of Day 5, the agent was live in staging, processing real test failures with a measured accuracy baseline and a clear path to production.

Production outcomes

The triage agent has been running in production since the workshop. It automatically classifies nightly end-to-end test failures, replacing manual first-pass triage with an automated first pass that engineers validate. For each failure, the agent generates a structured remediation report with actionable next steps rather than raw logs. The agent’s classification agreement with human triage has risen from 44% at initial deployment to 68% today. It continues to improve as the team iterates on the golden dataset and prompt engineering.

Since the triage agent entered production, the team has measured a 20% decrease in time blocking production deployment while test failures are analyzed. Because these tests gate Rescale’s weekly production releases, that reduction shows up directly in how quickly changes reach production. Engineers also spend less of the on-call rotation on repetitive classification.

Life after the workshop: From one agent to an AI-first practice

The workshop delivered one production agent, but its larger effect was on how Rescale approaches engineering work. The triage agent is part of a broader push at Rescale to deliver digital engineering capabilities for the AI era. Internally, Rescale is applying these same benefits realized from AI across its own engineering organization. AI-DLC gave Rescale’s engineers a structured, repeatable way to put that direction into practice.

Scaling AI-DLC across the organization

Rescale is evaluating an internal AI-DLC Center of Excellence, a small group that codifies best practices and helps other teams adopt the methodology independently.

The engineers who participated are already applying what they learned. One of the engineers noted that the process “will be part of my workflow going forward,” not only for building agents, but for any complex development work where AI can contribute.

Broader AI-native development

Rescale is now incorporating AI-DLC into the standard software development lifecycle for new engineering simulation products. The framework brings simulation-domain expertise, product requirements, platform architecture, validation, and operations into one structured design process. Teams resolve key questions early, capture reviewed decisions in executable specifications, and give coding agents focused work with clear acceptance criteria. This shortens the path from product concept to validated implementation while engineers remain accountable for product correctness.

The same approach is already being used in product-enabling platform work and agent systems:

  • HPC simulation application catalog management.
  • Container vulnerability tracking and remediation for government compliance requirements.
  • Workflow-based cloud coding agents.

Conclusion

For the triage agent, the most useful output of AI-DLC was not the code itself. It was the structured path from an initial idea to a reviewed system design: clarifying questions, scoped requirements, and evaluation criteria.

That specification gave coding agents a narrower, better-defined problem to solve. Instead of asking an agent to infer the architecture while implementing it, the team could use agents for focused construction against decisions that humans had already reviewed. The result was more focused, reviewable output that was easier to integrate and improve. For Rescale, that is the repeatable pattern: use AI-DLC to structure the design conversation, turn the decisions into a specification, and then use coding agents to accelerate implementation.

Key takeaways

  • Start with a real problem. Rescale’s triage agent succeeded because it solved an engineering challenge. The problem drove the solution, not the other way around.
  • Human oversight accelerates, not decelerates. Every architecture pivot that improved the system came from human validation of AI proposals. The mob format, where AI generates and humans validate, is faster than working alone.
  • The AWS stack provided each layer the agent needed. Amazon Bedrock supplied foundation-model access for classification in an environment Rescale was already using, so the team could build the triage workflow without taking on additional model-infrastructure overhead. The Strands SDK provided the agent framework, and Amazon EKS hosted the containerized agent within Rescale’s existing pipeline.

Get started with AI-DLC

  • Understand the methodology: Read the AI-DLC introduction blog and the adaptive workflows deep-dive.
  • Explore the service: Learn more about Amazon Bedrock.
  • Try it now: Clone the open-source AI-DLC workflow rules at github.com/awslabs/aidlc-workflows.
  • See it in action: Walk through a practical AI-DLC build with Amazon Q Developer.
  • Connect: Contact your AWS account team to discuss how AI-DLC can be tailored to your organization’s specific engineering workflows.

About the authors

item.title: [DeepInfra] Best API Providers for Granite-4.2-8B in 2026
item.content:encoded:
Best API Providers for Granite-4.2-8B in 2026

Published on 2026.10.22 by DeepInfra

IBM’s Granite-4.2-8b is an 8-billion-parameter reasoning model built for enterprise and developer use cases. It offers a 131,072-token context window and an Apache 2.0 license, which suits complex reasoning and long-context data processing in production.

Running an 8B model with a long context window means balancing inference cost, output throughput, time to first token (TTFT), and compliance needs. The right provider depends on which of those matters most.

This guide compares the top API providers, gateways, and deployment platforms for Granite-4.2-8b so you can match one to your architecture and budget.

Summary of Top Providers for Granite-4.2-8b

Here is a quick summary of the best platforms for Granite-4.2-8b, by need:

  • DeepInfra: Best overall for cost and developers who want the most affordable API access.
  • CoreWeave: Best for output-heavy workloads, with the lowest output price and the lowest first-chunk latency.
  • OpenRouter: Best for developers who want a single endpoint to access the model and compare it with others.
  • IBM: Best for enterprise workloads that need contractual protections and on-premises deployment.
  • Vultr: Best for organizations that want to self-host on high-performance cloud GPUs.
  • Hugging Face: Best for researchers and developers who want to download the open weights for local deployment or fine-tuning.
  • TrustedRouter: Best for production routing where prompts are not stored and provider failover matters.
  • LLM Gateway: Best for developers who want an alternative gateway with listed token prices.

Detailed Company Reviews

DeepInfra

Granite-4.2-8b on DeepInfra combines the lowest blended price with the highest measured output speed of the two providers Artificial Analysis tracks. Developers building cost-sensitive applications get a managed API for an 8B reasoning model without running any infrastructure.

Key features

  • Lowest blended price at $0.05 per 1M tokens, per Artificial Analysis
  • Input tokens at $0.06/M and output tokens at $0.25/M
  • Cached input tokens at $0.015/M, a 75% discount from the input rate
  • Highest measured output speed of the two tracked providers, at 120 tokens per second
  • Support for JSON output and function calling
  • Zero data retention and private endpoint deployments
  • 100% uptime on OpenRouter’s tracking of the DeepInfra endpoint

Differentiators for Granite-4.2-8b

Prompt caching suits the model’s 131K context window. At $0.015/M, cached input lets you resend large documents or system prompts without inflating your inference budget.

Output speed matters for a verbose reasoning model. Artificial Analysis measured 130M output tokens across its Intelligence Index runs, against a median of 82M for comparable models.

CoreWeave

CoreWeave is a GPU cloud that serves Granite-4.2-8b through an API. It suits workloads where output volume drives the bill.

Key features

  • Lowest output price at $0.15/M
  • Input tokens at $0.10/M and cached input at $0.05/M
  • Lowest median first-chunk latency of the two tracked providers, at 0.74 seconds
  • Support for tool calling and structured outputs

Differentiators for Granite-4.2-8b

A reasoning model writes a lot of output, so a $0.15/M output rate can offset the higher input price on output-heavy workloads. Tool calling and structured outputs suit agentic workflows and interactive chatbots.

Output speed is lower than DeepInfra’s, at 89 tokens per second against 120. CoreWeave fits cost-driven, output-heavy use better than speed-critical use.

OpenRouter

OpenRouter is a unified API aggregator that serves Granite-4.2-8b alongside many other models. It provides a single standardized endpoint with built-in routing.

Key features

  • OpenAI-compatible unified API
  • Input at $0.06/M and output at $0.25/M on the DeepInfra route, or $0.10/M and $0.15/M on the CoreWeave route
  • Support for the full 131,072-token context window
  • Automatic failover between providers, plus Balanced, Nitro, Floor, and Exacto routing modes

Differentiators for Granite-4.2-8b

Teams experimenting with different models can swap Granite-4.2-8b into an existing OpenAI-compatible stack. If one underlying provider goes down, requests route to the other, which preserves application stability.

OpenRouter reports 99.98% availability for the model over the last 72 hours.

IBM

IBM created Granite-4.2-8b and offers it through its enterprise AI platform, watsonx.ai. IBM aims this ecosystem at large organizations that need data privacy and legal protections.

Key features

  • Standard contractual intellectual property indemnification for IBM-developed models
  • Granite Guardian models that detect malicious content and harmful outputs
  • Transparency into training data and processes
  • On-premises deployment, which IBM describes as powering secure, on-prem AI

Differentiators for Granite-4.2-8b

Because IBM built the model, it extends its standard IP indemnification to Granite and documents its training data and processes. Organizations that need on-premises deployment with guardrails get both from IBM’s native ecosystem.

Vultr

Vultr is a cloud infrastructure provider for teams that prefer to self-host Granite-4.2-8b instead of using a managed API.

Key features

  • Private inference endpoints on NVIDIA HGX B200 GPUs
  • Support for the vLLM and SGLang inference engines
  • Starting price of $3.50 per GPU per hour
  • Support for the 128K native context window, with extension to 512K

Differentiators for Granite-4.2-8b

Self-hosting a model with a 131K context window needs ample GPU memory and memory bandwidth. Vultr pairs B200 GPUs with modern inference engines, and its benchmarks for the model were measured on B200 with vLLM.

Hugging Face

Hugging Face is the primary hub for the raw assets of Granite-4.2-8b. It is the starting point for any team that wants to inspect, download, or fine-tune the model.

Key features

  • Apache 2.0 licensed model weights
  • Quantized variants in FP8, NVFP4, MXFP4, and GGUF, published by IBM alongside the bfloat16 weights
  • Official launch post and model card with benchmark scores
  • Integration with Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang

Differentiators for Granite-4.2-8b

Multiple quantization formats let you run the model on edge devices, consumer-grade hardware, or optimized production servers. You can trade precision against memory footprint to fit your hardware.

TrustedRouter

TrustedRouter is an API gateway for production environments where privacy, failover, and provider choice matter.

Key features

  • OpenAI-compatible API, so you keep the OpenAI SDK and change the base URL
  • No stored prompt or output content at the gateway
  • Provider failover for requests that hit an unhealthy provider
  • Provider prices listed side by side, with the cheapest Granite-4.2-8b route at $0.1055/M input and $0.15825/M output
  • Pricing set at provider cost plus a 5.5% markup

Differentiators for Granite-4.2-8b

Privacy-conscious applications benefit from the gateway’s policy of storing no prompt or output content. The attestation covers the TrustedRouter gateway, not the underlying providers, so check each provider’s own policy.

LLM Gateway

LLM Gateway is an alternative API gateway with listed per-token rates for foundation models.

Key features

  • Input at $0.06/M, output at $0.25/M, and cached input at $0.015/M
  • Support for the 131,072-token context window and up to 131,072 output tokens
  • Reasoning and tool calling capabilities
  • DevPass, a flat monthly subscription for developers who code with AI agents

Differentiators for Granite-4.2-8b

LLM Gateway lists the same token rates as DeepInfra and the full 131,072-token window. It suits developers who want a gateway with published pricing and an optional subscription plan for agent-based coding.

Conclusion and Recommendations

Integrating Granite-4.2-8b into your application means aligning your infrastructure choice with your performance, privacy, and budget requirements.

  • Enterprise and compliance: IBM fits organizations that need IP indemnification, training data transparency, and on-premises deployment.
  • Self-hosting and fine-tuning: Download the weights from Hugging Face and deploy them on GPU infrastructure such as Vultr’s B200 endpoints.
  • Output-heavy workloads: CoreWeave offers the lowest output price and the lowest median first-chunk latency of the tracked providers.
  • Routing and redundancy: OpenRouter and TrustedRouter add automatic failover, and TrustedRouter stores no prompt or output content at its gateway.

DeepInfra offers the strongest balance of cost, reliability, and feature support for most teams. It combines a $0.05 blended price, $0.015/M cached input, 100% uptime on OpenRouter’s tracking, and the highest measured output speed. Because reasoning models shift spend toward output tokens, model your real inference costs against your own token ratios before you commit.

It is a 754-billion parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 40 billion active parameters per token, a 202,752-token context window, and up to 131K output tokens. The model is the direct successor to GLM-5, designed specifically for long-horizon autonomous […]</p>

Best Kimi K3 SaaS Tools & API Platforms<p>Kimi K3, with its 2.8 trillion parameters and 1M-token context window, represents a significant leap in large language model capabilities. However, deploying, accessing, and managing a model of this scale presents real infrastructure challenges. From optimizing inference latency and managing GPU compute costs to handling multimodal vision capabilities, selecting the right deployment platform is critical […]</p>

Best SaaS Tools and API Providers for GLM-5.2<p>GLM-5.2 represents a significant leap forward in open-weight models, particularly for complex reasoning, long-context processing, and agentic coding tasks. Deploying a model of this scale — especially with its massive 1-million token context window and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture — presents real infrastructure challenges. Managing memory bandwidth, optimizing time to first token (TTFT), and handling quantization […]</p>

item.title: [DeepInfra] Wan 3.0: Model Documentation & Integration Guide
item.content:encoded:
Wan 3.0: Model Documentation & Integration Guide

Published on 2026.10.22 by DeepInfra

Wan3.0 is an all-in-one video generation model from Wan-AI, hosted on DeepInfra. It covers reference-based generation, editing, replication, and driving in a single model, and it accepts images, video clips, audio, documents, and web links as input.

Use it for cinematic storytelling, social media content, and video editing. Every generation includes synchronized audio by default, and the model keeps characters stable and recognizable across a clip.

Key Capabilities

  • Omni-modal reference: Parses documents, web pages, and complex images to drive video generation.
  • Long clips with audio: Generates up to 30 seconds of video with a synchronized audio track by default.
  • Character consistency: Keeps subjects stable and recognizable for the full duration of a video.
  • Editing and extension: Handles style transfers such as clay art conversions, and extends existing videos forward or backward.

Technical Specifications and Benchmarks

Standard specifications

MetricSpecificationNotes
Maximum resolution1080P480P, 720P, and 1080P tiers
Frame rate30 fpsOutput is an MP4 video
Duration2 to 30 secondsSet -1 to let the model choose
AudioGenerated by defaultSet audio to false for silent output
Reference inputsImages, video, audio, files, linksUp to 20 reference assets per request

Quality benchmark

Artificial Analysis measures video quality through blind user votes in its Video Arena. Wan3.0 ranks first on both of its text-to-video leaderboards.

LeaderboardEloRank
Text-to-video with audio1,173 (95% interval 1,157 to 1,189)1
Text-to-video without audio1,1341

On the with-audio board, Wan3.0 leads Utopai X at 1,166 and Dreamina Seedance 2.5 at 1,159. The rank interval spans first to third, so the top models sit close together.

Comparison with Wan2.7

FeatureWan2.7Wan3.0
Input typesImage or reference video, depending on the modelText, images, video, audio, files, and web links
Maximum duration15 seconds30 seconds
Models on DeepInfraSeparate image-to-video and reference-to-video modelsOne model for every workflow
Price on DeepInfra$0.10 per second$0.20 per second

Both Wan2.7 models remain available, including Wan2.7 image-to-video. Alibaba introduced video editing in Wan2.7, and Wan3.0 carries it forward.

Getting Started

To use Wan3.0-Video, you need a DeepInfra account and an API key. DeepInfra applies a zero-retention policy to inputs and outputs.

Authentication

Create a key in the DeepInfra dashboard and pass it in the Authorization header of every request:

Authorization: Bearer <DEEPINFRA_API_KEY>

API endpoint basics

  • Base URL: https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/inference
  • Model path: /Wan-AI/Wan3.0-Video
  • HTTP method: POST
  • Content type: application/json

Making your first API call

The example below generates a short video with Python.

import os
import requests
 
url = "https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/inference/Wan-AI/Wan3.0-Video"
headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['DEEPINFRA_API_KEY']}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}
 
payload = {
    "prompt": "A cinematic drone shot flying over a misty pine forest at sunrise",
    "duration": 5,
    "resolution": "720P",
    "audio": True,
    "prompt_extend": True,
}
 
response = requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload)
print(response.json()["video_url"])copy

To guide a generation with reference media, add a media array. Refer to each asset in the prompt as Image 1, Video 1, and so on, numbered in the order the assets appear in the array.

payload = {
    "prompt": "Image 1 walks through a rainy neon street at night",
    "media": [
        {"type": "reference_image", "url": "https://example.com/character.png"}
    ],
    "duration": 8,
}copy

Configuration and Parameters

Each request needs either a prompt or media.

Common parameters

ParameterTypeDefaultDescription
promptstringEmptyText description of the video. Use Image n or Video n to reference assets in the media array.
mediaarrayEmptyInput media objects, each with a type and a url.
durationinteger5Video length from 2 to 30 seconds. Set -1 for a model-chosen duration.
resolutionstring1080POutput tier: 480P, 720P, or 1080P.
ratiostringadaptiveAspect ratio such as 16:9 or 9:16. Adaptive derives the ratio from input media.
audiobooleantrueGenerates a synchronized audio track.
prompt_extendbooleantrueRewrites the prompt to improve output quality.
watermarkbooleanfalseAdds an AI-generated watermark.
seedintegerNoneValue from 0 to 2147483647 for reproducible outputs.

Media entries use one of these types: first_frame, last_frame, reference_image, reference_video, reference_audio, file, or link. Reference types cannot be combined with first_frame or last_frame. When a request includes a reference_video, the input and output durations together must stay within 30 seconds.

Input limits

Input typeLimitFormats and notes
Text prompt20,000 charactersDescribes the scene, motion, and audio
Reference images10 imagesJPEG, PNG, BMP, and WEBP, up to 20 MB each
Reference videos5 clips, 15 seconds totalMP4 and MOV, up to 100 MB each
Reference audio5 clips, 15 seconds totalWAV and MP3, up to 15 MB each
Documents1 file, up to 50 pagesPDF, DOCX, PPTX, and Markdown, up to 100 MB
Web links1 linkPublic URLs that do not require a login

Response Format

The API returns a JSON payload with a link to the generated video. An inference_status object reports the status, runtime, and cost of the request.

{
  "video_url": "https://example.com/video.mp4",
  "request_id": null,
  "inference_status": {
    "status": "succeeded",
    "runtime_ms": 0,
    "cost": 0.0
  }
}copy

Pricing

Wan3.0-Video is billed at $0.20 per second of generated video. A 10-second clip costs $2.00, and a 30-second clip costs $6.00. DeepInfra lists the rate per second of generated output.

Conclusion

Wan3.0-Video combines omni-modal input with audio and video output in one model. Creators can turn text, images, and documents into finished video without assembling a multi-model pipeline.

  • Range: Generates up to 30 seconds of video with integrated audio and multi-modal references.
  • Control: Offers prompt_extend, adaptive aspect ratios, seeds, and optional watermarks.
  • Simple billing: Charges a single per-second rate for generated video.

DeepInfra also hosts other video models that accept reference inputs, such as ByteDance Seedance 2.0, so you can compare outputs through the same API.

Related articles

Reliable JSON-Only Responses with DeepInfra LLMs<p>When large language models are used inside real applications, their role changes fundamentally. Instead of chatting with users, they become infrastructure components: extracting information, transforming text, driving workflows, or powering APIs. In these scenarios, natural language is no longer the desired output. What applications need is structured data — and very often, that structure is […]</p>

GLM-5.3 Model Overview & Integration Guide<p>GLM-5.3 is a large-scale reasoning model from Z.ai, built for complex software engineering and long-horizon agent tasks. It handles text input and output across a 1,048,576-token context window, and is one of several hundred models in DeepInfra’s catalog. The model uses the same base as GLM-5.2. Every gain comes from post-training, which is where Z.ai […]</p>

Nemotron 3 Nano vs GPT-OSS-20B: Performance, Benchmarks & DeepInfra Results<p>The open-source LLM landscape is becoming increasingly diverse, with models optimized for reasoning, throughput, cost-efficiency, and real-world agentic applications. Two models that stand out in this new generation are NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Nano and OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-20B, both of which offer strong performance while remaining openly available and deployable across cloud and edge systems. Although both […]</p>

item.title: [AI21 Labs] How we cut GitLab Duo Code Review’s cost by 98%
item.content:encoded:
In Brief

We cut GitLab Duo Code Review’s cost by 98% on Martian’s Code Review Bench without losing review quality, and all of it came from optimizing the harness: which model each stage runs on and how much context each stage reads. Neither change gets there alone. The open-weight model stalled on a handful of oversized reviews, and compacting the context is what made them fit.

Figure 1. Cost against F1 for every setup in the results table. F1 stays within two points of the baseline throughout. The same compaction step saves 19% from the baseline and 84% after the model switch; on a log axis, arrow length reflects the percentage saved.

An agent’s cost is eventually set by its harness: which stages it runs, what each stage reads, and which model does the work. We took GitLab Duo Code Review, whose harness is source available, measured where its money sits, and, with our own agent helping run the experiments, changed one thing at a time until the bill stopped dropping.

But the real story is not the final changes in the harness; it’s the way we got there. Switching to a smaller model in every stage hurt the quality. Moving to an open-weight model on every stage cut 85% of the cost, but we didn’t stop there. While compaction looks marginal at first glance, the 98% only shows up with both, because the open-weight model’s deployment window decides which requests it can take at all. The model sets the price. The harness decides whether you get to use it.

We ran this on public pull requests, with no GitLab production traffic or customer data. Quality is F1 on one public benchmark, scored by two judges. Cost is token spend at published list prices, including for the model we serve ourselves, so it measures what the harness consumes. What our own infrastructure costs is a separate question. Configurations were chosen and tuned on the same 50 pull requests they’re scored on, so read these as measured results on this benchmark; how they hold on a new codebase is untested. The full methodology is at the end.

A pipeline with four stages

Duo Code Review, the Code Review Flow of GitLab Duo Agent Platform, reviews merge requests and posts comments. At the time of testing, it ran Claude Sonnet 5 by default, and GitLab published the flow, built on LangGraph, in its source-available ai-assist repository. That, plus a public benchmark, is why we chose it.

It runs four model stages, each with its own prompt and at most two tools:

  • Exploration lists the repository tree around the changed files.
  • File fetching reads related files: tests, callers, custom instructions.
  • Analysis turns what was fetched into notes.
  • Review reads the diff and most changed files in full, then posts comments.

Figure 2. Duo Code Review’s four stages. Each starts from a fresh prompt with at most two tools.

Every generic optimization we had built targets coding agents like Claude Code, which resend one growing conversation full of tool output and tool definitions. Duo Code Review’s stages are independent: each starts with a fresh prompt, carries at most two tools, and has no history to trim. Our defaults had nothing to act on and changed zero requests.

It turns out there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to harness optimization; each harness requires its own careful analysis.

Where the money goes

Figure 3. Where the baseline’s $0.589 per PR goes. The review is 65% of the bill, split almost evenly between what it reads and how much it reasons.

The review is 65% of the bill, and its output alone is a third of the total: free to think before it posts, Sonnet 5 writes about 18,600 tokens per review, nearly all reasoning. Exploration and fetching, which only decide which files to read, are 27%. Analysis is 9%.

The money mainly goes in three places: the context every stage reads, the mechanical stages, and the review’s reasoning. No single change reaches all three but each step below reaches one of them.

Finding 1: less context, more reasoning

Can we cut what the review reads without hurting it? Yes, and it saves less than arithmetic suggests.

The review stage builds its context including changed files in full, plus a diff where every line sits in a tag repeating its type and both line numbers. A unified diff marks the same line with one character.

We compacted both in front of the flow, with rules rather than a model: nothing is summarized. File windowing keeps each changed hunk plus 25 lines either side of both the old and new line ranges, and elides the rest. Diff compaction rewrites the per-line diff as a standard unified diff with the same hunks and line numbers.

The median review prompt fell from 59K to 32K tokens. Spending on review context fell further, by 62%, because the largest prompts shrank hardest.

Yet the review’s cost fell by only a fifth. With compaction on, Sonnet 5 also wrote more: about 23,800 output tokens per review instead of 18,600, nearly all reasoning. We haven’t isolated why, but it caps what compaction can save on its own. On its own, compaction took cost from $0.589 to $0.475, a 19.4% saving, at 47.2% F1 and 1.16x the latency.

Figure 4. Baseline against compaction. Spending on the review’s context falls 62%, but its reasoning output grows 28%, so the bill falls only 19%.

Finding 2: the open-weight model held on every stage

How far does changing models get you? That depends on which stage you change.

We started by moving Claude Haiku 4.5 onto one stage at a time. On exploration and fetching, it picked the same files Sonnet 5 did. Early tests on the other two were less kind: quality dipped with Haiku on analysis and dropped sharply with it on the review. Same model, very different results depending on where it sat. Kept on the two mechanical stages, Haiku cut the bill 15.4% at unchanged F1, and 34.6% with compaction.

That was as far as Haiku could go. It couldn’t hold quality on the review, where most of the money is, and at half Sonnet 5’s price it wouldn’t have moved the bill enough if it had. Reaching the review’s reasoning meant leaving the Claude family.

We then turned to an open-weight model: DeepSeek V4 Flash, the first one we tried, which we serve with vLLM on H100s. At Together AI’s list price it costs 14x less than Sonnet 5 per input token and 36x less per output token. With all four stages on it and compaction off, cost fell to $0.086, an 85.3% saving, at 48.4% F1 and 0.37x the latency. On this benchmark it held on every stage, review included.

Two harness settings made that hold. Reasoning effort was set by measurement (see “What didn’t help”). And about one review call in seven on DeepSeek ended without posting; GitLab’s own correction step retried each one, so every review was posted, and the retries are in the costs.

Why the saving stopped at 85%

Our DeepSeek deployment accepts prompts up to 256K tokens; anything longer stays on Sonnet 5 so the review completes. The model supports 1M, but serving that window takes a more complex deployment, and its quality at very long contexts is still debated. Without compaction, some review prompts reach 480K, and 3 of the 50 PRs cross the limit, producing 11 fallback calls.

Figure 5. With every stage on the open-weight model and no compaction, 3 of 50 PRs (6%) exceed the 256K deployment and fall back to Sonnet 5. Those 11 calls carry 77% of the remaining $0.086 per PR.

Six percent of pull requests carried 77% of what was left. And the prompts that overflow are the largest reviews, large for exactly the reasons in Finding 1.

So compaction goes back in, this time to make prompts fit. The largest review prompt drops from 480K to 109K. Every review fits. Nothing falls back. Cost reaches $0.0135 per PR, 97.7% below baseline, at 47.2% F1 and 0.35x the latency, with the second judge within half a point.

Figure 6. Cost per PR along the way. The best setup on Claude reaches $0.385, the open-weight model on every stage reaches $0.086, and adding compaction brings it to $0.0135: 98% below baseline, at 47.2% F1 against 46.4%.

At that point compaction’s own token saving is about $0.006 per PR. What it buys is fit. In front of Claude, compaction is a cost optimization. In front of a 256K deployment, it keeps every review on the open-weight model.

A 1M deployment would also have removed the fallback. It would not have shrunk what every review reads, and it would have leaned on the model at the lengths where its quality is least settled.

What didn’t help

What we triedWhat we found
Raising reasoning effortAt “max” on 30 trial reviews, recall rose from 38.9% to 52.8% while F1 moved from 35.0% to 35.4%, at 3.5x the latency: more findings, more cost, no better reviews
Prompt cachingLittle to reuse. Requests within a stage share their instructions, but the stages share no prefix with each other, so the diff and files every stage reads can’t be reused across stages
A lower-priced model for exploration and fetchingNot worth testing. In the final setup those stages cost $0.005 of $0.0135 per PR, so even a free model would add about one point to the saving

Results

SetupF1Cost per PRCost vs baseline
Staying on Claude
Baseline: Sonnet 5 on every stage46.4%$0.5890%
Compaction only47.2%$0.475−19.4%
Haiku 4.5 for exploration and fetching46.3%$0.498−15.4%
Haiku 4.5 for exploration and fetching, plus compaction46.0%$0.385−34.6%
Adding the open-weight model
DeepSeek for exploration and fetching, plus compaction45.9%$0.370−37.1%
DeepSeek for everything except the review, plus compaction45.1%$0.317−46.1%
DeepSeek on every stage48.4%$0.086−85.3%
DeepSeek on every stage, plus compaction47.2%$0.0135−97.7%

Any stage not named runs on Sonnet 5. No setup moved F1 by more than 2 points on either judge. The final setup’s reviews are more precise than the baseline’s (46.8% vs 41.9%) but catch slightly fewer issues (recall 47.6% vs 52.0%), and at about 9,000 tokens against 18,600, run at about a third of the latency.

Summary

  • The bill sat in three places, each needing a different change: shared context, mechanical stages, and the review’s reasoning.
  • Haiku 4.5 held quality on the two mechanical stages and lost it on analysis and the review.
  • With compaction, the median review prompt shrank 46% while reasoning output grew 28%.
  • Three of 50 PRs carried 77% of the remaining cost until compaction made every review fit the deployment’s window.

Compaction on its own is worth 19.4%. Added after the model change, the same compaction is worth 84% of what was left, because by then its job was making prompts fit.

That interdependence is what makes harness optimization hard, and why it pays off. The settings in this study kept changing each other’s value. Compaction was worth a fifth of the bill on Sonnet 5 and decided the outcome on a 256K deployment. Haiku was safe on two stages and hurt quality on the other two. Getting to 98% meant searching configurations as a whole, and that search is where the saving came from.

The specific settings belong to this agent, and they’re already dated: GitLab has moved Duo Code Review to Sonnet 5.5 since we ran this. The method travels better. Measure cost per stage before changing anything. Change one variable at a time, and re-test earlier changes after each new one lands. Most teams won’t have a public benchmark to work against; we’d expect the same loop to work on a slice of live traffic, and once a configuration holds on most of it, it becomes a line in the harness.

Appendix: How we measured

Everything in the table below was fixed before the first run. Our own agent helped run the search inside those rules, proposing, executing, and scoring configurations.

What we tested onMartian’s Code Review Bench, full offline set: 50 real pull requests from Sentry, Grafana, Cal.com, Discourse, and Keycloak, with 173 human-verified “golden” comments, the issues a good review should catch
How a review is scoredA judge model matches the agent’s comments to the golden ones. Precision: how many of its comments match. Recall: how many golden comments it found. F1 balances the two. Claude Opus 4.5 judges with Martian’s prompts, GPT-5.2 as a cross-check
What “comparable” meansEach configuration reviews each PR 3 times. Comparable means F1 is less than 5 points below baseline even at the pessimistic end of its 95% confidence interval, on both judges
How cost is pricedPublished prices per million input/output tokens, no caching discount: Sonnet 5 2/10, Haiku 4.5 1/5. We self-host DeepSeek V4 Flash, so we price it at Together AI’s public rate, 0.14/0.28, instead of our own serving cost
BaselineThe agent as shipped, Sonnet 5 on every stage: 46.4% F1, $0.589 per PR (code_review flow 2.0.0, ai-assist commit 5272972)

To check our scoring, we ran it on GitLab’s own recorded reviews of these PRs, which Martian publishes: 52.3% F1 against Martian’s 54.2%. Those came from a different configuration, so they validate our scoring and tell us nothing about our baseline. These are public PRs, so their content may have been in training data. What we can rule out is the review models reproducing the answers from the question: given only each PR’s title, URL, and commit link, both score about 4% F1. Every file the agent read came from pinned offline copies.

Thanks to GitLab’s team for publishing the Duo Code Review flow and its benchmark results, which made this study possible.

item.title: [Modular (原 BentoCloud/BentoML)] Modular: MAX is now source available and open to everyone
item.content:encoded:
October 22, 2026

MAX is now source available and open to everyone

Modular Team

Product

Today, we're excited to announce a major milestone for Modular: the complete MAX source code is now publicly available, alongside a radically simplified MAX License.

Developers can now explore, modify, and extend the entire MAX stack. Building on our open source kernels, models, and serving infrastructure, this release opens the remaining core components that power MAX's heterogeneous capabilities: the graph compiler, runtime, and hardware backends. These include support for CPUs and GPUs.

Under the new license, you can build and distribute commercial products with MAX without licensing fees or royalties. We’re also opening MAX to community contributions, starting with bug fixes and expanding over time. We’re also actively supercharging MAX with agentic infrastructure development that will increase our overall development approach.

This milestone builds on our progressive approach to opening our stack. We started with the Mojo standard library in 2024, followed by MAX's kernels, models, serving infrastructure, and APIs throughout 2025. In August of this year, we fully open sourced the entire Mojo compiler and toolchain. Today, we complete the picture by making the remaining MAX compiler, runtime, and hardware backends source available.

As Modular enters a new chapter within Qualcomm, we’re accelerating our mission to democratize heterogeneous compute. In the next few months, we will launch an alliance program, with a goal of uniting developers and hardware vendors around a single software platform. Opening MAX is the first step toward that shared ecosystem.

The new MAX License

We designed the new MAX License to balance two priorities: enabling the community to build with more flexibility, and balancing the long-term sustainability of MAX and its ecosystem.

That starts with giving developers the freedom to build. You can use, modify, extend, and build commercial products with MAX, without licensing fees or royalties. Our goal is to remove barriers to adoption and give developers, researchers, and hardware vendors the freedom to innovate on top of the entire stack.

Equally important is ensuring that the ecosystem can thrive over the long term. Our team has spent decades building and maintaining major open source projects, and we've seen the challenges they face. Fragmentation is a common pitfall, especially for foundational infrastructure like MAX. MAX’s core goal is to unify the programming model across hardware, and that goal becomes much harder to achieve if every platform develops its own incompatible version.

We designed the license with these considerations in mind. As with Mojo, we expect our approach to continue evolving as the technology matures and we hear more from the community.

What the MAX License covers

Many MAX components are already open source under Apache 2.0. These include the MAX kernel library in Mojo, Mojo interfaces for programming accelerators, Python APIs for the serving CLI and modeling, MAX models, and more. All of these components will remain under Apache 2.0.

The new MAX License covers the MAX internals we’re making source available today, plus the MAX binaries we distribute. Each source file includes a header identifying the license that applies to it.

Here’s what the MAX License allows:

  • Unlimited MAX usage on any hardware, without licensing fees: Build with MAX on any hardware, for free.
  • Contribute back to MAX: Fork MAX for the purposes of contributing back to the main MAX project.
  • Build libraries and applications on top of MAX: Create projects and libraries using MAX and license them however you choose. Components of MAX, such as the kernels (Apache 2.0), the graph compiler (MAX License), and device backends (MAX License), retain their licenses and you can license your code as you see fit.

There a few limitations:

  • AI-assisted reimplementation of MAX: You can't use any part of MAX as input to an AI system to produce a reimplementation of MAX. We want to build a community and pull people together, not be the foundation for many AI-driven forks.
  • Commercial hosted inference services: If you use MAX for hosted inference or training services that you sell to customers, you must prominently display the “Modular Accelerated” wordmark on your product to recognize our contribution to your commercial products.
  • Publication and distribution of modified source code: You can't publish or distribute modified MAX source code, except by forking MAX for the purpose of contributing changes back to the main project. We know that there are many fierce competitors in the AI landscape, and hope to replicate LLVM’s success of getting people to build on a shared codebase that can service many different companies' needs, better than any one can build for themself.

Our intent is to encourage experimentation and innovation while ensuring that MAX continues to evolve as a unified software foundation. Developers are free to modify and experiment with MAX, and we want to make it as easy as possible to contribute improvements back to the project. The license’s distribution restrictions are designed to prevent fragmentation into incompatible versions of MAX, not to discourage individual developers from exploring new ideas. We recognize that there are many legitimate reasons to experiment with modifications that aren’t ready for upstream contribution, and we’ll continue working with the community to make sure our development and contribution processes support that innovation.

MAX may also collect usage telemetry to help us improve the product. We handle personal information in accordance with our Privacy Policy, which describes users’ rights under applicable data protection laws, including the EU and UK GDPR and the California Consumer Privacy Act. As with most software licenses, MAX is provided as-is, without warranties.

For more details on the MAX License, explore the FAQ and read the full license.

What comes next

With the full MAX codebase now source available, we’re also opening MAX to community contributions starting today. Initially, we’ll accept bug fixes, with plans to expand to refactors and other changes over time, following the same gradual approach we took with the Mojo standard library and compiler.

Our next step is to bring MAX and Mojo to the broader AI ecosystem. At ModCon, we announced the Modular alliance program, bringing together hardware vendors, model labs, and data center operators around a common software foundation.

Partners who contribute engineering resources, compute, or early model checkpoints will help shape the future of MAX, with a voice in governance and conformance standards, input into the roadmap, priority for upstream contributions, early access to model checkpoints, ownership of dedicated hardware backends, and more permissive licensing.

We’ll share more about the alliance in the coming months. If you’re interested in getting involved, reach out at alliance@modular.com.

To learn more about the new MAX License, join Modular cofounders Chris Lattner and Tim Davis for a live Q&A on November 10 at 10 AM PT. RSVP here.

Get started

  • Browse the MAX source on GitHub
  • Read the full MAX License
  • Read the MAX License FAQ
  • Install MAX with pip install max[all]
  • Check out the contributor guide to submit a bug fix
  • Build MAX from source
  • Share your feedback on the Modular forum or in Discord

We look forward to seeing what you build with MAX. If any part of the license remains unclear, we want to hear from you. Your feedback shaped this release, and it will continue to guide the steps that follow.
