item.title: [Modular (原 BentoCloud/BentoML)] Modular: Modular 26.7: Opening up MAX
item.content:encoded:
October 22, 2026

Modular 26.7: Opening up MAX

Modular Team

Product

The headline of Modular 26.7 is one we've wanted to write for a long time: this release opens the MAX graph compiler, MAX runtime, and device extensibility hooks for everyone. This means that MAX is now fully source-available, and can be built and modified by hardware innovators, researchers, and everyone else who loves making accelerators go "brr." This release also brings an eager mode that gets you debugging custom ops in a fraction of the time, decision model support, and the next step in Mojo's growth into a systems programming language.

MAX is now fully source-available

At our recent ModCon conference, we committed to opening up MAX, and we're delivering on that promise.

The full source for MAX is now available: hardware backends, the graph compiler, the runtime, and more. Our new MAX License is intentionally permissive: you can use, modify, extend, and build commercial products with MAX, without licensing fees or royalties. If you've wanted to bring up MAX on your own accelerator, this is where to start, and you can see the existing implementation for NVIDIA, AMD, Apple Silicon, and CPUs as a reference point. We plan to release source for the MAX plugins for other chips, including Qualcomm Dragonfly and Google TPU, in the coming months.

Why not Apache 2.0?

The MAX License allows nearly everything Apache 2.0 does: use, modify, extend, and build commercial products with MAX, with no fees or royalties. The difference comes down to fragmentation. We’ve spent decades maintaining major open source projects and have seen the challenges they face. MAX aims to unify the programming model across hardware, and incompatible platform-specific versions would undermine that goal. The Modular alliance program is how we solve this, giving hardware vendors and partners a shared path to build on MAX without splintering the ecosystem. As with Mojo, we expect our approach to evolve as the technology matures and we hear from the community.

There's far more in the MAX source code than we can cover here, so we wrote a separate post on what's included and what you can build with it.

What's new in MAX

Eager mode for faster development

MAX has long had an advanced graph compiler that performs automatic fusion and other optimizations for peak performance. But during development, fast iteration often matters more than peak performance. MAX now has full eager mode support, including your custom ops, and it shares a single code path with the graph compiler, so the code you run in eager mode is the same as what you compile and ship.

Declare an op once, call it directly on a Tensor, then reuse it unchanged inside a compiled Module. That makes the development loop much faster: on a slice of Gemma 4 31B, eager mode reaches the first token in about 30 seconds, compared to about 110 seconds compiled.

Here’s an example of how eager mode works with custom ops:

python

n, w, c = custom.Symbols("n", "w", "c")
downsample = custom.declare(
    "downsample",
    inputs={"x": custom.TemplateType(DType.float32, [n, w, c])},
    outputs=[custom.TemplateType(DType.float32, [n, w // 2, c])],
    custom_extensions=["path/to/kernels"],
)

# Eager: runs immediately.
y = downsample(Tensor.ones([2, 8, 3]))        # shape (2, 4, 3)

# Compiled: same op inside a Module.
class Encoder(Module):
    def forward(self, x: Tensor) -> Tensor:
        return downsample(x) * 2.0

model = Encoder().compile(TensorType(DType.float32, ["batch", 8, 3], device=Encoder().device))
y = model(Tensor.ones([2, 8, 3]))             # same op, now compiled

Support for System One/decision models, new modalities, and more models

There’s been a lot of recent excitement about the new modality of System One/decision models, due to their ability to enable zero-shot classification in a very inexpensive manner. MAX has added initial support for these decision models, including Decider 2B, through the new v1/decisions and v1/systemone API endpoints.

MAX has also added support for MiMo-V2.6-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, and Muse-Glimmer, with KDA and sparse MLA.

In addition to new capabilities, we continue to improve existing model families. Several ops that used to round-trip through the CPU now run entirely on the GPU, which gives a 2.6x prefill speedup for Qwen and GLM models.

Mojo 1.2: growing into a systems language

With 1.0, Mojo proved itself as a language for high-performance code across heterogeneous hardware. Now we're leaning into the next phase of the Mojo roadmap: Mojo as a systems programming language.

Pattern matching

Mojo 1.2's flagship new feature is pattern matching. The match statement lets you replace long chains of conditionals with clear, structured cases, and the compiler can check that you've handled every one of them.

python

def classify_point(p: Tuple[Int, Int]) -> String:
    match p:
        case 0, 0:
            return "origin"
        case x, 0 if x < 0:
            return String("negative x-axis:", x)
        case x, 0:
            return String("x-axis:", x)
        case 0, y:
            return String("y-axis:", y)
        case x, y:
            return String("point:", x, ",", y)

As a bonus, it also works at compile-time:

python

def classify_type[T: AnyType]() -> String:
    comptime match T:
        case == Int:
            return "integer"
        case == String:
            return "string"
        case _:
            return "other"

More expressive traits and constraints

Structs can now explicitly opt out of trait conformance (for example, by declaring themselves not Movable), and where clauses accept an else branch so you can state exactly why a constraint failed. Both make generic code easier to read and easier to debug.

See the Mojo changelog for the full list of changes in 1.2.

Get started

  • Upgrade with pip install --upgrade max
  • Read the MAX License blog post and FAQ
  • Explore the full MAX 26.7 changelog
  • Check out the full Mojo 1.2 changelog

With the whole stack open, we can’t wait to see what you build. Share it on the Modular forum.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] HCLTech joins the Claude Partner Network as a Global Premier…
item.description: Full title: HCLTech joins the Claude Partner Network as a Global Premier partner
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic is partnering with HCLTech (opens in new tab), a global technology company with more than 230,000 people in 60 countries. HCLTech will build agentic solutions on Claude for its clients through a dedicated Anthropic Business Unit and Center of Excellence, embed Claude in HCLSoftware products, and integrate Claude and Claude Code into AI Force, the platform it uses to run IT services for clients. HCLTech becomes a Global Premier Partner (opens in new tab) in the Claude Partner Network.

HCLTech provides solutions for financial services, manufacturing, life sciences and healthcare, technology, semiconductor, telecom and media, retail and CPG, and mobility and public services. In these environments, a mistake is expensive and every change needs to be reviewed, logged, and approved. The partnership is built to put Claude into that work with the controls designed for those environments.

How HCLTech is putting Claude to work

HCLTech is bringing Claude into its business in three places and is designing each with guardrails and human review.

  • A dedicated Anthropic Business Unit and Center of Excellence. HCLTech’s forward-deployed engineers will set up secure sandbox environments where clients can test Claude against their own systems and data before deploying. The Center will train client workforces, help engineering teams adopt AI-native practices, and build the organizational controls for running agents safely at scale.
  • Claude inside HCLSoftware products. HCLSoftware becomes an Anthropic independent software vendor (ISV) partner and will embed Claude in select products across cybersecurity, automation, business process applications, and application development. The first are HCL BigFix for endpoint management, HCL AppScan for application security testing, and the Actian AI analyst for data and analytics.
  • Claude and Claude Code in AI Force. AI Force is how HCLTech delivers IT support, code remediation, and digital employee services for the enterprises it serves. Claude and Claude Code go into that platform with policy guardrails, exception handling, and human oversight for high-impact changes. Agents handle the routine work, and HCLTech engineers review and approve anything that touches a client’s production systems.

“Few technology companies combine the scale of a global systems integrator with the product depth of an ISV,” says C Vijayakumar, CEO and Managing Director at HCLTech. “That gives us a rare advantage to securely engineer and deploy Agentic AI at scale and deliver the business outcomes that matter most to our clients. Our partnership with Anthropic further strengthens our capabilities to achieve the same.”

"AI can only be as useful as it is trustworthy, and we build Claude to give companies the confidence to bring it into their most sensitive and valuable work,” says Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President at Anthropic. “HCLTech manages those kinds of systems for banks, hospitals, telecom companies and manufacturers, and we’re excited to partner with them as they integrate Claude and Claude Code. This partnership — and our broader commitment to advancing capability and safety together — is how AI will change the way entire industries run for the better.”

To learn more about working with Anthropic partners, visit the Claude Partner Network (opens in new tab).

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Introducing Claude Duet
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re opening a research preview of Claude Duet, a new app where Claude works as a proactive agent. It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away, and checks with you before it acts on your behalf. We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track.

It’s available as a standalone app on iOS and Android, and on claude.ai. For this research preview, Claude Duet is included in Pro and Max plans and uses the same usage limits as the rest of Claude. To get access, join the waitlist (opens in new tab).

Put your attention where it matters most

We designed Claude Duet to be a partner you can trust. Professionals of all kinds have to juggle many decisions a day, and we think they’ll find Claude Duet most useful. It helps you prioritize where to spend your time and energy, and to leave room for the ambitious projects that felt impossible or daunting before.

What makes Claude Duet so helpful is its judgment. We designed it around Claude Opus 5.5 (opens in new tab) and built it to be resourceful and to decide what needs you, what can wait, and when to check with you first.

Each morning, it sends you a short brief on the most important items across your connected apps. Throughout the day, it keeps tabs on those apps and messages you only when something needs your attention. You can also hand it tasks of all shapes—from simple administrative tasks of scheduling meetings to more complex ones, such as building dashboards with dozens of tools, creating financial or sales forecasts, prototyping, and building web apps.

Safety and discretion are built in

Claude Duet draws on years of security, safety, and privacy work on agents, both our own and the infrastructure businesses use to run theirs:

  • Claude Duet draws on our framework for trustworthy agents (opens in new tab), which also guides agents like Claude Code and Claude in Chrome.
  • Claude Duet’s handling of credentials follows the design we use for Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab), so it never directly sees your passwords or sign-in tokens.
  • Actions are approved by our auto mode classifier (opens in new tab), the same safeguard that protects Claude and Claude Code from taking steps you didn’t ask for.
  • Claude Duet’s defenses against hidden instructions and prompt injection come from our browser-use research (opens in new tab), and our models and safeguards also cover this more broadly.
  • We run adversarial tests for Claude Duet’s security infrastructure. Red teams and an external firm penetration tested Claude Duet, and it’s covered by our public bug bounty program (opens in new tab).

How Duet handles sensitive information. We’re also releasing Claude Duet with a new dedicated classifier and safety system prompt that checks each message and guards against leaks of sensitive information. An agent that reads email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where information should go. This new classifier and prompt are designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information, including credit card numbers and government identification. Other sensitive information, such as health or personal finances, are let through only when you’ve explicitly instructed Claude Duet to send it.

We’re continuing to develop and strengthen these protections, and will share more details about how Claude Duet is designed for safety in the coming days.

How testers are using Claude Duet

People at Anthropic have been using Claude Duet to accomplish more, but also to leave more room for thinking and being present. Boris Cherny, who leads our Claude Code team, talks through his mental to-do list with Claude Duet on walks, instead of saving the work for his desk. Chelsea Larsson, who leads our model and product behavior design team, hands Claude Duet her to-do list before leaving to be with her kids and it saves the results for an evening report. And the team behind Claude Duet uses it to build the product. Karan Ahuja, who leads the team, works with it to schedule user interviews, partner with him on prototypes, and even ship code.

We gave small business owners and entrepreneurs early access to Claude Duet, and some have been using it to help run their businesses. Here’s what some of them said:

Jess gets a rundown from Claude Duet each morning. One day, without being asked, it flagged a property showing that was on her calendar for the wrong day. “[This is] exactly the kind of thing I want caught without having to ask,” she said.

Jess Provencher, broker and owner, Pro Homes

Amin owns Shahs of Kabob in South Florida with about 110 employees. He’s used Claude Duet for accounting, customer support, and marketing, and has worked through his invoices store by store. “It brings it all together,” he said. “I don’t need to open up 100 tabs.”

Amin Ebrahimi, owner, Shahs of Kabob

Mya had a call coming up with a potential client. Claude Duet saw it on her calendar and prepared a brief. It also noticed the call fell right before her flight and offered to move it. “I didn’t realize that it was right before my flight,” she said. “I love that proactivity.”

Mya Dalton, a brand strategist

How Claude Duet works

Your context from Claude is the foundation. Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work. What changes is how you work together: Claude Duet comes to you first, and you can message it through typing or voice in one ongoing thread, so a quick reply and a weeklong project both start in the same place.

Work continues when you step away. Claude Duet has a virtual machine with its own browser, so it doesn’t require your laptop or phone to be on. Describe a task in a short message, and it works out which apps to use and what steps to take in the background. You’ll receive a notification when the task is complete or needs your review.

Receive a message when something needs you. Claude Duet checks your connected accounts every few hours, because checking nonstop would use up your plan’s limits much faster. We’re continuing to test its judgment about when to message you, and we’ll keep tuning it based on what testers tell us. You can also tell it what you want to hear about and how often.

Important decisions stay with you. Claude Duet reads, drafts, and prepares work on its own. But before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document, or deletes anything, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your approval. A few things are off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities or moving money between accounts. You’re also able to disconnect any app Claude Duet has access to.

Connect with the tools your business runs on. Claude Duet can use the over 6,000 connectors and plugins in the Claude Marketplace (opens in new tab) to:

  • Find the Gmail and Slack messages you’ve missed and help you reply.
  • Check Intuit QuickBooks or Stripe for unpaid invoices and draft reminders.
  • Prepare and run payroll in Gusto, with hours, bonuses, and reimbursements filled in.
  • Draft a job posting and, once you edit and approve, post it to LinkedIn.
  • Help prepare agreements and send them for review and signature through Docusign.
  • Draft follow-up emails using the contact and deal history in HubSpot.
  • Turn your product launch into a social campaign in Canva.
  • Set up, design, and manage your Shopify store. Coming soon, a richer visual editor will let you design your storefront and preview it before anything goes live.

You can also use Claude Duet to purchase things for your business using Link, Stripe’s digital wallet. Claude Duet confirms the item with you, and Link asks you to approve the spend. It then pays with a virtual card, so your real card number isn’t shared. It can also use Shop Pay from Shopify to check out at online stores. Coming soon, with your permission, it will be able to sign in to sites with logins you’ve saved in 1Password.

Join the research preview

This is an early version of Claude Duet, and it still might misread a thread or miscalibrate what’s urgent. We built its core functionality around work, so personal errands, such as booking tickets, aren’t quite as strong, and it can’t yet show you its browser. For now, Claude Duet lives in its own app, separate from the main Claude app. What we learn from early users will shape how the two work together.

During the research preview, Claude Duet shares your plan’s usage limits with the rest of Claude, and it uses them differently than a typical conversation does. Its background checks count toward those limits, and larger tasks, like building a financial model or a deck, require more model turns and background work.

We’re starting today with Pro and Max users in the US. Join the waitlist (opens in new tab) and we’ll email as soon as Claude Duet’s ready for you.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Claude Security now scans continuously and tracks fixes
item.content:encoded:
Since Claude Security entered public beta in April, thousands of organizations have used it to find over a million vulnerabilities.

Instead of waiting for someone to start a scan, Claude Security now keeps up with your repositories as your code changes, keeps track of which findings get fixed, and uses what your team tells it about your environment to decide what matters. Claude Security is powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos, with no Cyber Verification Program access required.

The latest version of Claude Security is available today in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers. Organizations receive $25,000 in free usage credits each month, for two months. The offer applies to usage through December 31, 2026. You can view full terms in the Help Center.

Continuous monitoring keeps up with your code

A scan captures one moment, and code changes every day. Teams told us they wanted coverage that stays current without anyone having to schedule it.

Create a project, connect your repositories through the Claude GitHub app (including GitHub Enterprise Server) or with an access token from GitLab and other Git providers, and choose the branch and scope for each. Claude runs a deep baseline scan, then scans changes regularly based upon their risk and complexity, so your list of findings stays close to the current state of your code.

A project can hold multiple repositories, so Claude can catch issues that live between services, like a backend that trusts input a client was supposed to validate.

Findings are marked fixed when the fix ships

Most fixes happen outside the tool that found the issue. Claude Security checks open findings against the code that changed and marks them fixed when the fix lands, whether your team fixed it in Claude Code or in a separate process. If Claude Security finds the issue again later, the finding reopens automatically.

Your team’s knowledge shapes the scan

Every environment has controls a scanner can’t see from the code alone. Teams wanted a way to tell Claude Security about those controls, and to look across services that depend on each other. Now, each project has a knowledge base where you can describe how your code is deployed, which security policies apply, and anything a new security engineer on your team would need to know.

Claude Security also generates a threat model from your code that your team can review and edit. Subsequent scans use those threat models to decide what’s worth flagging. Added context also helps Claude Security skip risks your environment already handles.

Severity and exploit paths for every finding

Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project’s threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what’s actually reachable first. Findings can include a diagram of the attack path.

Findings reach your tools, with controls for larger rollouts

The new API lets you integrate Claude Security into your existing workflows. You can list and read projects and findings, resolve or reopen findings, and create and manage projects and their repositories. Users can create a personal access token in Claude Security settings, and it can only see and change what the user can. Webhooks can also notify your systems when a new finding lands.

Claude Security is also available as an MCP connector in Claude.ai and Claude Code. An engineer can pull up a finding, ask Claude about it, start the fix, and mark it resolved in the same session.

New role-based access controls let admins decide who can view projects, triage findings, and create projects. Organizations can open Claude Security to more teams that own the code without giving everyone access to create projects.

Getting started

The latest version of Claude Security is available in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers starting today. Admins can enable it in the admin console and set who on their team can access it.

Use the Getting Started Guide to set up your first project, and visit the Help Center for more details.

Organizations receive $25,000 in free usage credits each month, for two months. The offer applies to usage through December 31, 2026. You can view full terms in the Help Center.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Ben…
item.description: Full title: Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
item.content:encoded:
Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control.

“I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.”

Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover.

More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960.

“When Chris found evidence that the universe was expanding at a rate no one expected, he and his team followed the data even when it went against the prevailing wisdom of the field. As AI starts to transform how science itself is done, Chris’s intellectual honesty, rigor, and commitment to the truth are the values we want shaping the future of this technology, and I’m grateful he’s bringing his deep expertise to the Trust,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic.

Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation, which means we’re structured to balance commercial growth with our public benefit purpose. The Trust exists to help us hold that balance over the long term. It has the authority to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, and Trustees advise the board and our leadership on critical decisions, particularly those involving risks and societal impacts of AI.

This week we published our first Public Benefit Report, a public account of how we’re working toward our charter and where we’re falling short. The Trustees helped define the five charter pillars it measures us against, and the report closes with their assessment of our progress to date. Subject to stockholder approval, we’ve also committed to setting aside a portion of Anthropic’s shares to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows.

“Helping the world build powerful AI safely and making sure it meaningfully improves people’s lives both depend on a deep understanding of science and on leading with integrity,” added Neil Buddy Shah, Chair of the Long-Term Benefit Trust. “Not only has Chris worked on some of the hardest problems in science, but he has consistently been a high-integrity leader of large, complex, collaborative scientific endeavors across academia, government, and the national laboratories. That will be of great value to the Trust as we support Anthropic in developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”

Stubbs, the Trust’s first physicist, joins Shah, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and former Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke. Trustees are independent of the company’s management and investors.

item.title: [Mistral AI] Mistral Advances AI for Engineering with NVIDIA
item.content:encoded:
Company

Mistral Advances AI for Engineering with NVIDIA

October 21, 2026

By Mistral

5 min read

Copy url to clipboardCopied

Thinking

Summary

Mistral and NVIDIA are collaborating to revolutionize engineering workflows by integrating Mistral’s AI models with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and physics modeling tools, enabling faster simulations and closed-loop AI-driven design. The partnership will introduce public benchmarks and open datasets to standardize evaluations for physics and agentic AI in computer-aided engineering, while leveraging NVIDIA’s Omniverse for 3D simulation and asset creation. Building on their existing work, including the development of Mistral Large 4, the initiative aims to push the boundaries of AI-powered engineering across industries like aerospace, automotive, and semiconductors.

Mistral is collaborating with NVIDIA to develop a new generation of AI-native engineering workflows powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing. Combining Mistral Large 4, with Mistral’s data generation, and physics modeling pipelines, accelerated by NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries and NVIDIA Warp, the initiative aims to accelerate engineering simulation and enable closed-loop workflows that connect simulation, AI model development and engineering design. Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to integrate Mistral's models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for GPU-accelerated 3D scene generation and SimReady asset creation.

A central focus of the collaboration is the development of public benchmarks and open datasets for evaluating physics models. These benchmarks will give researchers, developers and industrial teams a shared foundation to compare model accuracy and performance and build and validate automated CAD-to-simulation workflows.

"For too long, the pace of engineering has been set by the pace of simulation. With Mistral's open-weight models and physics AI capabilities, combined with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing stack, we’re giving engineers faster simulation cycles, as well as open benchmarks rigorous enough to validate agents on real CAE and EDA work.” Neil Ashton, VP of Computational Engineering, Mistral

Beyond physics AI, Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to develop dedicated evaluations and benchmarks for agentic AI in computer-aided engineering (CAE) and electronic design automation (EDA) to accelerate the application of AI for engineering within aerospace, automotive and semiconductor use-cases. These benchmarks will assess agents’ ability to use engineering tools, complete multistep workflows and produce technically correct results, while measuring execution time and computational cost.

Through this work, Mistral and NVIDIA will help define standards for agentic and physics AI evaluations in engineering, establishing consistent, reproducible methods for assessing capabilities and tracking progress. Powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing, libraries and tools, Mistral will redefine AI for engineering, transforming how engineers design, simulate and build the next generation of products.

“The next wave of engineering breakthroughs will come from exploring ideas that were once too complex or time-consuming to test,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “By combining Mistral’s advanced open models and deep expertise in physics AI with NVIDIA accelerated computing and libraries, we’re helping engineers push the boundaries of design—with shared industry benchmarks to build confidence in what AI can do.”

Building on the ongoing NVIDIA and Mistral partnership

The industrial engineering collaboration builds on an ongoing partnership between NVIDIA and Mistral spanning open model development, domain-specific AI and the infrastructure needed to bring these capabilities into production.

The companies previously co-developed Mistral NeMo and are now working together through the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition to develop a frontier base model that will continue to advance the open weight frontier. This shared foundation will enable developers and enterprises worldwide to specialize AI for their industries, languages and regions, supported by contributions of data, evaluations and domain expertise from coalition members.

Mistral recently introduced the public preview of Mistral Large 4, known as Le Chonk, its largest and most capable frontier model to date. With approximately 1 trillion total parameters and 49 billion active parameters, the multimodal model was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral-operated data centers in Europe. It advances capabilities across coding, agentic workflows and multimodal understanding, with weights planned for release at the end of October.

Alongside model development, Mistral and NVIDIA are expanding the infrastructure that powers AI training, customization and inference. Mistral is bringing additional NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure online in support of Mistral’s compute roadmap targeting 1 GW of capacity by 2030.

This expansion strengthens Europe’s role in developing and delivering AI for the world. By connecting European infrastructure and research with open models, specialized engineering capabilities and customer applications, Mistral and NVIDIA are helping enterprises build AI around their own expertise and scale it to serve markets worldwide.

item.title: [Cohere] Introducing Rerank 5: precise, efficient enterprise document…
item.description: Full title: Introducing Rerank 5: precise, efficient enterprise document retrievalGive your AI the most relevant context for each request, now with passage-level precision.
item.content:encoded:
Oct 21, 2026

8 minute read

Introducing Rerank 5: precise, efficient enterprise document retrieval

Give your AI the most relevant context for each request, now with passage-level precision.

Key takeaways

  • State-of-the-art retrieval: Rerank 5 Pro leads on major public benchmarks, while Rerank 5 Fast delivers near-leading performance at lower cost.
  • Strong across enterprise domains: Rerank 5 establishes itself as a leader across finance, healthcare, scientific research, parsed documents and multilingual retrieval.
  • Context Focus: new to Rerank 5 - a single Rerank call returns the most relevant passages within each document, cutting LLM token costs with minimal loss in answer quality.
  • Calibrated relevance scores: consistent scores across queries and domains let teams set one threshold to decide what reaches the LLM.
  • Deploy anywhere: available through the Cohere API, Model Vault, Microsoft Foundry, Amazon SageMaker, privately in your own VPC or on-premises, and to all North users. Get started with just a few lines of code.

Introduction

Today, we're releasing Rerank 5, our most advanced enterprise retrieval models yet, available in Pro and Fast tiers.

Rerank 5 helps teams find the right information, send the most relevant context to their LLMs, and give customers more tailored search experiences. With Rerank 5 Pro, we’ve set a new standard in reranking quality, especially on reasoning-intensive search, visually rich documents, and key enterprise domains. Rerank 5 Fast brings that quality to latency- and cost-sensitive workloads. Both models introduce Context Focus, which pinpoints the most relevant spans of text within documents, going beyond document- or chunk-level retrieval to surface precisely the information that matters.

Every token your LLM reads is a token you pay for, and retrieval decides which tokens those are. As agents run more searches over longer documents, retrieval has become a key lever enterprises have over their AI cost, latency, and answer quality.

Rerank 5 joins Embed 5 and Parse 5 as part of our latest generation of search models. It is generally available today on the Cohere API and Model Vault, Microsoft Foundry, Amazon SageMaker, and to all North users. API pricing is $0.05 per 1M tokens for Pro and $0.02 for Fast.

Performance

Rerank 5 Pro leads public benchmarks such as ViDoRe V3, nanoMTEB, BRIGHT, and BEIR - outperforming every competing model tested. Of the 46 composite datasets evaluated, Rerank 5 Pro ranked first on 39 and placed at least second in 43. Models are evaluated using RCP-nDCG@10, a Cohere-developed methodology designed to address limitations in traditional nDCG caused by incomplete relevance judgments (qrel coverage).

The advantage is particularly pronounced on BRIGHT, a benchmark testing reasoning-intensive retrieval, where identifying relevant documents requires deeper understanding beyond keyword or semantic similarity. Rerank 5 Pro scores 82.2, outperforming Voyage AI Rerank 3 by 5.8 points and Rerank 4 Pro by 12.4 points, its largest generational gain across the four headline benchmarks. Pro also leads the strongest external competitor by 1.6 points on ViDoRe V3, 1.8 on BEIR, and 3.4 on nanoMTEB. These gains are increasingly important for agentic workflows, where complex, multi-step queries demand the ability to reason about relevance and return evidence that may not closely resemble the original query.

Rerank 5 Fast delivers substantial quality gains in the speed-optimized tier. In all four benchmarks, it outperforms Voyage AI Rerank 3 Lite and Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B, as well as the much larger Qwen3-Reranker-8B and previous-generation Rerank 4 Pro.

Headline benchmarks. Reranking quality (RCP-nDCG@10) on four public benchmarks: ViDoRe V3 (8 datasets), BEIR (13), BRIGHT (12) and nanoMTEB (13). Scores are averaged across each benchmark's datasets.

Domain-specific performance

Across specialized enterprise domains, Rerank 5 demonstrates consistent leadership. In finance and economics, Rerank 5 Pro leads competition on visual retrieval from financial documents (ViDoRe Finance), numerical reasoning over financial reports (FinQA), and complex economics questions (BRIGHT Economics). This is where its lead is largest, outperforming Voyage AI Rerank 3 by 9.6 points.

Similar results extend across healthcare, scientific research, and energy-focused retrieval, where benchmarks test the ability to surface relevant information from specialized scientific literature, biomedical research, and climate-related content. See the full list of results here.

Reranking quality (RCP-nDCG@10) on finance and economics datasets.

Reranking quality (RCP-nDCG@10) on healthcare and life sciences datasets.

Reranking quality (RCP-nDCG@10) on scientific research datasets.

Reranking quality (RCP-nDCG@10) on energy and sustainability datasets.

Multilingual

Rerank 5 Pro improves on Rerank 4 Pro in every language we evaluated, with gains of at least two points in Spanish, French, German, Arabic and Korean. It ranks first on 14 of the 19 non-English languages in our internal evaluation suite, including all six of the priority business languages shown below.

Against the competition, Pro leads Voyage AI Rerank 3 in every one of these languages. Its widest margins are in Japanese (+2.7), French (+2.3) and Arabic (+2.3). Rerank 5 Fast outperforms Voyage AI Rerank 3 Lite across all six, by as much as 4.5 points in Arabic. See the full results across all 19 languages here.

ModelSpanishFrenchGermanArabicJapaneseKorean
Cohere Rerank 5 Pro91.290.590.689.789.491.8
Cohere Rerank 5 Fast88.688.688.686.586.889.9
Voyage AI Rerank 389.488.289.487.486.789.9
Cohere Rerank 4 Pro88.688.188.687.589.389.8
Voyage AI Rerank 3 Lite86.084.786.382.083.886.6
Qwen3-Reranker-8B85.484.086.284.485.988.0
Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B76.974.278.074.678.680.8

Multilingual. Reranking quality (RCP-nDCG@10) by language on our internal evaluation suite across six selected languages. The entire suite consists of 20 world languages and 74 datasets.

Parsed PDFs

On retrieval tasks involving content extracted from PDFs, an important capability for enterprise document search, Pro achieves the highest average score of 89.9 in the evaluated suite. This puts it ahead of Voyage AI Rerank 3 (88.4) and Rerank 4 Pro (88.3). Fast follows closely at 88.5, marginally outperforming both models.

Parsed PDFs. Reranking quality (RCP-nDCG@10), averaged across 47 datasets of text parsed from PDFs. Documents were parsed using Gemini 1.5 Flash.

Latency + Throughput

Rerank 5 Fast is built for volume. Under sustained load, Fast reranks about 187 standard-length documents (1,000 tokens) per second on an NVIDIA A100 GPU - delivering 2.9x the throughput of Pro.

Fast also delivers nearly 3x faster response times than Pro, making it ideal for latency-sensitive applications and agents that run many searches per task. Pro remains best suited for applications where ranking quality takes priority over speed.

Document throughput and median request latency for Rerank 5 Fast and Pro on a single NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU via the Cohere API, with 96 documents per request at a concurrency of 8, over 1,000 requests per document length. Document lengths are approximate.

Context Focus: unlock smarter token economics

As documents grow longer and AI agents retrieve information from more sources, the amount of context passed to LLMs continues to increase. Yet, often only a few sentences within each document are relevant to the query. Processing unnecessary content drives up token costs, increases latency and can introduce noise that reduces answer quality.

Context Focus, a new optional capability launching with Rerank 5, goes beyond identifying relevant documents to pinpoint the specific passages that matter most. Configurable thresholds let developers balance context reduction with evidence retention, while a single Rerank API call returns both document-level relevance scores and scored text spans. Applications can then pass only the most relevant evidence to an LLM, without adding steps to the retrieval pipeline.

Decouple context from answer quality

We measured how answer quality varied as Context Focus removes more of the retrieved text across 30 question-answering datasets. Removing half the context sacrificed only 2 percentage points of answer quality (96% retained), and removing three-quarters lost just 7 (87% answer quality retained). Context Focus therefore works like a dial: moderate settings are close to free, and teams that need bigger savings can trade some quality for up to 10x less context.

Answer quality as retrieved text is removed. Each model picks its top 5 documents from the same pool of 50 candidates, then removes text at a range of thresholds (one dot per threshold): Rerank 5 with Context Focus, the baselines with their own compressors. Qwen3.5-9B answers from what remains, and Qwen3.5-35B grades the answer. x-axis: share of retrieved tokens removed; y-axis: average judge score; both averaged over 30 single-turn QA datasets from ViDoRe, UNICORN, BRIGHT-Pro and agentic QA (up to 500 queries each).

We then gave a search agent a retrieval stack built up one step at a time, starting from keyword search (BM25). Adding Rerank 5 Pro raised accuracy from 46% to 49%. Turning on Context Focus then cut tokens and raised accuracy further. At the default threshold (0.1), tokens per task fell by 19% and accuracy rose to 57%. At 0.4, tokens fell by 34%, lower on every dataset, and accuracy reached 58%. Altogether, the full stack with Context Focus at 0.4 used 35% fewer tokens than BM25 alone, at higher accuracy (58% vs 46%). On the six deep-search benchmarks, it used 41% fewer tokens, and accuracy rose from 39% to 52%, with every benchmark improving on both measures. ​

Search-agent results, averaged over 17 datasets including six deep-search benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, MedBrowseComp, WebWalkerQA, SealQA, HERB and DRBench), with 50 questions per dataset. We follow the evaluation setup of BrowseComp-Plus. The agent is glm-5-3-flash, with search as its only tool and 5 results per search. Retrieval starts with BM25, and Rerank 5 Pro reorders the top 100 with Context Focus switched off. Context Focus is then shown at the default threshold (0.1) and at 0.4, each applied on top of Rerank 5 Pro. Accuracy is the percentage of questions answered correctly. Tokens are the average total per task, summed over every LLM call in the run: input, output and reasoning tokens. The prompt for each call includes the full conversation so far, and cached tokens are included.

Calibrated relevance scores

With Rerank 5, a score of 0.7 now means a 70% chance the document is useful.

Every reranker returns a relevance score, but until now those scores were mostly good for sorting. What counted as a "good" score changed from model to model. Teams had to tune a cutoff for each model and re-tune it on every upgrade.

Rerank 5's scores are calibrated out of the box: the relevance_score returned with each result reads as the probability that the document is useful, with no change to your request or the response format. Pro and Fast also agree on where the line is: "more likely useful than not" is a score of 0.50 for Pro and 0.45 for Fast.

Rerank 5's raw scores read as probabilities. Documents are sorted into ten bins by score, and each line connects a model's bins: the bin's average score (across) against the share of its documents judged useful (up). On the dotted diagonal, a score is exactly a probability; lines below it overstate relevance, and lines above it understate it. Scores are used as returned, with no recalibration. Left: blind human graders, 2,262 documents; useful = a mean grade of "Useful" or higher on a five-point scale (Off-topic, Topical, Useful, Answers, Complete). Right: NIST TREC-DL assessors, 20,646 documents; useful = grade 2 ("highly relevant") or higher on NIST's 0–3 scale.

We checked this against two independent sets of human judgments that no model was trained on: a blind panel of graders and NIST's TREC Deep Learning assessors. On both, Rerank 5 follows the diagonal far more closely than any other reranker. Competing models sit below it, overstating relevance: documents Voyage AI Rerank 3 scored around 0.55 were only 24% useful to the human graders.

The table below sums this up as expected calibration error (ECE): the average gap between a model's scores and the real share of useful documents, where 0 is perfect. Rerank 5's is about 0.06 on both sets of judgments; every other reranker we tested has nearly four times that error or more. Calibration doesn't cost ranking quality, either: Rerank 5 Pro and Fast rank first and second in average precision on both.

Expected Calibration ErrorJudge
ModelHumansNIST
Cohere Rerank 5 Pro0.0580.057
Cohere Rerank 5 Fast0.0580.058
Cohere Rerank 4 Pro0.3840.309
Voyage AI Rerank 30.2340.307
Voyage AI Rerank 3 Lite0.2260.325

Expected Calibration Error sums up each line in the charts above: the average distance of its dots from the diagonal, weighted by how many documents each dot represents. In other words, how far a model's scores are from the real share of useful documents. Lower is better; 0 is perfect.

Why it matters

  • Filter by relevance, not by count. Instead of passing a fixed top-k to your LLM, keep every document above the threshold. Narrow queries pass a few documents, broad ones pass more, and the model sees less noise.
  • Know when nothing relevant came back. If no document clears the threshold, an agent can rewrite the query or say it doesn't know, instead of answering from whatever ranked first.
  • One threshold across domains and model sizes. Across BRIGHT, NanoBEIR, and ViDoRe V3, the default stays between 0.47 and 0.53 for Pro, and Pro and Fast are within 0.05 of each other.

Start reranking

Rerank 5 Pro and Rerank 5 Fast are generally available through the Cohere API, Model Vault, Microsoft Foundry (Fast, Pro), and Amazon SageMaker (Fast, Pro), and to all North users. For private deployments in your own VPC or on-premises, speak to a member of our team.

Rerank 5 sits on top of the retrieval stack you already have. It works with any keyword, vector or hybrid search, with no re-indexing, and is available through frameworks including LangChain, Haystack, Elasticsearch and Weaviate. Read the documentation.

Start by creating an API key, then use the code snippets below to quickly make your first query.

#rerank with Context Focus
import os
import requests

query = "How much did card provisions rise in Q3?"

documents = [
    "Market update. Commercial real estate prices fell 6% this year as office "
    "vacancies climbed. Analysts expect refinancing pressure on landlords to "
    "persist into next year.",
    "Q3 credit quality. Net charge-offs held steady at 0.42% of average loans. "
    "Commercial real estate loans stood at $14.3 billion, or 9% of total loans. "
    "Office properties accounted for $2.1 billion of that balance. Card "
    "provisions rose $85 million on higher delinquencies.",
    "Q3 mortgage lending. Residential mortgage originations rose 11% as rates "
    "eased. The average loan-to-value ratio on new lending was 68%.",
]

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.cohere.com/v2/rerank",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['CO_API_KEY']}"},
    json={
        "model": "rerank-v5.0-pro",
        "query": query,
        "documents": documents,
        "top_n": 2,
        "relevant_spans": {"mode": "enabled", "threshold": 0.4, "max_spans": 10}, #toggle Context Focus
    },
)
response.raise_for_status()

for result in response.json()["results"]:
    document = documents[result["index"]]
    print(f"{result['relevance_score']:.2f}  {document[:60]}...")
    for span in result.get("relevant_spans") or []:
        print(f"      {span['score']:.2f}  {document[span['start']:span['end']]}")

Last thoughts

Try Rerank 5 inside a full retrieval stack. Compass Cloud, our managed search and retrieval platform, brings parsing, embedding, hybrid search and Rerank together in one service, with Cohere managing the infrastructure. It's now in private beta for teams building retrieval-heavy and agentic applications. Request access.

Follow us on X and LinkedIn for the latest from Cohere, and email search@cohere.com with any other questions.

item.description: Full title: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required

Enterprise + Article

Published October 21, 2026

6

Joshua Przybylko

jprzybylko

nvidia

Jure Leskovec

profjure

nvidia

Matthias Fey

rusty1s

nvidia

Federico Lopez

flopeznv

nvidia

Valter Hudovernik

valterh-nv

nvidia

Akihiro Nitta

akihironitta-nv

nvidia

Ramona Bendias

RBendiasN

nvidia

Ardrian Wong

aw777

nvidia

TL;DR

NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers up to 10,000 historical examples as context and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models library or as an NVIDIA NIM.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596
  • Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview

The Shift to Structured Data Foundation Models

Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications.

The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons:

Better accuracy today: As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational.

Simplicity and agility: One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization.

Agents that can predict: LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions.

Today, we are introducing Kumo Relational (paper, documentation), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required.

How Kumo Relational Works

Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation (e.g., "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort.

Kumo Relational is a Relational Foundation Model that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning, reading up to 10,000 context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target (e.g., "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units").

![Overview of the NVIDIA Kumo Relational system: (a) database integration, (b) a prompting interface that turns natural language into a predictive query, and (c) automatic context generation feeding the NVIDIA Kumo Relational model, which scales horizontally across tenants.]

Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference.

To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works:

![Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input with task, users, orders and items tables; (b) column and row attention within tables with injected context targets; (c) graph attention and cross-sample attention across tables.]

Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables.

Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL), a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage.

Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently, alternating column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates.

Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, interleaved with cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs.

How Kumo Relational Was Built

Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures.

The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. Members of the Kumo team helped develop PluRel and co-authored the original paper. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited, and the PluRel paper shows that pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases.

Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations. When maximum accuracy matters, Kumo Relational can also be fine-tuned on a specific dataset and task.

Performance

In this paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. On the RelArena-α leaderboard, which compares relational models and systems on RelBench V1, it also sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front out of the box:

![Scatter plot of the RelArena-α leaderboard: relative accuracy as Elo across tasks (y-axis) versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (x-axis, log scale). Kumo Relational sits on the Pareto front at about 17 seconds and Elo 1,842. The highest-scoring entry, rt-plurel, reaches Elo 1,878 at about 7,300 seconds, roughly 430 times slower. Every other foundation model, feature-engineering system, and supervised model scores lower and runs slower than Kumo Relational.]

Figure 3. RelArena-α leaderboard: Elo across tasks versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (log scale). Kumo Relational is about 430× faster than the highest-scoring entry at similar accuracy.

The paper also reports that on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark, Kumo Relational surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and recent tabular foundation models by about 25%, and fine-tuning extends its lead over AutoGluon to 16%. It also holds up under hard conditions: it performs well with as little as 0.2% of the training data as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely degrades when many noisy columns are added.

Limitations

Kumo Relational performs best on data with meaningful relationships and temporal dynamics, such as user behavior over time. On tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models may still edge out in-context predictions, which used at most 10,000 context examples in our benchmarks. Fine-tuning of the foundation model is designed for exactly this case. Predictive signals must also be reachable within a limited number of hops, so start with a focused query over a few relevant tables and expand the graph as needed.

Demo

Kumo Relational runs in-context learning natively over databases: in memory, through database and warehouse connectors, or through a custom graph engine that handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s. It is available in NVIDIA's newly released, GPU-native structured-data-models library, the same open-source library that powers our sister model, Kumo Tabular. The library downloads the weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, so you can load the model in a GPU-backed notebook and predict directly from it. The code below passes context examples, prediction entities, and their related tables to the model:

# pip install structured-data-models
import sdm

model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device="cuda")
pred = model(
    # In-context training table (fkeys/timestamps/targets):
    x_context=...,
    y_context=...,
    # Prediction examples (fkeys/timestamps):
    x_query=...,
    # Multi-table information for context/prediction entities:
    related_context_tables=...,
    related_query_tables=...,
)

See the library's relational examples for complete RelBench and SAP SALT pipelines, including how to sample each entity's related tables.

To run the model as a separate service instead, deploy it as an NVIDIA NIM and point the open-source structured-data-models-client at it from your notebook. You write the prediction in PQL, and the client gathers the context examples and related tables, then sends the request:

# pip install 'structured-data-models-client[relational]'
import sdm_client

client = sdm_client.SDMClient(url="http://localhost:8001")  # NIM URL
query = sdm_client.PredictiveQuery(
    # Prediction task in Predictive Query Language (PQL):
    "PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) FOR EACH users.user_id",
    # Multi-table data as pandas DataFrames (keys/links inferred):
    {"users": ..., "orders": ...},
)
pred = client.predict(
    # Context examples and related tables for the entities to predict:
    query.materialize(indices=[1, 2, 3]),
    model=sdm_client.KumoRelational(),
)

See the client's example notebooks for end-to-end runs against a local NIM and on Databricks.

Start Building with NVIDIA Kumo Relational

NVIDIA Kumo Relational is available today. Read the research paper, explore the quickstart notebook, or start making predictions on your own data. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license and the model weights under the OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1. NVIDIA believes Trustworthy AI is a shared responsibility, and we have established policies and practices to enable development for a wide array of AI applications. When downloaded or used in accordance with our terms of service, developers should work with their supporting model team to ensure this model meets requirements for the relevant industry and use case and addresses unforeseen product misuse. Please report model quality, risk, security vulnerabilities, or NVIDIA AI concerns here.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596
  • Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview
  • Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/structured-data-models/
  • Client code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client
  • Client PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/structured-data-models-client/
  • Weights: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Relational
  • Quickstart notebook: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client/blob/main/examples/local/relational.ipynb
  • Related Research: Predictive Query Language (PQL), PluRel, Kumo Tabular

Acknowledgements

We thank the entire Kumo team for their invaluable support. Special thanks go to Josh Przybylko, Adi Wadaskar, Hema Raghavan, Manush Murali, Raja Rao DV, Keti Jovanovska, Zack Drach, Vanja Josifovski, Myungwhan Kim, Blaž Stojanovič, Siyang Xie, Alan Krumholz, Effy Fang, Abdullah Al-chihabi, Disha Dubey, Devan Johnson, Joseph Oliveira, Angela Liu, Miha Pelko, Vedaant Jain, Sally Liu, Aleksandar S. Sokolovski, Alex Porter, and Ramona Bendias.

item.title: [Hugging Face] How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Co…
item.description: Full title: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

Team Article

Published October 21, 2026

15

Bernardo França de Aguiar

bernardoaguiar

Dharma-AI

Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso

GabrielPimenta99

Dharma-AI

Bruno Duarte

brunoduarte01

Dharma-AI

Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves

falves9101

Dharma-AI

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

A Vocabulary Built for Everyone

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Why Existing Solutions Fell Short

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

How We Solved It

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

What Changed in the Grader

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

Beyond the Grader

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

Sources

  • Dharma-AI. "VocabX: Cost-Weighted Vocabulary Adaptation for Domain-Specific Language Models." In preparation (2026).
  • Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Fast vocabulary transfer for language model compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2022).
  • Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Multi-word tokenization for sequence compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2023).
  • Smith, Jimmy T.H., et al. "In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs." arXiv:2607.15232 (2026).

Further Reading

  • Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order
  • GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft
  • Why Specialization Is Inevitable
  • Specialization Beats Scale: A Strategic Variable Most AI Procurement Decisions Overlook
  • Text Degeneration: A Production Failure Mode That Most Benchmarks Do Not Track
